## Abstract

We defend a position we summarize in five words: Reality exists; knowledge is authored. Against idealism, we hold that there is a world independent of any observer, which punishes us when we misjudge it. Against naive realism, we hold that everything we say about that world beyond what reaches the senses is written by us: patterns noticed, orders projected and consensus built. We develop three concepts to keep the two halves of the position apart. An SOB, a scientific observational boundary, is a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. A placeholder is an invented entity parked in a gap to make the books balance; we give four tests that separate the placeholders that get found from those that never do. The Existential Boundary is the line between observed reality and what needs to be experienced to be understood; it runs through the observer, not the instruments, and science has no error bar for it.

We argue from these that all scientific knowledge of the observed world is correct at best and never certain, that certainty belongs only to what we invent, and that the familiar crises of modern physics, from dark matter to the black hole interior, are what happens when placeholders are painted on SOBs and called discoveries.

## 1. Introduction

> As long as we’re human, something has been overlooked.

Science presents its findings as a view from nowhere, as if the universe had been photographed by no one. Every observation is in fact made by someone, from somewhere, with equipment built by evolution for keeping a moving animal alive, not for finding the truth. This paper asks what follows if that is taken seriously, and answers in five words: **Reality exists. Knowledge is authored.**

The first half rules out idealism. The world was here before us and will outlast us; fire burns whatever we agree about it. The second half rules out the assumption, common in popular science and often in science itself, that our best descriptions are the world. Everything we know beyond the raw givens of sense was written by us, tested by us and agreed on by us. Some of it is superbly reliable. All of it has authors.

Holding both halves at once requires a vocabulary that keeps them apart, and most of this paper builds one. Section 2 identifies what reaches us directly. Section 3 shows how the rest is authored. Section 4 catalogues the impediments between any observer and Reality. Sections 5 to 7 introduce the paper’s three concepts, the SOB, the placeholder and the Existential Boundary. Section 8 draws the consequence for the standing of scientific knowledge. Sections 9 and 10 call witnesses and meet objections.

## 2. What we sense, and what we assume

> We know what we sense. We assume what it is.

Strip away every theory, equation and name, and ask what reaches us before any explanation at all. We count seven givens: **matter, motion, light, heat, sound, duration and life.** We feel the resistance of matter when we push against it. We see motion and light, and feel heat on the skin. We hear sound. We feel things last. And we know life, our own, from the inside.

Three things commonly treated as basic are not on the list. _Space_ is not sensed; we sense things in it and through it, but never space itself. _Time_ is not sensed; we feel duration, but the thing on the clock is a count of regular motions. _Energy_ is not sensed; it is a number we calculate that stays constant through every change, a superb piece of bookkeeping that no one has ever seen. Each is an assumption about what the givens are, not a given.

The first act of the mind after sensing is a question: what is that? The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long. The instinct to question is the _sine qua non_ of survival; a creature that never asks what moved in the grass does not live long enough to learn the answer. Every level of knowledge above the senses is built on that first pairing of question and answer, and the answer is always ours.

## 3. How knowledge is authored

> All observation is self-centered. Reality does not possess a self.

We get from the seven givens to the body of human knowledge in three steps: **we detect motion, we observe pattern, we project order.** The motion is Reality; it reaches us whether we like it or not. The pattern is the first thing we write: motion someone has noticed repeating. The order is the second thing we write: the laws, the causes, the _because_.

The planets show the steps at work. Kepler described their pattern. Newton projected an order onto it and called it gravity. Einstein projected a different order onto the same pattern and called it curved spacetime. The planets did not change, and neither did the pattern. Only the order changed, because the order was always ours. This is a claim about authorship, not accuracy. Some of our orders are astonishingly accurate. They still have authors.

No single author wrote our knowledge. One person notices the moon returning; a village agrees to count the returns and call them months; nations sign a treaty fixing the length of a meter. Every name, scale and law in use today was drafted by someone, argued over by many and kept because it worked well enough for enough people. Human observation is entirely reduced to consensus scales and frameworks.

Science is the finest example, not an exception. Karl Popper, one of its great defenders, wrote that “the objectivity of scientific statements lies in the fact that they can be inter-subjectively tested.” Objectivity, on that account, is not a view from nowhere. It is a view from everywhere at once: the widest consensus we know how to build, under the strictest rules we can devise. That is the highest compliment we can pay science, and it is also a statement of what science is.

Why write any of it? Because every pursuit serves survival. Counting began with livestock, geometry with measuring fields and astronomy with knowing when the river would flood. Knowledge is the first line of defense, the sword and shield of survival.

## 4. The impediments

> Experience is real. Knowledge is optional.

Before asking what Reality is, we have to take stock of what stands between any observer and it. Life predates brains: for about three billion years, most of life’s history, there was no brain anywhere on Earth. The observer is a latecomer, and it arrived with equipment built for one job, keeping a moving creature alive. We count twelve impediments in four groups.

| Group | Impediment | What it does
| The body | 1. Senses built to survive | We see a thin sliver of the light that exists and hear a narrow band of sound; the brain errs toward false alarms, so we see threats and patterns that are not there
| The body | 2. Senses that filter out peril | We feel none of the Earth’s spin, its orbit or the Sun’s journey around the galaxy; the brain stops reporting whatever is constant
| The body | 3. A mind too small for the scale | Built for dozens and hundreds; a billion seconds is nearly 32 years, and the cosmos deals in numbers far beyond
| The self | 4. The reference point | Every observer needs a “here,” and wherever you stand there is a horizon; horizons belong to observation, not to Reality
| The self | 5. The eye that can’t see itself | The observer can never observe the observer; “You cannot see the seer of seeing,” as an Upanishad put it about 2,700 years ago
| The self | 6. Projection | We hang our wishes for order, repetition and permanence on whatever we observe: perfect circles, incorruptible heavens, a smooth universe
| The tools | 7. Language | It freezes happenings into nouns and sends us hunting for the noun; “time,” “nothing” and “the self” become things to be found
| The tools | 8. Logic and mathematics | Made for the marketplace and superb on repetition; they break down at one-offs such as the first instant, where they divide by zero
| The tools | 9. Instruments | They extend the senses but are designed by survival-tuned brains, aimed where those brains expect to find something, and read through the same projections
| The frame | 10. Isolation | Only 24 people have traveled far enough to see the whole Earth; every other observation of the cosmos was made from home
| The frame | 11. Brevity | Our lives and instruments are brief; every observation is a still frame of something that never stops moving
| The frame | 12. The framework | All knowledge is framework-dependent; agreement does not rescue us, since other observers share our framework

Every observer carries all twelve. We use a framework we invented to define a Reality that created us.

## 5. SOBs: the walls

> An SOB is a wall. A placeholder is a ghost painted on the wall.

**Definition.** An SOB, a scientific observational boundary, is a place where our methods of observation run out, though something surely lies beyond.

**Examples.** Four are central. The first instant of the universe, where the equations stop. The inside of the objects called black holes, which no signal can leave. The edge of the observable universe, beyond which no light has had time to reach us. And the self, where every signal in the brain can be traced up to the point of experience, and the trail stops. To these we add the far future, which no one will witness, and the wall inside logic itself, which Kurt Gödel found in 1931 when he proved that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains truths it cannot prove.

**Three properties.** First, an SOB is a feature of observation, not of Reality. It marks the reach of whoever is looking, not the end of the world; a sailor’s horizon is real, but it is not a cliff. Second, an SOB claims nothing except a limit. It does not say what lies beyond, only that we cannot see it. Third, the reason for every SOB is in us: where we stand, how long we live, what we see with.

**The right response.** At an SOB, the honest answer is “maybe.” We can dream past it; we cannot see past it. Dreams carried back across the wall are legitimate, and some have come true: John Michell imagined dark stars in 1783, Democritus imagined atoms around 400 BC, and Einstein imagined riding a beam of light at sixteen. They must be labeled as dreams, _pending_, until evidence and consensus build around them.

The concept is our contribution. Philosophy has long discussed the limits of knowledge in general; what the SOB adds is a name for the specific places in science where observation stops, and a rule for what may and may not be said there.

## 6. Placeholders: the ghosts

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

**Definition.** A placeholder is an invented entity parked in a gap to make the books balance. An SOB says “we cannot see past here.” A placeholder says “there is something here we cannot see.”

Placeholders are not automatically bad. In the 1840s Uranus wobbled off its predicted course, Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams predicted an unseen planet, and in 1846 Neptune was found almost exactly where Le Verrier said. In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli proposed the neutrino to balance the energy books, and it was caught in 1956. But in 1859 Le Verrier blamed Mercury’s wobble on another hidden planet, Vulcan. It was hunted for some sixty years and was never there. The wobble was explained in 1915, when Einstein rethought gravity. The luminiferous ether was another placeholder, required by the equations, never detected, and gone within twenty years of the Michelson-Morley experiment.

**Four tests.** We propose four questions that separate the placeholders that get found from those that never do.

1. **Does it claim a thing?** An SOB claims only a limit. A placeholder claims that something exists, and so it carries a burden of proof.
2. **Does it make a definite prediction?** Neptune had to be in one patch of sky; the neutrino had to show up in one kind of detector. A good placeholder sticks its neck out.
3. **Is there a clock?** Neptune was found on the first night someone looked with the prediction in hand; the neutrino took twenty-six years. A placeholder that has gone half a century without being found deserves a hard look, not a bigger budget.
4. **Is it redefined after every miss?** This is the surest sign of a bad ghost. When a search comes up empty and the answer is that the ghost must be lighter, heavier, shyer or stranger than thought, it has stopped being a prediction and become a habit.

**Ghosts on the walls.** The deepest mischief begins when the two concepts are confused: when an SOB is treated as a gap waiting to be filled and a placeholder is painted on it. The ghost then borrows the permanence of the wall. Today’s largest placeholders sit exactly on SOBs. Inflation is painted on the first instant. Dark matter is painted on the outskirts of galaxies, where the tested rules of gravity give out. Dark energy is painted on the far edge of the observable universe. Emergence is painted on the self. Each fills a place where we cannot see with something we cannot see, and each has been searched for, redefined and searched for again.

Respect the wall. Question the ghost.

## 7. The Existential Boundary

> You can’t know before you feel.

**Definition.** The Existential Boundary is the line between observed reality and what needs to be experienced to be understood. An SOB is where our instruments stop. The Existential Boundary is where the observer stops. On the near side we know the measurement; on the far side we know what it means.

**The swim.** One of the authors, sailing on a warm day, once dived off the transom for a swim without telling the helm, surfaced and watched the boat sail away: a speck in an endless sea under a more endless sky. He had known all his life that the sea was big. In that moment he knew it for the first time, in the body and beyond argument, not as a fact but as an actuality. The boat came back. The knowledge stayed.

**Four rungs.** Between a number and its meaning there is a ladder with four rungs. The _measurement_: the sea is so many miles wide. The _description_: the sea is vast. The _experience_: the vastness is around you. The _meaning_: you know what the vastness means for a living thing inside it. Instruments supply the first two rungs superbly. The third requires a body in the place. The fourth requires stakes, because vastness only means something to a body that can be lost in it.

**What science leaves out.** Science corrects its instruments with great care. It calibrates them, estimates their errors and publishes the margins. There is one distortion it never builds in: the fact that the observer has never experienced the thing described. No paper carries an error bar for that. Every description of the cosmos, including descriptions of a space in which isolation is total, has been made from the warmest, safest and most connected seat in the universe. Apollo 8’s crew went a quarter of a million miles to explore the Moon and, in Bill Anders’s words, “discovered the Earth.”

**The relation to experience.** The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long. For most of human history that was the whole system of learning: the ones who survived the experience kept the answer and passed it on. The Existential Boundary marks the answers no instrument can supply, because they can only be lived.

## 8. Correct, never certain

> We can be certain of what we invent, never of what we observe.

The consequence of the preceding sections is that every scientific statement about the observed world is, at best, correct, and never certain. We are not saying science is unreliable. We are saying what the most reliable knowledge can be. Seven reasons converge.

1. **Induction.** David Hume showed in 1739 that no number of observed cases proves the next case. A law that has held a billion times has not been shown to hold the billion-and-first.
2. **Underdetermination.** Pierre Duhem showed in 1906, and W. V. O. Quine generalized, that any body of evidence is consistent with more than one theory. The planets fit Newton’s order and Einstein’s.
3. **Theory-laden observation.** What an instrument records is read through the theory that designed it. Observation and interpretation cannot be fully separated.
4. **The record of reversals.** Larry Laudan showed in 1981 that many of history’s most successful theories, the ether and the caloric among them, were later abandoned. Success has never guaranteed survival.
5. **Probability needs repetition.** Statistical confidence requires repeated trials. The universe happened once. Its origin cannot be repeated, and claims about it carry no confidence in the sense the word has elsewhere in science.
6. **Laws are situational.** Every law has been tested in some range of scale, speed and density. Projected beyond that range it becomes a prediction, and prediction does not equal truth. It is local and non-transferable.
7. **The observer is human.** All twelve impediments of section 4 travel with every observation.

**Where certainty lives.** There is one kind of knowledge we can be sure of: the things we invented. The rules of chess, the definition of a meter and the theorems of mathematics, given their axioms, are certain because we made them. The trouble begins when certainty is borrowed from an invention and lent to an observation, so that a solution exact on paper is taken for a description exact in nature. That loan underlies the black hole interior and the singularity at the first instant.

If this is right, it should change three expectations: our expectation of science, science’s expectation of itself and our common expectation of reality.

## 9. Supporting witnesses

> Intelligence should always be respected, no matter what form it comes in.

The position is our own. Parts of it have distinguished witnesses.

**Kant.** In 1783 Immanuel Kant wrote that the understanding “does not derive its laws from nature, but prescribes them to nature.” Behind every drawing of the world lies what he called the thing in itself, which we never see directly. Our SOBs are local, scientific instances of his general wall.

**Fleck and Kuhn.** In 1935 the Polish physician Ludwik Fleck described the thought collective, a group whose shared way of thinking makes certain questions invisible to its members. In 1962 Thomas Kuhn described normal science, in which anomalies are shelved until they pile too high. Both describe consensus as the medium in which knowledge is authored.

**Popper and Lakatos.** Popper made falsifiability the mark of science and defined objectivity as intersubjective testability. Imre Lakatos distinguished progressive research programs, which predict new facts, from degenerating ones, which add patches to explain away failures. Our four tests for placeholders are a field version of Lakatos’s distinction.

**Nagel and Jackson.** In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat, and argued that no amount of physical description captures the answer. In 1982 Frank Jackson imagined a scientist who knows every physical fact about color but has never seen red, and asked whether she learns something when she does. Both point at the Existential Boundary.

**Van Fraassen.** Bas van Fraassen’s constructive empiricism, set out in _The Scientific Image_ (1980), holds that science aims at theories that fit what is observable, and that accepting a theory need not mean believing its claims about the unobservable. Our “correct, never certain” is close kin.

## 10. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: the thesis refutes itself.** If all knowledge is authored, so is the claim that all knowledge is authored.

_Reply._ It is, and it says so. Authored does not mean arbitrary, and a claim can apply to itself without collapsing. The thesis is offered as correct, never certain, like everything else it describes. What would refute it is a piece of knowledge about the observed world that no one wrote: a law with no author, a pattern noticed by no one. We know of none.

**Objection 2: this is relativism.** If knowledge is consensus, any consensus is as good as any other.

_Reply._ Only if the world is silent, and it is not. Agree all you like that the fire is cold; it will still burn you. Agree that the leopard is friendly; it will still eat you. We draw where the world gives us handholds, and the best drawings are the ones that keep us alive. Consensus is disciplined by consequences. Reality has no voice, but it has consequences.

**Objection 3: the success of science would be a miracle if its theories were not true.** Hilary Putnam put this “no miracles” argument in 1975: the best explanation of science’s predictive success is that its theories are approximately true.

_Reply._ Success shows that an order fits the patterns where it has been tested. Ptolemy’s order predicted the planets for some 1,400 years and was wrong about what moves. Laudan’s record of successful theories later abandoned shows that success and truth come apart. The thesis grants the success fully. It denies only that success certifies the story told about it.

**Objection 4: SOBs get crossed.** In 1835 Auguste Comte declared that we could never know what the stars are made of. Within twenty-five years, spectroscopy had told us.

_Reply._ Comte confused a hard place with a wall. The distinction matters, and our definition draws it: an SOB is a place where our _methods_ run out, and some of those places are walls by the physics of how signals travel, not by the state of our instruments. Nothing will ever bring a signal from beyond the observable edge or from inside a horizon. Where a boundary turns out to be merely hard, so much the better, and the “maybe” we recommend at an SOB leaves room for that.

**Objection 5: experience is irrelevant to physics.** The Existential Boundary concerns how things feel, and physics concerns how they are.

_Reply._ Physics is done by people, and what they find worth asking, funding and believing depends on what the numbers mean to them. A cosmos described with no stakes becomes a cosmos described with myths: numbers too large to feel stand in for the things themselves, as the ancients put the sky on Atlas’s shoulders. The Existential Boundary does not change a measurement. It changes what the measurement is taken to show.

## 11. Conclusion

> Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

We have defended a position in five words. Reality exists: there is a world that was here before us, that does not care what we believe, and that answers every misjudgment with consequences. Knowledge is authored: everything we say about that world beyond seven raw givens is written by us, in three steps, from motion to pattern to order, and kept by consensus.

To hold both halves, we offered three concepts. The SOB names the walls where observation stops. The placeholder names the ghosts painted on them, and four tests tell the good ghosts from the bad. The Existential Boundary names the line no instrument can cross, between what is measured and what must be lived to be understood. From these we drew the conclusion that knowledge of the observed world is correct at best and never certain, and that certainty belongs only to what we invent.

What seems clearly not right is a science that presents authored orders as Reality itself, paints ghosts on its walls and calls them discoveries, and describes a cosmos it has never felt with a certainty it has never earned. The better question is not “what is Reality?” which no observer can answer from inside. It is who is asking, from where, with what, and what they have overlooked. When you run out of authors, you have found the one true question: why is there anything at all? And one author always remains, the one who asks.

## Abstract

We propose that space is a single material medium and that everything physics calls a particle or a field is a motion of that medium. The proposal is old in outline. It is the ether, taken one step further, so that matter is made of the medium and does not merely move through it. We argue that it does better work today than when it was abandoned. It explains why the two kinds of mass, inertial and gravitational, are equal to one part in a million billion: both are the same resistance of the medium. It explains gravity as a pressure gradient instead of a curved geometry. It offers a physical reading of the radial acceleration relation, under which the observed motion of stars in 153 galaxies follows from their visible matter alone, without dark matter. It dissolves wave-particle duality: the wave is the medium moving and the particle is the medium meeting resistance. And it gives a natural account of why matter and antimatter appear in pairs.

We meet the main objections: the null result of Michelson and Morley, the equality of the speeds of gravity and light, the mass still missing in galaxy clusters, and the pattern in the cosmic microwave background, which the standard model fits with dark matter. Some of these the proposal answers. One of them, the microwave background, it does not yet answer, and we say what an answer would require. We close with tests that could tell the medium apart from spacetime.

## 1. Introduction

> Space is the singular field of Reality.

Modern physics rests on four entities that have never been observed directly. Dark matter holds galaxies together. Dark energy speeds up the expansion. Inflation smoothed the early universe. And the wave function, which in the standard reading has no definite value until it is measured, governs every particle. Each was introduced to close a gap between theory and observation. Each has been hunted, redefined and hunted again.

This paper argues that the four share a root. Since the early twentieth century physics has treated space as something other than a substance. In special relativity it is a frame. In general relativity it is a geometry, welded to time into spacetime, that bends and tells matter how to move. In quantum field theory it is the arena in which dozens of separate fields overlap without interacting. In each case, space has properties but is not a thing.

Yet space behaves like a thing. It carries light at a fixed speed, set by its electric and magnetic properties. It holds a zero-point energy. It produces measurable forces between uncharged plates. We take that behavior at face value. Our thesis is that **space is a single material medium, the only substance there is, and that everything physics calls a particle or a field is a motion of that medium.** We call it the singular field.

Section 2 states the thesis. Sections 3 to 7 apply it to light and inertia, to gravity, to galaxies, to quantum behavior and to the origin of matter. Section 8 calls its supporting witnesses, section 9 meets the objections, and section 10 proposes tests. A companion paper, The Exhaust Stroke, applies the same premise to the expansion of the universe.

We write as natural philosophers. The thesis is a physical picture, not a finished mathematical theory, and where a claim is our best guess we label it _pending_.

## 2. The thesis

> We measure the reaction, never the reactors.

The thesis has five parts.

1. **One substance.** There is a single material medium filling everything, which ordinary language calls space. It is not a container for matter. It is what matter is made of.
2. **Fields are modes of the medium.** What quantum field theory treats as separate fields, the electromagnetic field, the electron field, the quark fields and the rest, are different kinds of motion in the one medium: stresses, twists, vibrations and currents. A pond can carry ripples, whirlpools and sound at once without being three ponds.
3. **Particles are its excitations.** A lasting particle, such as an electron or a proton, is a stable knot: a region where the medium is wound tight and ringing at a fixed frequency. The frequency is the particle’s identity. The electron rings about 120 billion billion times a second. Light is a disturbance crossing the medium at the one speed the medium allows. Most of the short-lived particles found in colliders are splashes, made when lasting knots are struck together hard.
4. **Properties are reactions.** Every measurement in physics records an encounter between two things. Mass is how hard a thing is to move, charge is how it pushes on another charge, and color is the light a surface sends back. A property is how a thing reacts to pressure. On the thesis, these are reactions of the medium to itself: one region of it meeting the resistance of another. The medium itself is never measured, only its reactions. It stands behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond.
5. **Motion is basic.** The medium is always in motion, and nothing needs to set it moving. Time is not a dimension woven into the medium. It is the count we keep of the motion.

The thesis keeps the predictions of existing theory wherever they have been tested. Its claim is about what those predictions describe. General relativity describes the medium’s pressure gradients exactly; it misnames them as the curvature of a geometry. Quantum mechanics describes the medium’s reactions exactly; it declines to say what is reacting.

## 3. Light, inertia and the two masses

> A property is how a thing reacts to pressure.

**Light.** In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell showed that the speed of light follows from two measured properties of empty space, its electric permittivity and its magnetic permeability. The speed is fixed because the medium that carries light has fixed properties, exactly as the speed of sound in air is fixed by the air’s stiffness and density. Physics kept Maxwell’s equations and dropped the medium. The thesis puts it back: the speed of light is the speed at which the singular field passes on a disturbance.

**Inertia.** On the thesis, a particle is a knot in the medium, and moving it means moving the knot through the stuff it is tied in. The medium resists changes in the knot’s motion, not the motion itself. A knot coasting at a steady speed carries its pattern with it, the way a wave crosses a pond without the pond dragging it to a stop. Changing that speed means reshaping the surrounding medium, and the medium pushes back. That push-back is inertia.

Standard physics is closer to this picture than its language admits. The masses of the fundamental particles are attributed to the Higgs field, which fills all of space and resists the motion of particles that interact with it. And about 99 percent of the mass of a proton is not the mass of its three quarks but the energy of their motion and binding: trapped motion, in the language of the thesis.

**The two masses.** Physics has two definitions of mass. Inertial mass measures how hard a body is to accelerate. Gravitational mass measures how strongly gravity pulls on it. Nothing in Newton’s mechanics requires them to be equal. Newton tested their equality with pendulums and found no difference. In 2022 the MICROSCOPE satellite found them equal to about one part in a million billion. Einstein built general relativity on that equality as a starting principle. Neither he nor anyone since has explained it.

The thesis explains it. Inertial mass is the medium’s resistance to a change in a knot’s motion. Gravitational mass, as section 4 argues, is the knot’s response to a pressure gradient in the same medium. Both are the same interaction between a knot and the stuff it is made of, measured in two situations. They are equal because they are one quantity, not because of a coincidence that a principle has been built on.

## 4. Gravity without geometry

> All laws are situational, not universal.

General relativity says that mass curves spacetime and that bodies follow the straightest paths through the curvature. The equations are superbly accurate. The picture is harder to accept. A geometry is a description of relations, and time is a measure of motion. Welding the two into a fabric and crediting the fabric with pushing matter about turns a calculating device into an agent.

**The compression.** On the thesis, a massive body is a large concentration of knots, and it changes the state of the medium around it, which becomes denser close to the body and thinner farther out. A second body in that region feels less push from the side facing the first body than from the open side, and is driven inward. Gravity is a pressure gradient in the medium: not an attraction, but a compression.

The idea is old. Nicolas Fatio de Duillier, a friend of Newton’s, proposed a mechanical explanation of gravity around 1690, and Georges-Louis Le Sage developed it in the eighteenth century. Their versions relied on streams of tiny particles bombarding bodies from all sides, and they failed: the bombardment should have slowed the planets and heated them. The thesis does not depend on bombardment. The medium is continuous, and a steady pressure gradient exerts force without drag, as a body at rest in a still ocean feels the pressure of the water without being worn by it.

**Light and clocks near mass.** A denser medium near a massive body slows the light that crosses it. The result is that light bends as it passes the body, the way it bends entering water, and arrives late. Both effects are measured. The bending of starlight by the Sun was first measured in 1919. The delay of radar signals passing near the Sun was predicted by Irwin Shapiro in 1964 and confirmed by bouncing radar off Mercury and Venus. Arthur Eddington noted in 1920 that the bending could be computed by treating the space around the Sun as a medium of slightly higher refractive index. In 1957 Robert Dicke showed that a vacuum with a variable refractive index reproduces the classic tests of general relativity, and Harold Puthoff extended the treatment in 2002.

The same density that slows light slows every rhythm in the region. Clocks run slower near a massive body, as Robert Pound and Glen Rebka measured in 1959 over the height of a building and as the GPS satellites confirm every day. On the thesis, this is not time itself running slowly. It is every knot in the region ringing more slowly in a denser medium, including the knots that make up the clock.

In the regime where general relativity has been tested, the thesis keeps its numbers. What it changes is the account of what the numbers describe: a material under pressure, not a geometry under strain.

## 5. Galaxies

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

**The rule.** Stars at the outer edges of spiral galaxies orbit faster than the visible matter can account for. The standard answer is a halo of dark matter, about five times as massive as the ordinary matter, which has not been detected in some forty years of laboratory searches. In 2016 Stacy McGaugh, Federico Lelli and James Schombert compiled 2,693 measurements in 153 galaxies of every size and type. They found that the observed acceleration at every point is fixed by the acceleration the visible matter alone would produce, through a single relation with a characteristic scale of about 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ meters per second squared. The scatter is small and mostly due to measurement error. In their words, the dark matter contribution “is fully specified by that of the baryons.”

A halo of independent, invisible matter has no reason to arrange itself in lockstep with the visible matter of every galaxy, from dwarfs to giants. The standard account can reproduce the relation in simulations only with careful tuning of how galaxies form. Mordehai Milgrom predicted the relation in 1983, decades before the data, by proposing that the law of gravity itself changes below that acceleration scale. His proposal, MOND, describes what happens. It does not say why.

**The medium’s character.** The thesis offers a reason. Close to a star, the pressure gradient is steep, and it overwhelms any property of the medium itself, much as a gale flattens a lake and hides its currents. Where the gradient falls below a certain gentleness, the medium’s own response shows through, and the motion departs from what the steep-gradient law predicts. The threshold is a property of the medium, the same everywhere, which is why one scale fits all 153 galaxies.

One further clue supports a medium. The acceleration scale is close to the speed of light multiplied by the expansion rate of the universe, divided by 2π. On the standard account this is an unexplained coincidence between a galactic number and a cosmic one. On the thesis, both numbers are properties of the same material, so their kinship is expected. _Pending._

**The Bullet Cluster.** The strongest evidence for dark matter as a substance is the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters that passed through each other. Most of their ordinary mass is hot gas, which collided and stalled in the middle; the galaxies sailed through. Maps of gravitational lensing, published by Douglas Clowe and colleagues in 2006, show the lensing centered on the galaxies, not the gas. The standard reading is that invisible matter traveled with the galaxies.

The thesis reads the same evidence through the difference between diffuse and compact matter. A medium displaced by a body responds to how the body is packed as well as to its mass. Compact matter, stars in galaxies, makes sharp, focused displacement. Diffuse gas spread over millions of light-years makes a broad, shallow one. In a slow, settled system the difference averages out. In a violent collision at thousands of kilometers per second it need not. This reading is qualitative and _pending_ a calculation. We note that the collision speed itself has been argued to be improbably high on the standard account (Lee and Komatsu, 2010).

## 6. Quantum behavior

> The thing is a fundamental force meeting the resistance of a material space.

**The puzzle.** In 1801 Thomas Young showed that light passing through two slits makes bands of light and dark, as waves do. In 1905 Einstein showed that light also arrives in separate packets. In 1989 Akira Tonomura’s team at Hitachi sent electrons through a two-slit apparatus one at a time. Each landed as a single dot at an unpredictable place, and the dots built up into bands. Each electron arrives like a particle, and the crowd lands like a wave. A century of interpretation has not settled what this means. A 2025 survey by the journal _Nature_ of more than a thousand physicists found no interpretation of quantum mechanics with majority support.

**The reading.** On the thesis there is one substance doing two things. The wave is the medium moving: a disturbance that spreads through both slits at once because the medium is on both sides of the barrier. The particle is the medium meeting resistance: when the spreading disturbance reaches a detector, a screen or an atom, the exchange happens at one place, and that place is the dot. Neither the wave nor the dot is the thing itself. The thing itself is the medium, caught traveling and caught arriving.

The dot’s position is unpredictable because it depends on the detailed state of the medium and the detector at the moment of contact, which no measurement can fully capture. Quantum mechanics records how often each outcome occurs. It is the bookkeeping of the medium’s reactions, and it is exact. It says nothing about what is reacting, and the thesis supplies that.

**Observation.** The standard reading says a measurement collapses a spread of possibilities into one outcome. Erwin Schrödinger’s cat, from 1935, was meant to show how strange that is: a cat that is a blend of dead and alive until someone looks. On the thesis, reactions do not wait for a physicist. The atom meets the trigger, the trigger meets the vial, and every part of the box meets the air and the walls, continuously. Observation is what material does whenever it touches material. Standard physics has moved toward the same view under the name of decoherence: interaction with the surroundings, not a conscious observer, is what makes outcomes definite.

**A respectable relative.** The closest established theory is pilot-wave mechanics, proposed by Louis de Broglie in 1927 and developed by David Bohm in 1952. In it, particles always have definite positions and are guided by a real wave. Its cost, confirmed by tests of John Bell’s 1964 theorem that culminated in the 2022 Nobel Prize, is that the guiding wave connects distant places instantly. For a picture in which everything is one continuous medium, a connection that does not respect distance is less surprising than it is for a picture of separate particles in empty space.

In 2005 Yves Couder and Emmanuel Fort showed that oil droplets bouncing on a vibrating bath of oil, guided by the waves they make, reproduce several quantum behaviors, including interference patterns built up one droplet at a time. Later experiments found that some of these analogies, the two-slit pattern among them, are less clean than first reported. The droplets do not prove the thesis. They show that a particle guided by a wave in a real medium is a working physical picture, not a metaphor.

## 7. Origins

> One force, four theaters, one movie.

**Pairs.** Whenever energy becomes matter, it comes out in pairs: a particle and its antiparticle, opposite in charge and equal in mass. Carl Anderson found the first antiparticle, the positron, in 1932, and Patrick Blackett and Giuseppe Occhialini watched light turn into electron-positron pairs the following year. No experiment has ever produced a single particle of matter from energy alone.

On the thesis, a pair is the simplest knot the medium can tie: a twist and its opposite, which together leave the surrounding medium undisturbed. That is why charge always balances and why matter never appears singly. A twist cannot be put into a continuous material without an equal counter-twist somewhere.

**Which comes first?** Our essays have offered two readings of how the medium and its knots began, and this paper has to choose. In the first (No. 67), the medium is primary and particles are bubbles it throws up. In the second (No. 68), the first pairs are primary and the medium is woven between them, as Leibniz argued that space is only the relations among things. We adopt the second for the beginning and the first for everything after it. The first pairs that held, instead of annihilating, wove the first fabric between them. Once woven, that fabric is the singular field of sections 2 to 6, and every later particle is a knot retied in it. The medium is a product of the first pairs, and the medium of every pair since. _Pending._

**The leftovers.** When matter meets antimatter, both vanish into light. The early universe should therefore have annihilated itself completely. It did not. Counting the photons in the microwave background against the particles of matter shows that for every billion or so pairs, one extra particle of matter survived. Every star and every living thing is made of that remainder. Physics has no accepted explanation for the excess. The thesis does not supply one either. It names the question differently: not why matter won, but why, out of a billion pairs, one knot held when its twin did not.

**One force.** As the early universe cooled, the push running through the medium met different kinds of resistance and appeared as four different forces. Physics has already shown that two of them are one: in the 1960s Sheldon Glashow, Steven Weinberg and Abdus Salam unified electromagnetism and the weak force, and the carriers of the weak force were found at CERN in 1983. The strong force is expected to join them at higher energies. Gravity is the holdout only because general relativity treats it as geometry. On the thesis it is the medium pushing back, which is the same kind of thing as the others.

## 8. Supporting witnesses

> Criticism is fair. Controversy is destructive.

The ether was never refuted so much as set aside, and some of the physicists who set it aside later had second thoughts.

**Lorentz.** Hendrik Lorentz’s theory of the electron, completed around 1904, kept a stationary ether and showed that bodies moving through it contract and their clocks slow in exactly the way that hides the motion. It makes the same predictions as special relativity. Physics preferred Einstein’s version because it did without the unobservable medium, a choice of economy, not of evidence.

**Einstein.** In a 1920 lecture at Leiden, Einstein said that general relativity gives space physical qualities, and concluded that “space without ether is unthinkable.” His ether had no parts that could be tracked through time, so it was not a material in our sense. But he conceded the point the thesis begins from: space is something.

**Dirac.** In a 1951 letter to _Nature_ titled “Is there an aether?”, Paul Dirac argued that quantum mechanics removes the main objection to the ether, and that the new electrodynamics he was developing was “rather forced to have an aether.”

**The refractive vacuum.** Robert Dicke (1957) and Harold Puthoff (2002) showed that a vacuum with a variable refractive index reproduces the classic tests of general relativity: the bending of light, the radar delay, the slowing of clocks and the advance of Mercury’s orbit. Their work is the nearest quantitative model to section 4 of this paper.

**Condensed-matter vacua.** Grigory Volovik’s _The Universe in a Helium Droplet_ (2003) shows how particles, gauge fields and an effective gravity emerge from the motions of a superfluid, and the field of analogue gravity has built laboratory systems in which sound in a fluid behaves like light near a black hole. Frank Wilczek, in _The Lightness of Being_ (2008), describes empty space as a material medium he calls the Grid, and treats it as the primary ingredient of physical reality.

**Superfluid dark matter.** Lasha Berezhiani and Justin Khoury (2015) proposed that dark matter is a superfluid whose collective behavior reproduces Milgrom’s rule inside galaxies while acting as ordinary dark matter in clusters. It is the closest modern proposal to section 5. It differs from the thesis in keeping dark matter as a separate substance. The thesis has one substance, and the behavior Berezhiani and Khoury attribute to a superfluid it attributes to space.

## 9. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: Michelson and Morley found no ether wind.** In 1887 their interferometer showed no difference in the speed of light along and across the Earth’s motion. A medium should have produced one.

_Reply._ Only if rulers and clocks are made of something other than the medium. On the thesis, every ruler, every clock and every atom in an interferometer is a knot in the same medium that carries the light. When the apparatus moves, its knots are reshaped by the medium in the same proportion as the light’s passage is affected, and the effect cancels. Lorentz showed this in mathematical detail before relativity was published. The null result rules out a medium that matter moves through. It does not rule out a medium that matter is made of.

**Objection 2: Lorentz invariance is tested to extreme precision.** Any preferred frame of rest, which a medium seems to supply, should show up somewhere. Searches for it have found nothing, to very high precision.

_Reply._ The same answer applies. If all matter and all measuring devices are made of the medium, no experiment built from them can detect motion relative to it. The thesis predicts the null results; it does not merely survive them. We note that the cosmic microwave background does define a rest frame, which every astronomer uses, and the Earth’s motion through it is measured at about 370 kilometers per second. Nature supplies a preferred frame; physics declines to give it significance.

**Objection 3: gravitational waves.** In 2017 the merger of two neutron stars was seen in gravitational waves and in light. The two arrived within seconds of each other after traveling 130 million years, which fixes the speed of gravity equal to the speed of light to within a few parts in a million billion. Gravitational waves also have two transverse polarizations, which a simple refractive medium cannot produce.

_Reply._ The equal speeds favor the thesis: if light and gravitational waves are both disturbances of one medium, they should travel at one speed. On the standard account the equality is built in by assumption. The polarizations are a real demand. A medium that carries transverse waves must resist shear, as the elastic-solid ethers of the nineteenth century did, and a model in which the medium has only a variable refractive index, such as Dicke’s or Puthoff’s, is not enough. The thesis requires a medium with shear resistance, and its mathematical form is _pending_.

**Objection 4: galaxy clusters.** Milgrom’s rule removes most of the missing mass in galaxies but not in clusters. Robert Sanders found in 2003 that MOND reduces the discrepancy in clusters by a factor of three or four but leaves a residue: a cluster still appears to hold roughly twice as much mass as its stars and gas.

_Reply._ The residue is real, and the thesis inherits it. Two answers are available. Some of the missing cluster mass may be ordinary matter not yet counted, such as diffuse gas or massive neutrinos, which are known to exist and to have mass. Or the medium may respond differently in the hot, dense, violent environment of a cluster than in the quiet outskirts of a spiral galaxy. Neither answer has been worked out. _Pending._

**Objection 5: the microwave background.** This is the hardest objection, and we state it without softening. The cosmic microwave background shows a pattern of hot and cold spots whose detailed statistics, the acoustic peaks, are fitted with great precision by a model in which, before the background was released, there was about five times as much non-interacting matter as ordinary matter. The relative heights of the peaks are the main evidence that this extra component does not interact with light. No model without dark matter has yet matched the peaks as well.

_Reply._ The thesis does not yet answer this objection. To answer it, the medium would have to respond, in the hot early universe, in a way that mimics a pressureless component that does not interact with light. That is not impossible. The superfluid models of section 8 do something similar, by having one substance behave like dark matter on large scales and like modified gravity in galaxies. But no such calculation exists for the thesis, and until one does, the microwave background stands as the strongest evidence against it.

**Objection 6: this is reinterpretation, not physics.** Where the thesis keeps the predictions of general relativity and quantum mechanics, it changes nothing measurable.

_Reply._ Partly true, and not a weakness. Choosing between readings of the same equations matters when the readings point in different directions for research. The thesis also does more than relabel. It explains the equality of inertial and gravitational mass, which the standard account assumes. It explains why one acceleration scale governs every galaxy, which the standard account must tune for. And it makes predictions of its own, which section 10 lists.

## 10. Predictions and tests

> If science can read the stars, it ought to be able to sense the wind.

1. **The equivalence of the two masses is exact.** If inertial and gravitational mass are one quantity, no experiment will ever find them different, at any precision or for any materials. A confirmed violation would refute the thesis. General relativity makes the same prediction, but as an assumption.
2. **One acceleration scale for every galaxy.** The rule of section 5 should hold for every kind of galaxy, including faint, diffuse galaxies and the small galaxies that form from debris thrown out in collisions. The standard account expects these tidal dwarfs to carry almost no dark matter, since the debris comes from the disk of the parent galaxy and not its halo. If they follow the same rule as other galaxies, as early observations of the system NGC 5291 suggested, the medium reading is favored.
3. **The scale changes with cosmic time.** If the galactic acceleration scale is a property of the same medium as the expansion, and tracks the expansion rate, it should have been larger in the past, when the expansion was faster. Rotation curves of distant galaxies, now being measured by the James Webb Space Telescope and the ALMA array, can test this. The standard account offers no reason to expect a change.
4. **Black hole shadows.** Where gravity is strongest, a medium and a geometry need not agree. The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged the shadows of the dark objects at the centers of the galaxy M87 and of our own galaxy. On the thesis, the shadows should differ in size from the predictions of general relativity by a few percent, a difference within the reach of the next generation of telescopes. What lies inside the shadow is behind an SOB and will never be seen; the shadow’s edge is not. The size and sign of the difference depend on the mathematical form of the medium, which is _pending_.
5. **The dark matter searches stay empty.** Laboratory detectors have searched for dark matter particles for about forty years, each generation more sensitive than the last, without a confirmed detection. The thesis predicts that they will go on finding nothing, because there is nothing separate from the medium to find.
6. **Wide binary stars.** Pairs of stars orbiting each other at thousands of times the Earth-Sun distance feel accelerations below the galactic threshold. If the medium’s character shows at low accelerations everywhere, and not only in galaxies, these pairs should orbit slightly faster than Newton’s law predicts. Analyses of the Gaia satellite’s data have reached opposite conclusions, and the test is _pending_ better data.

## 11. Conclusion

> Reality exists. Knowledge is authored.

Physics abandoned the ether for a sound reason: no experiment could detect motion through it. That reason does not touch a medium that matter is made of, because instruments made of the medium cannot detect their own motion through it. With that objection answered, the case for a material space is stronger than the case for a geometric one at several points. It explains why the two kinds of mass are equal. It gives gravity a mechanism. It explains why a single acceleration scale governs the motion of stars in every galaxy, without an invisible halo tuned to match. It makes sense of the particle that travels as a wave and arrives as a dot. And it accounts for the fact that matter is made in pairs.

The thesis has open accounts, and we have listed them: the mathematical form of a medium that carries transverse gravitational waves, the mass still missing in galaxy clusters, and above all the acoustic peaks of the microwave background. These are the places where work on the thesis should begin.

What seems clearly not right is the current arrangement, in which space is denied the status of a substance while being credited with energy, pressure, fluctuations and the power to bend, and in which the gaps this leaves are filled with ingredients nobody has found. The singular field fills them with the one thing every measurement has ever touched.

The better question is not what dark matter is made of. It is whether space is made of something, and if it is, how much of what physics has hunted for a century was the medium all along.

two-the-primacy-of-pairs:
## Abstract

At every scale we can observe, in matter, in living things and in thought, reality comes in pairs. We argue that this is not a coincidence of description but a feature of existence: two is the smallest number that can make a difference, and to exist is to be different from something. Charge comes in two kinds and always balances. Energy becomes matter only as particle and antiparticle. Living things copy themselves by pairing the rungs of a double ladder, and most animals are built on a left and a right. The mind is a difference detector, and its first act after sensing is a pair: a question and its answer.

One, on this view, is not something we can ever observe. It is the undivided, the state before the first distinction, and it lies behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary. We examine the one great pair that failed to balance, matter over antimatter by one part in a billion, which left behind everything that exists, and the proposal that the total energy of the universe is zero: a nothing that split into a plus and a minus. We meet the objection that the mind sees pairs because it is built to, which we partly accept, and propose tests.

## 1. Introduction

> Two rights always create a wrong. Two maybes don’t.

Up and down. Left and right. Night and day. True and false. Plus and minus. North and south. Life and death. Mom and Dad. Everywhere we look, at every scale, reality comes in twos: not in threes, fives or tens, but in pairs.

The ancients noticed first. Heraclitus, around 500 BC, saw opposites everywhere and bound together: “The road up and the road down are one and the same.” The Pythagoreans built the world from a table of ten opposites. The Tao Te Ching taught that being and non-being produce each other, and gave the world its most famous pair symbol, yin and yang. Genesis opens not with God making things but with God dividing them: light from darkness, the waters above from the waters below, the sea from the dry land.

Our thesis is that **two is the basic integer of existence, because existence is difference and two is the smallest number that makes one; and that one, the undivided, is what lies before the first distinction, beyond observation.** If that is right, it answers two questions together: why everything that exists comes in pairs, and why the first instant is hidden from us. It also suggests what didn’t Bang.

Section 2 argues from logic and mathematics, sections 3 to 5 from matter, life and mind. Section 6 examines the pair that failed to balance and section 7 what came before the first pair. Sections 8 to 10 call witnesses, meet objections and propose tests.

## 2. The smallest difference

> All observation is self-centered. Reality does not possess a self.

**Two makes a difference.** One thing alone cannot be compared with anything. The moment there are two, there is a difference: this and that, here and there, more and less. Baruch Spinoza put it in three words in 1674: “determination is negation.” A thing is a thing only because of what it is not. Draw a circle and you have made two things at once, an inside and an outside.

**Language and logic.** Ferdinand de Saussure showed in the early 1900s that words mean nothing on their own, only by contrast: “in language there are only differences.” Aristotle’s first law of thought holds that nothing can be both true and false in the same respect. In 1854 George Boole built an algebra on those two values, and less than a century later it became the 1 and 0 inside every computer. Gottfried Leibniz had already worked out binary counting in 1703, and saw in it an image of creation: God as one, nothing as zero, everything built from the two. In 1989 John Wheeler proposed “it from bit,” that every physical thing is at bottom information, and a bit is a pair: yes or no.

**Does one exist?** The Greek mathematicians thought not. Euclid defined a number as “a multitude composed of units.” One was the unit, the stuff of numbers, not a number itself, and Aristotle called it the measure of number. For them, counting began at two. Modern foundations reach a curious echo. In the 1920s John von Neumann built the numbers from nothing: zero is the empty set, one is the set containing the empty set, two is the set holding both. In the foundations of mathematics, one is nothing, wrapped.

We draw the conclusion the Greeks implied. One is not a thing we can ever meet. The moment anything is observed, it is set apart from something else, and there are already two. One is the number of what we cannot observe: the undivided. It lies behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond.

## 3. Pairs in matter

> We measure the reaction, never the reactors.

**Balanced books.** Electric charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative, and the total never changes. Magnets have two poles; cut one in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south. In 1931 Paul Dirac showed that a single magnetic pole would be consistent with quantum theory, and it has been searched for ever since, most recently at the Large Hadron Collider, without success. Isaac Newton stated the rule in 1687: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. In 1918 Emmy Noether proved that every symmetry of nature produces a conservation law, so that something can only be moved from one side of the ledger to the other. Nature keeps double-entry books.

**Matter from light.** In 1928 Dirac’s equation predicted that every particle has an opposite twin. In 1932 Carl Anderson found the first, the positron. Since 1933 physicists have watched light turn into matter, and it never produces one particle. It produces a pair. When the pair meets again, both vanish, and two flashes of light fly off in opposite directions. Hospitals use those paired flashes every day in PET scanners.

**Pairs that bind.** The chemical bond that holds water together is a pair of electrons shared between atoms, spinning in opposite directions, as Gilbert Lewis described in 1916; Wolfgang Pauli’s exclusion principle is the reason electrons pair up. In superconductors, electrons travel in pairs, as Leon Cooper showed in 1956, and flow without resistance.

**Pairs that stay linked.** Two particles created together remain correlated however far apart they travel. Einstein doubted it in 1935. Experiments have since confirmed it beyond argument, and the 2022 Nobel Prize in physics recognized them.

**Complementarity.** Niels Bohr spent his life on the fact that light and matter behave as wave and as particle, two descriptions that exclude each other yet are both needed. When Denmark knighted him in 1947 he chose the yin-yang for his coat of arms, with the motto _Contraria sunt complementa_: opposites are complementary. In our companion paper The Singular Field we read the pair as one substance caught traveling and caught arriving.

**Conjoined, not attracted.** Physics says opposites attract: positive draws negative, north draws south. “Attract” is a name for an effect at a distance, and like “gravity” it hides the mechanism. The evidence describes something else. Opposites are not two things drawn together across empty space. They are conjoined: one disturbance with two faces, made together and never found apart.

The magnet is the hardest witness. Cut it and each piece has both poles, and no lone pole has ever been found. Quarks are never seen alone; pull two apart and the effort makes a new pair, so the separation produces two conjoined pairs instead of one divided one. A single burst of light can become an electron and a positron at the same instant, and when the two meet again they vanish back into light. That is not attraction ending in a collision. It is a pair rejoining. And every positive charge ever made has arrived with its negative. What looks like a pull between opposites is the tendency of the two faces of one twist in the medium to be whole again.

## 4. Pairs in life

> Evolution rests on two facts: smart and lucky.

**The double ladder.** DNA, described by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, is a double strand whose every rung is a pair: A with T, G with C. When a cell divides the ladder unzips and each half rebuilds its partner. Life copies itself by pairing.

**Left and right.** For more than 500 million years the great majority of animals have been bilateral, built on a left and a right. We have two eyes and two ears because the brain finds depth and direction by comparing what the pair reports.

**Mom and Dad.** Sexual reproduction is at least a billion years old; the oldest known example is a tiny red seaweed. Every human carries 23 pairs of chromosomes, one of each pair from each parent. Why sex exists at all is still open. Graham Bell called it the queen of problems in evolutionary biology, and John Maynard Smith named its twofold cost: a creature that clones itself passes on all its genes and needs no partner. The leading answer, the Red Queen, says that parasites constantly evolve to crack whatever lock a species carries, and sex reshuffles the lock every generation.

**Why two sexes.** One hypothesis, put forward by Laurence Hurst and W. D. Hamilton in 1992, is that every cell carries power plants, the mitochondria, with genes of their own, and if both parents passed theirs on the two sets could compete inside the offspring. So one parent supplies them and the other does not. Tellingly, some fungi, which mate without merging their cells, have thousands of mating types instead of two. _Pending._

**Smart and lucky.** Evolution itself runs on a pair. Lucky is the variation, the random change. Smart is the keeping of what works. Neither is enough alone, and every survivor has been both.

## 5. Pairs in the mind

> The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long.

**A difference detector.** The nervous system reports change and contrast and stops reporting whatever stays the same. Walk into a house and you smell it; live there a week and you do not. Everything we perceive, we perceive as a difference: light against dark, sound against silence, this against that. A mind built that way can only see a world of pairs.

**Question and answer.** The first act of the mind after sensing is a matched pair. The senses deliver something moving in the grass; the mind asks what it is, and experience, if the creature lives long enough, supplies the answer. The instinct to question is the _sine qua non_ of survival. Every later level of knowledge, pattern, order and law, is built on that first pairing.

**Caution and curiosity.** At the root of every living mind sits the pair that keeps it alive. A wild rat meeting a new food takes a nibble, waits to see whether it gets sick, then comes back for more. Curiosity says try it; caution says carefully. Every foraging animal chooses again and again between the patch it knows and the patch it does not. All curiosity and the first snake gets you; all caution and you starve in the cave. The same pair runs through reproduction: cloning is caution, keeping what worked, and sex is curiosity, gambling on new combinations. When the pair breaks, caution hardens into certainty and curiosity runs into recklessness.

**The engine.** In our companion paper The Exhaust Stroke the universe itself runs on a pair of strokes: gathering, which we call gravity, and dispersal, which thermodynamics calls entropy. The power stroke and the exhaust stroke, a recycling system. The pattern that runs through matter, life and mind runs through the cosmos as a whole.

## 6. The pair that didn’t balance

> Things break and stuff happens.

**The puzzle.** If energy makes matter only in pairs, the early universe should have made matter and antimatter in exactly equal amounts, and every particle should have met its twin and vanished, leaving nothing but light. That is not what happened. There are no antimatter galaxies. Counting the photons of the microwave background against the particles of matter shows about a billion and a half photons for every surviving particle. For roughly every billion pairs that annihilated, one extra particle of matter survived. Every star, every planet, every horse and every one of us is made of that remainder.

**What physics knows.** In 1967 Andrei Sakharov listed the conditions any explanation must meet, among them a difference in how matter and antimatter behave. Such a difference was found in 1964 by James Cronin and Val Fitch. But the known differences are far too small to account for the surplus. The excess of matter is one of the great unsolved problems in physics.

**A reading.** The standard account places the Big Bang first, then the separation of matter and antimatter, then their mutual annihilation, as three stages. We propose that they may be one event. The Big Bang may have been the separation itself: the moment the undivided first split into a pair, matter and antimatter, unequally, with the antimatter wholly consumed in the same instant and a sliver of matter left behind. In the 1960s Hannes Alfvén and Oskar Klein proposed a universe that began as a mixture of matter and antimatter in separate regions. It was set aside because the borders between such regions would glow, and none are seen. If the antimatter was consumed in the very event that made it, there would be no borders left to glow, which is the universe we observe. Why the split was unequal remains the open question. _Pending._

**The leftovers.** In our companion work we put the emphasis on the survivors. The pairs came as two, but what survived came one at a time, a single stray for every billion pairs, and those singles set the ball rolling. On this reading antimatter is the mother of Two: she gave herself up entirely in the event, and everything that exists is what she left behind. Her light still fills the sky as the microwave background.

## 7. What didn’t Bang

> Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

If everything that exists comes in pairs, what was there before the first pair? What split? What didn’t Bang?

**Zero, split.** In 1973 Edward Tryon proposed in _Nature_ that the total energy of the universe may be exactly zero: the positive energy of all its matter balanced, to the last decimal, by the negative energy of gravity. If so, the beginning was not something coming from nothing. It was a nothing splitting into a plus and a minus that still add up to zero. One observation is consistent with this. A universe with zero total energy should be spatially flat, and the Planck satellite measured the curvature of space to be zero to within about two parts in a thousand. Consistency is not proof. _Pending._

**The One.** Philosophers reached for the same thing in their own terms. In the third century Plotinus taught that behind every pair stands “the One,” beyond all opposites, from which all things flow. In 1440 Nicholas of Cusa wrote that in the infinite all opposites coincide, and titled his book _On Learned Ignorance_. In 1952 the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, whose exclusion principle is the reason electrons pair up, and the psychiatrist Carl Jung published a book together seeking a single reality beneath mind and matter; Jung borrowed the alchemists’ name for it, the _unus mundus_, the one world.

**Why we cannot see it.** Here the argument turns back on the observer. A mind that perceives only differences can see only pairs. The undivided, if it exists, has no opposite to show against. It is not hidden because it is far away. It is hidden because a mind like ours has nothing to compare it with. What didn’t Bang may be the last SOB of all, invisible not by accident but by the way observation works.

One is what didn’t Bang. Two is the first thing that did.

## 8. Supporting witnesses

> Intelligence should always be respected, no matter what form it comes in.

The thesis is our own. Its witnesses span twenty-five centuries.

**The ancients.** Heraclitus on the unity of opposites; the Pythagorean table of ten opposites; the Tao Te Ching’s account of the Tao giving birth to one, one to two, two to three and three to the ten thousand things; and the dividing God of Genesis.

**The logicians.** Aristotle’s law of non-contradiction, Spinoza’s “determination is negation,” Leibniz’s binary, Boole’s two-valued algebra, Saussure’s differences and Wheeler’s bit.

**The physicists.** Newton’s third law, Noether’s theorem, Dirac’s antimatter and Bohr’s complementarity, each describing a world that keeps double-entry books.

**The biologists.** Watson and Crick’s double helix, Maynard Smith’s twofold cost of sex and Hurst and Hamilton’s account of two sexes.

What none of them did is put the pairs of matter, life and mind together with the claim that one is unobservable in principle, and read the first instant as the first split.

## 9. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: nature also comes in threes.** A proton is three quarks, quarks carry one of three color charges, matter comes in three generations and space has three dimensions.

_Reply._ Threes exist, and the thesis does not deny them. It claims that two is basic, the smallest difference. Several threes resolve into balance: the three colors in a proton combine to neutral, and a meson is a quark paired with an antiquark. Where a three does not resolve, it leaves a remainder. In “You Are Not Me” we argued that odd numbers are where disparity, and with it conflict, begins: three is where politics starts, two against one. The threes support the thesis by showing what happens when the pairing is incomplete.

**Objection 2: the pairs are in the mind.** A mind built as a difference detector will find pairs wherever it looks. The pattern may be ours, not nature’s.

_Reply._ We partly accept this, and section 7 depends on it. Projection is one of the twelve impediments every observer carries. But some pairs are measured, not perceived: light turning into exactly two particles, charge always balancing, the two flashes from annihilation landing on opposite sides of a scanner. Those are counted by instruments. The honest position is that the pattern belongs to nature and to us, and that we cannot cleanly separate the two shares.

**Objection 3: this is numerology.** Any number can be found everywhere by selective listing.

_Reply._ The pairs listed here include laws, not coincidences: conservation of charge, Noether’s theorem and pair production are exact and measured. Numerology predicts nothing. The thesis predicts what will not be found, in section 10.

**Objection 4: the total energy of the universe is not well defined.** In general relativity there is no agreed way to add up the energy of an expanding universe, so “exactly zero” may have no meaning.

_Reply._ A fair technical point, and the reason we label the zero-energy proposal pending. Its observational companion, the flatness of space, is well measured and consistent with it.

## 10. Predictions and tests

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

1. **No lone magnetic pole will be found.** Dirac showed in 1931 that a single magnetic pole is allowed by quantum theory, and searches continue at the Large Hadron Collider and in cosmic rays. The thesis predicts that every magnet will always have two poles.
2. **No lone particle from energy.** No process will ever turn energy into a single particle of matter, or create net electric charge. Every creation will be a pair.
3. **The surplus will come from a pair.** Whatever explains the excess of matter will be a difference in how twins behave, a process in which matter and antimatter are made or destroyed together but unequally, not the creation of matter alone.
4. **Space will stay flat.** As measurements of the curvature of space improve, the thesis, through the zero-energy reading, predicts that the curvature will remain consistent with zero.
5. **The first instant will stay hidden.** No observation will ever recover a state before the first distinction. If a signal from “before” is ever claimed, the thesis predicts that on examination it will turn out to come from after the split.

## 11. Conclusion

> We can be certain of what we invent, never of what we observe.

We know a great deal about what pairs do. They mark one thing off from another, which is what it means to exist. They hold matter together and keep nature’s books balanced. They let life copy itself and outwit its parasites. They give us depth and direction, and the pair of caution and curiosity keeps every living thing alive. Question and answer, the first pair the mind makes, is the root of all knowledge, and gathering and dispersal, the two strokes of the cosmic engine, keep the universe in motion.

What we do not know is where pairs come from. That lies on the far side of the last SOB, with the One that didn’t split. Perhaps one was never a number, only the name for what we cannot see. Perhaps the universe is a nothing that divided, or the leftover of a pair that did not balance.

What seems clearly not right is a description of the first instant as a single thing, a point or a singularity, when nothing observed has ever been single. The better question is not what banged. It is what split, and why it split unequally.

With the function in hand and the origin out of reach, we can have our milk and cookies and sleep soundly through the night, until the day comes round again, which is, of course, the other half of a pair.
