## Abstract

The objects at the centers of galaxies, and the remnants of the largest stars, are among the best-observed things in astronomy. They are also described in terms that no observation could ever confirm: an event horizon nothing can return through, an interior where space and time exchange roles, a central point of infinite density, and a faint evaporation too cold ever to detect. We separate the observations from the description. What is observed is a dense, dark concentration of mass, matter falling toward it and heating, part of that matter thrown back out in jets, and the ripples from pairs of such objects merging. Nothing observed requires a hole.

We propose that these objects are what they appear to be: the densest concentrations of matter in nature, gathering mass and heat, and ejecting some of it. Read through our companion papers, they are the gathering stroke of a cosmic recycling engine, and possibly the early stage of an eruption on the scale of the one our own expansion began with. We examine why the hole persists in the face of so little evidence for it, meet the strongest objection, which is the absence of light from any surface at the center of our galaxy, and propose tests that could tell a dense object from a hole. We also separate two kinds the word “black hole” lumps together and give them names: galactic accumulators, which gather, store and release at the centers of galaxies, and collapsed stellar cores, the graves of single stars.

## 1. Introduction

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

The black hole is one of the most familiar ideas in science and one of the least examined. It has everything a good story needs: a door that opens one way, a place where time stops, a point of infinite density, a slow evaporation, and a paradox about lost information that has occupied some of the best minds in physics for half a century. It is taught as fact in schools, staged in films and photographed, we are told, by a telescope the size of the Earth.

This paper takes the story apart one piece at a time and asks, of each piece, whether anything has been observed. Our method is that of a detective reopening a cold case: keep every piece of evidence, throw out the theory, and see where the evidence points. Our thesis is that **the evidence describes a dense, dark object gathering matter and heat, and that the hole, with everything said to lie inside it, is an inference from an equation, not an observation.**

Section 2 lists what is observed and section 3 what is inferred. Section 4 traces how the hole entered physics before the evidence did. Section 5 states the thesis and connects it to our companion papers. Section 6 asks why the story holds. Sections 7 to 9 call witnesses, meet objections and propose tests.

## 2. What is observed

> We measure the reaction, never the reactors.

Strip away the vocabulary and the record is this.

- **A dense mass at the center of our galaxy.** For three decades, teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked stars orbiting an unseen point called Sagittarius A*. The orbits fix its mass at about four million times the Sun’s. The star S2 passes within about 120 times the Earth-Sun distance of it and, at its closest in 2018, moved at about 7,650 kilometers per second. The work earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in physics.
- **Rings of light around dark centers.** The Event Horizon Telescope, an array of radio dishes spread across the Earth, imaged the center of the galaxy M87 in 2019 and Sagittarius A* in 2022. Both images show a bright ring around a darker middle. For Sagittarius A*, the dark region is smaller than the orbit of Mercury.
- **Matter falling in and heating.** Gas spiraling toward these objects is heated until it radiates across the spectrum, in some cases outshining every star in its galaxy. Quasars, the most luminous steady sources in the universe, are powered this way.
- **Matter thrown out.** Jets of particles leave some of these objects at nearly the speed of light. The jet from M87 is about 5,000 light-years long. Winds and jets heat the surrounding gas and limit how many stars the host galaxy can form.
- **Growth in step with the galaxy.** The mass of the central object tracks the mass of its galaxy’s central bulge closely, as if the two grew together.
- **Ripples from mergers.** Since 2015 the LIGO and Virgo detectors have recorded gravitational waves from pairs of dense objects, each of several to dozens of solar masses, spiraling together and merging.
- **Smaller cousins.** In binary star systems such as Cygnus X-1, a visible star orbits a dark companion too massive to be a neutron star, and gas pulled off the visible star glows in X-rays as it falls.

Every item on this list describes a dense, dark mass and what happens to matter near it. None describes an interior, a horizon in the sense of a one-way surface, a singularity or an evaporation.

## 3. What is inferred

> We can be certain of what we invent, never of what we observe.

The standard description adds four things to the record, and none of them has been observed.

**The horizon.** The event horizon is defined as a surface from which nothing, not even light, can return. If such a surface exists, it is the purest SOB in nature: a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. By definition no signal from inside can ever reach us. Yet the inside has been described in remarkable detail.

**The interior.** Inside the horizon, the equations of general relativity exchange the roles of space and time, so that the center stops being a place ahead of the traveler and becomes a moment in his future, as unavoidable as next Tuesday. Physicists still disagree about whether a traveler would cross the horizon unharmed or be burned on the threshold, a dispute that has run since Ahmed Almheiri, Donald Marolf, Joseph Polchinski and James Sully published their “firewall” argument in 2012. The disagreement is about a place that cannot, by definition, be observed.

**The singularity.** At the center the equations run to infinity. No one has measured an infinity; it is what an equation produces when it has stopped describing anything. The singularity is that breakdown given a location. It has a twin at the beginning of the universe, built the same way from the same equations run backward.

**The evaporation.** In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that, if quantum fields are added to the picture, a black hole should glow faintly and slowly lose mass. For an object of the Sun’s mass the glow corresponds to a temperature of about sixty billionths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than the microwave background around it, so such an object absorbs far more than it emits, and the glow will never be detected. The popular explanation, in which pairs of particles appear at the horizon and one falls in, is a heuristic picture, as Hawking himself said. For fifty years physicists have argued over what happens to the information carried by what falls in. The argument concerns a place nobody can see and an effect nobody can measure.

Each of these four elements comes from the mathematics, not from the telescopes. That does not make them false. It makes them unverified, and three of them are unverifiable in principle.

## 4. How the hole got there

> Prediction does not equal truth. It’s local and non-transferable.

The hole entered physics as mathematics, and the evidence arrived decades later to find the picture waiting.

In 1783 the English clergyman John Michell imagined a star so massive that light thrown up from its surface would fall back, like a stone. He called it a dark star. It was a solid body with a surface, dark only because its light could not get away. Pierre-Simon Laplace made the same suggestion in 1796.

In 1916, weeks after Einstein published general relativity, Karl Schwarzschild found the first exact solution of its equations, for the space around a single mass. The solution has a radius at which its terms break down. For decades most physicists, Einstein and Arthur Eddington among them, regarded that radius as a mathematical artifact that real matter would never reach. In 1939 Einstein published a paper arguing that such objects could not form in nature. In the same year J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder showed that, in the equations, a collapsing ball of pressureless dust would fall inside the radius and keep going.

The idea lay quiet until the 1960s. Quasars were identified in 1963 and demanded a compact, powerful engine. In 1965 Roger Penrose proved that, under general relativity, collapse past a certain point must end in a singularity. In 1967 John Wheeler popularized the name “black hole,” and the name did as much work as the mathematics. From then on, everything that came near had to fall in, be swallowed and be lost. In the early 1970s Cygnus X-1 was identified as a dark companion too massive to be a neutron star, and the hole had its first object.

The order matters. The equation came first, the name second and the evidence last. When the evidence arrived, it was read into a picture that already existed. Astronomers who study the process directly use a plainer word for what they see. They call it accretion, which means gathering.

## 5. The thesis

> A new Big Bang gathering mass and heat, like Old Faithful getting ready to erupt.

We propose that the objects called black holes are the densest concentrations of matter in nature, with no hole, no interior of exchanged space and time, and no singularity. Four claims make up the thesis.

1. **A presence, not an absence.** Four million solar masses in a region smaller than Mercury’s orbit is the opposite of a hole. The name describes what we cannot see, not what is there.
2. **No exchange of space and time.** The exchange happens in general relativity because it welds a material thing, space, to a measure of motion, time, and calls the result one fabric. In a material space, as our companion paper The Singular Field argues, the center of a dense object is the place where the medium is compressed most, and a place stays a place. The infinities at the center mark where the equations stop describing anything; they are not a property of the object.
3. **Gathering, not swallowing.** Matter falling toward the object is heated, much of its energy leaves as light, some is thrown back out in jets and winds, and the rest stays on as mass. As far as anyone can tell, nothing is lost. The objects grow, by accretion and by merging, which is what the mass-bulge relation and the gravitational-wave mergers record.
4. **Gathering toward release.** In our companion paper The Exhaust Stroke we describe the universe as a recycling engine with two strokes: dispersal, which thermodynamics calls entropy, and gathering, which we call gravity. These objects are the gathering stroke at its most extreme. Mass piles up, heat rises, giants merge into larger giants, and some of what is gathered already escapes in the jets. The Big Bang is described as matter flying apart from extreme density. Here is matter gathering back into extreme density. We propose that these objects may be the quiet phase of an eruption, the way a geyser gathers water and heat underground between eruptions, and that on the largest scale the next eruption may resemble the hot, dense state from which our own expansion began. _Pending._

**Two kinds, two names.** Physics files two different things under one name. The stellar objects, roughly five to a few dozen times the Sun’s mass, are each what is left when one massive star collapses: a single event at the end of a single life. They grow little, and nothing about them suggests a store that fills and releases. We call them **collapsed stellar cores**, or plainly, graves. The objects at the centers of galaxies, millions to billions of times the Sun’s mass, grow by gathering over billions of years, keep pace with the growth of their galaxies, and flare when fed, as quasars and jets. They store and they release. We call them **galactic accumulators**, or plainly, middens: the heap where a galaxy’s leftovers pile up, where its history is layered, and which, like any heap large enough, heats from within and can flare. The James Webb Space Telescope has found central objects already enormous a few hundred million years after the beginning, too early to have grown from stellar seeds, and astronomers now consider that the two kinds may form by different routes. On our reading they are not two sizes of one thing. They are a grave and a midden.

We do not know what these objects are inside. Nobody does. The thesis claims only that a dense, gathering object accounts for every observation in section 2, and that the hole accounts for no observation the dense object does not.

## 6. Why the story holds

> Why does science keep serving phony Kool-Aid?

If so little of the story is observed, why is it taught as fact? We offer suggested causes, not accusations.

**The equation came first.** When the evidence arrived in the 1960s and 1970s, it was poured into a picture that had been waiting since 1916. Evidence that arrives into an existing picture is read as confirming it.

**Certainty was borrowed.** The mathematics of general relativity is exact. Its certainty belongs to what we invented, the equations, and it was lent to what we observe, the objects. A solution that is exact on paper came to sound like a description that is exact in nature.

**Careers live inside the hole.** Whole fields, information paradoxes, horizon thermodynamics and the holographic programs built on them, take the interior as their starting point. Nobody saws off the branch he is sitting on.

**The story sells.** A place where time stops fills lecture halls, documentaries and grant committees in a way that a dense, dark object never will.

**Doubt looks like ignorance.** After sixty years of textbooks, questioning the hole sounds like failing to understand it. That is the most effective protection any idea can have, and it has nothing to do with evidence.

The public is not to blame. It was handed the cup and told it was science.

## 7. Supporting witnesses

> Criticism is fair. Controversy is destructive.

The thesis is our own. Several lines of work support parts of it.

**Einstein.** His 1939 paper in the _Annals of Mathematics_ argued that the Schwarzschild radius could not be reached by real matter, because the particles of a collapsing cluster would need to move faster than light to stay in orbit there. The argument was later judged incomplete, but Einstein’s instinct, that nature does not make holes, is the instinct of this paper.

**Horizonless compact objects.** A substantial literature, reviewed by Vitor Cardoso and Paolo Pani in 2019, studies dense objects that look like black holes from outside but have no horizon. Pawel Mazur and Emil Mottola’s gravastar (2001) replaces the interior with a region of vacuum energy surrounded by a thin shell of matter. Samir Mathur’s fuzzballs (2005) replace the horizon and singularity with a tangle of strings. Boson stars are made of a dense field with no surface at all. These proposals differ from ours and from each other, but together they establish that a dense object without a hole can reproduce what telescopes see from outside.

**Accretion astronomy.** The astronomers who model what is actually observed, gas falling, heating, radiating and being ejected, work almost entirely outside the horizon. Their models describe gathering. They need the interior for nothing.

## 8. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: no light from a surface.** This is the strongest evidence for a horizon, and we state it at full strength. If the object at the center of our galaxy had a surface, gas falling onto it would release its energy there, and the surface would glow. In 2009 Avery Broderick, Abraham Loeb and Ramesh Narayan used the measured size of Sagittarius A* and limits on its infrared light to show that any such surface emits less than 0.4 percent of the energy released by the gas falling in. For a surface to stay that dark, the gas would have to send more than 99.6 percent of its energy somewhere else before landing. They concluded that the observations all but require a horizon.

_Reply._ The argument assumes that what lands on a surface is turned into heat and radiated in a steady state, as it would be on a star. A surface lying just outside the critical radius would send its light out through such a steep gradient that the light would be stretched and delayed enormously, and the steady state might take longer to reach than the age of the universe. Proponents of horizonless objects have made this argument for their own models. The thesis adds a second possibility: in a material medium, matter reaching extreme density may be returned to the medium rather than heated, as a knot unwinds rather than burns. Neither answer has been calculated for our picture. The objection stands as the main open account of this paper. _Pending._

**Objection 2: the images match the predictions.** The rings imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope have the sizes general relativity predicts for black holes of the measured masses.

_Reply._ The ring is light orbiting and escaping just outside the critical radius. Any object compact enough to have such orbits casts a similar shadow, hole or no hole. The images test the shape of the space outside the object, which the thesis does not dispute. They do not see inside it.

**Objection 3: the ringing after mergers.** When two dense objects merge, the new object settles with a characteristic ringing in its gravitational waves. The observed ringing matches the predictions for a hole. Some horizonless models predict faint later echoes, and claims to have found them, beginning with Jahed Abedi, Hannah Dykaar and Niayesh Afshordi in 2017, have not been confirmed.

_Reply._ The main ringing is set by the space just outside the object and is shared by any compact enough object. Echoes depend on what lies inside, and their size depends on the model. Their absence rules out some horizonless models, not all of them, and the detectors are improving.

**Objection 4: the singularity theorems.** Penrose proved in 1965 that collapse past a certain point must end in a singularity.

_Reply._ Under general relativity, applied all the way to infinite density, and with assumptions about the energy of matter. The theorems show where general relativity stops being able to describe a collapse. They do not show what nature does when it reaches that point, any more than a calculator’s error message shows that division by zero produces something.

**Objection 5: “dense object” says nothing.** A hole is a precise model. A dense object of unknown structure is not.

_Reply._ Precision about the unobservable is not a virtue. The thesis makes a definite negative claim, no hole and no singularity, a definite role, gathering toward release, and definite tests. What the object is inside lies behind an SOB, and we say so.

## 9. Predictions and tests

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

1. **No evaporation, ever.** The thesis predicts that no Hawking radiation will ever be found, from any object, because there is no horizon to produce it. The prediction is safe from refutation for large objects, which are too cold to detect. It becomes testable if small dense objects, such as primordial ones from the early universe, are ever found: their predicted final bursts would not occur.
2. **Echoes and departures in the ringing.** As gravitational-wave detectors improve, the settling of merged objects should eventually show structure that a hole does not produce: faint echoes, or small departures from the hole’s predicted tones. The thesis predicts that some departure will be found.
3. **Shadows that differ.** In a material medium the shape of space very close to the object need not match general relativity exactly. The next generation of the Event Horizon Telescope should measure the shadows of M87 and Sagittarius A* precisely enough to detect a difference of a few percent.
4. **The record of gathering.** The thesis treats these objects as stores of gathered mass and heat. It predicts that their growth histories, measured across cosmic time, will show them gaining mass steadily by accretion and merger, with nothing ever lost, and that the largest of them sit in the regions of the universe where gathering has gone on longest.
5. **Release at the largest scale.** If these objects are the quiet phase of eruptions, then somewhere, at some time, gathered mass at extreme density lets go on a large scale. We do not expect to see it, and we will not be here when it happens. The prediction is recorded for the sake of completeness and labeled honestly: it lies behind an SOB of time. _Pending._

## 10. Conclusion

> Whatever it is, we won’t be here to see it. That counts for something.

Everything astronomers have observed about the objects called black holes describes a dense, dark mass and the matter around it: stars racing around an unseen center, mass packed tighter than anything else known, rings of light around dark middles, jets thousands of light-years long, and ripples from merging pairs. Matter is drawn in and heated, much of it turns to light, some is thrown back out, and the rest stays on as weight.

The hole, the one-way door, the interior where space becomes time, the singularity and the evaporation are all inferred from an equation that came fifty years before the evidence, and three of them can never be observed. We have proposed that the objects are what the evidence shows: the densest gatherings of matter in nature, and the gathering stroke of a recycling universe. They come in two kinds, and we have named them: the galactic accumulator, a midden that gathers and flares, and the collapsed stellar core, a grave. We have one serious open account, the darkness of the center of our own galaxy, and we have said so.

What seems clearly not right is a description that tells us more about the inside of these objects than about anything we can see. The better question is not what happens to information that falls into a hole. It is what the object is, if the hole was only ever a word.

Never seen, never proven and far from convincing.

the-smooth-universe-is-an-assumption:
## Abstract

Modern cosmology assumes that on the largest scales the universe is the same everywhere and in every direction. The assumption, called the cosmological principle, was not discovered. It was chosen in the 1920s because Einstein’s equations could not otherwise be solved for the whole universe, and it was given its name in the 1930s. We argue that it combines two claims of very different standing. The first, that our observable patch looks even when averaged over large enough volumes, can be tested, and the tests are mixed. The second, that everything beyond the edge of what we can see resembles what is inside it, can never be tested, because the edge is an SOB, a scientific observational boundary.

We review the evidence that is straining the first claim: structures larger than the model allows, a dipole in the distribution of distant quasars twice the size the model predicts, and a persistent disagreement between measurements of the expansion rate. We argue that averaging, which makes the universe look smooth, is a bookkeeping method, and that cosmology has forgotten it chose the method. We propose instead a universe that is lumpy and in motion at every scale we can see, lawful in its overall patterns and random in its particulars, the way a sandpile or an earthquake record is.

## 1. Introduction

> All laws are situational, not universal.

Ask an astronomer what the universe is and the answer comes without hesitation: 13.8 billion years old, expanding and speeding up, five percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter, 68 percent dark energy, and smooth on the largest scales. Then look up. Nothing is smooth. Stars cluster in galaxies, galaxies in clusters, and clusters string along filaments around voids hundreds of millions of light-years across, all of it spinning, falling and colliding.

The standard answer is that the lumps disappear when averaged over large enough volumes, the way the ocean looks flat from orbit even in a gale. Every number in the astronomer’s answer depends on that averaging. The age, the expansion rate and the proportions of dark matter and dark energy are all parameters of a model that begins by assuming smoothness.

Our thesis is that **the smooth universe is an assumption that has forgotten it is one.** It was adopted to make the mathematics solvable. Part of it can be tested, and the tests are increasingly unfriendly. The rest can never be tested at all. What the evidence describes is a universe lumpy and in motion at every scale we can see, lawful in pattern and random in detail.

Section 2 shows how smoothness was chosen. Section 3 separates its testable and untestable parts. Section 4 reviews the cracks, and section 5 the averaging problem. Section 6 states the thesis. Sections 7 to 9 call witnesses, meet objections and propose tests.

## 2. How smoothness was chosen

> Prediction does not equal truth. It’s local and non-transferable.

In 1917 Einstein applied general relativity to the universe as a whole for the first time. To make the problem tractable he assumed matter was spread evenly, and to keep the universe from moving he added a constant to his equations. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann, and in 1927 Georges Lemaître, solved the equations for an evenly filled universe that expands or contracts. In full generality the equations could not be solved for the real distribution of matter. With the universe made the same everywhere and in every direction, they could.

In the 1930s the British astrophysicist Edward Milne gave the assumption its name, the cosmological principle. A convenience became a foundation. Every later cosmological model, including the current standard model, is built on the Friedmann-Lemaître solutions, and every number it produces assumes the universe is smooth on average.

The point is not that Friedmann and Lemaître were wrong to make the assumption. Simplifying to make a problem solvable is how physics gets started. The point is that the simplification was made for the sake of the mathematics, not because anyone had measured the universe and found it smooth. A tool chosen for convenience has hardened, over a century, into a description of nature.

## 3. Two claims in one

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

The cosmological principle bundles two claims, and they deserve to be judged separately.

**The testable claim: our patch is even on average.** Inside the observable universe, the region light has had time to cross, we can count galaxies and measure the background radiation. Here the evidence is real and some of it supports smoothness. The microwave background arrives at the same temperature from every direction to about one part in a hundred thousand. In 2012 Morag Scrimgeour and colleagues counted galaxies in the WiggleZ survey and found that above about 70 to 80 megaparsecs per h, roughly 300 million light-years, the counts grow with volume as an even distribution requires. We accept that evidence. It shows that our patch, averaged on those scales and by those methods, looks even. Section 4 shows that other evidence points the other way.

**The untestable claim: everything beyond looks like here.** Beyond the edge of the observable universe no instrument will ever reach. The edge is an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. The cosmological principle asserts that what lies beyond resembles what lies within. No observation can confirm or refute that, ever. It is the biggest assumption in science, painted on the biggest wall.

Even within the patch, there is a subtler limit. We see the universe only along the paths light has taken to reach us, looking back in time as we look out in distance. George Ellis pointed out decades ago that from a single vantage point, a universe that is smooth everywhere cannot be fully distinguished from one that merely looks the same in every direction from where we stand. Cosmology resolves the ambiguity by assuming we occupy no special place. That is a reasonable assumption. It is still an assumption.

## 4. The cracks

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

**Structures too big.** In a smooth universe built by the standard model, nothing should be much larger than about 1.2 billion light-years. In 2021 Alexia Lopez, then a doctoral student at the University of Central Lancashire, reported the Giant Arc, a crescent of galaxies about 3.3 billion light-years long. In 2024 she reported the Big Ring, about 1.3 billion light-years across. Earlier, astronomers mapping gamma-ray bursts had claimed a structure, the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, spanning roughly ten billion light-years. Each claim is disputed. If any one holds, the scale at which the universe becomes even is larger than the model allows.

**A dipole too large.** The Earth moves at about 370 kilometers per second relative to the microwave background. That motion should make distant objects appear slightly more numerous in the direction we are heading, by a predictable amount. In 2021 Nathan Secrest and colleagues counted about 1.36 million quasars and found the excess more than twice as large as predicted, at a significance of 4.9 standard deviations. Either the universe is not as even as the model requires, or the rest frame of the matter differs from the rest frame of the radiation. The standard model allows neither.

**Expansion rates that disagree.** Measured from nearby supernovae, the expansion rate comes out about 9 percent higher than the rate inferred from the microwave background under the standard model. Years of checking have not closed the gap.

**Dark energy as a misreading.** In December 2024 a team led by David Wiltshire analyzed 1,535 supernovae without assuming smoothness, allowing the clock rates in empty voids and dense walls to differ. They reported that the need for dark energy disappears. The result is contested and _pending_.

**A placeholder that won’t sit still.** In March 2025 the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument reported growing evidence that dark energy changes over time. A constant that varies is a strange constant. Mustapha Ishak, one of the collaboration’s leaders, put the question plainly: “Is it just that we are missing something big in the model of our universe and we just don’t know it?”

None of these cracks is conclusive alone. Together they describe a model under strain at exactly the point where it rests on its founding assumption.

## 5. The averaging problem

> Things break and stuff happens.

At any instant every collision, every swirl and every thermal jiggle in the universe is happening at once. The universe does not pause its motion to run an average. To find smoothness, the cosmologist takes a volume of space, cancels opposing motions against each other, and averages the density until one clean number remains. Then the smooth model is fitted to the averages.

Averaging is a respectable method. Thermodynamics throws away nearly all the detail of a gas and still runs every engine on Earth. Nobody needs the path of every air molecule to forecast tomorrow’s weather. The net figure is not a lie; it is useful.

But useful is not the same as real, and in cosmology the method has a specific flaw. General relativity is not linear. The average of the solutions for a lumpy universe is not the same as the solution for the averaged universe. Ellis raised this “fitting problem” in 1984, and Thomas Buchert later showed that the difference, called backreaction, can in principle mimic an acceleration of the expansion. How large the effect is in the real universe is disputed. That it exists is not.

There is also a problem of time. A spiral galaxy looks serene only because it takes hundreds of millions of years to turn. Our lives and our instruments are brief, and every image we have is a still frame of something that never stops moving. A smooth average of still frames is a portrait of our own limits as much as of the universe.

The bookkeeper is not wrong to average. He is wrong to forget that he did. When the books stop balancing, as they do at the edges of galaxies and in the expansion rate, the honest response is to suspect the method of summary. Cosmology’s response has been to add entries, dark matter and dark energy, until the ledger closes.

## 6. The thesis

> Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

We propose that the universe is lumpy and in motion at every scale we can observe, and that its regularity lies in its patterns, not in its smoothness. Three claims make up the thesis.

1. **Lawful in pattern, random in detail.** In 1987 Per Bak and his colleagues showed that a pile of sand fed one grain at a time organizes itself into a critical state in which avalanches of every size occur, many small and few large, in fixed proportions. No one can predict the next avalanche, yet the distribution of all of them follows a strict law. Earthquakes follow the same kind of law, as Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter found in the 1940s, and so do solar flares. We propose that the distribution of matter in the universe is of this kind: no scale at which it becomes featureless, but a statistical regularity across scales. The regularity is real and can be measured. The smoothness is a product of the averaging.
2. **Structure made by the engine.** In our companion paper The Exhaust Stroke we describe the universe as a recycling engine whose two strokes are gathering, which we call gravity, and dispersal, which thermodynamics calls entropy. An engine of that kind does not settle into evenness. Gathering makes walls and clusters, dispersal empties voids, and the pattern is renewed continually. A lumpy, moving universe is what the engine predicts.
3. **The ongoing event.** The standard account treats the Big Bang as something that happened, safely in the past, after which the universe settled. On the thesis there is no settling. Every atom of ordinary matter is still in motion from that event, and what we call different scales are different sizes of the same churning. We are not living after the Big Bang. We are living in it.

The thesis keeps the evidence of section 3. Our patch, averaged at around 300 million light-years, looks even by the counts that have been made. The thesis reads that as a property of the averaging scale and the survey, not as proof that the universe is smooth beyond it. _Pending._

## 7. Supporting witnesses

> Criticism is fair. Controversy is destructive.

The thesis is our own. These witnesses support parts of it.

**The fractal school.** In the late 1980s Luciano Pietronero and colleagues argued that galaxies are distributed as a fractal, with no scale at which they become even. Francesco Sylos Labini and others pressed the case through the 1990s. Larger surveys since then have found a transition toward evenness, so the strong form of their claim is out of favor. Their weaker point, that the universe is clumpy far beyond the scales once assumed and that homogeneity must be shown rather than assumed, has been borne out.

**The averaging critics.** George Ellis framed the fitting problem in 1984, and Thomas Buchert built a formal theory of how averaging a lumpy universe alters its apparent expansion. David Wiltshire’s timescape model, developed from 2007, treats the voids and walls of the real universe separately and finds that much of the apparent acceleration can come from the difference.

**Simulations without the assumption.** Since 2016, groups led by Eloisa Bentivegna and Marco Bruni, and by James Mertens, John Giblin and Glenn Starkman, have run the full equations of general relativity on lumpy model universes without assuming smoothness. The method exists. Cosmology no longer needs the assumption for want of tools.

**The anomaly hunters.** The Planck satellite’s own team catalogued features of the microwave background that sit uneasily with perfect isotropy, among them a large cold spot and a difference in power between two halves of the sky. Each is modest in significance. Together with the quasar dipole, they form a pattern that perfect smoothness does not predict.

## 8. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: the microwave background is smooth to one part in a hundred thousand.** That is the most even thing ever measured, and it comes from every direction.

_Reply._ It shows that the radiation reaching us is nearly the same in every direction. That is isotropy around one point, ours. Homogeneity, sameness everywhere, follows only with the added assumption that we occupy no special place. The radiation also dates from an early epoch, before most of the structure we see had formed. A smooth early universe does not make a smooth present one.

**Objection 2: homogeneity has been measured.** Galaxy surveys such as WiggleZ find the transition to evenness at about 300 million light-years.

_Reply._ They find it within our patch, by a particular counting method, over the volume surveyed. The same patch contains the Giant Arc, the Big Ring and the quasar dipole, which the transition at that scale does not allow. Two sets of measurements disagree, and the disagreement is evidence.

**Objection 3: the big structures are statistical flukes.** In a large enough survey some apparent structures will appear by chance, and several of the claimed giants have been challenged on those grounds.

_Reply._ A fair point, and the reason we call each claim disputed. The dipole is not a structure of that kind; it is a count over more than a million objects across the whole sky.

**Objection 4: the standard model fits the data superbly.** It fits the microwave background, the clustering of galaxies and the supernovae with six parameters.

_Reply._ It fits them with about 95 percent of the universe in components nobody has detected. A fit is not a description. Ptolemy’s model predicted the planets for some 1,400 years. When Copernicus’s book appeared in 1543, an unsigned preface told readers its ideas need not be true, only useful for calculation. “It works” justifies a tool. It does not justify a story.

**Objection 5: without smoothness there is no cosmology.** The assumption is what makes the subject possible.

_Reply._ That was true in 1922. It is not true now. Numerical relativity can evolve lumpy universes directly, and statistical physics can describe systems that are regular in pattern without being smooth. A cosmology of patterns is harder than a cosmology of averages. It is not impossible, and it would be honest about what it assumes.

## 9. Predictions and tests

> If science can read the stars, it ought to be able to sense the wind.

1. **Bigger structures will keep turning up.** As the Euclid mission, the Rubin Observatory and DESI map larger volumes, the thesis predicts more structures exceeding the standard model’s size limit, and fewer of them explained away.
2. **The scale of evenness will grow with the survey.** If the universe is regular in pattern but not smooth, the scale at which it appears even will depend on the volume and method used. The thesis predicts that larger, deeper surveys will place the transition at larger scales, or fail to find a stable one.
3. **The dipole will hold.** The thesis predicts that the excess dipole found in quasars will be confirmed with independent tracers, such as radio galaxies, and that it will not shrink to the size predicted by our motion alone.
4. **The expansion rate will depend on direction.** If the universe is lumpy on large scales, the local expansion rate should differ measurably between directions, and the disagreement between expansion rates should prove to be partly a matter of where one looks.
5. **Averaging will account for part of the acceleration.** Analyses that drop the smoothness assumption, such as the timescape model and numerical relativity, will find that part of the apparent acceleration of the expansion comes from averaging a lumpy universe. Our companion paper The Exhaust Stroke attributes the rest to the net of dispersal over gathering.

## 10. Conclusion

> Respect the wall. Question the ghost.

The smooth universe was adopted in the 1920s because the equations needed it, named in the 1930s and built upon ever since. It has two parts. The part that can be tested, that our patch looks even when averaged, has support and is under growing strain: from structures too large, from a dipole too strong and from expansion rates that will not agree. The part that cannot be tested, that the universe beyond the edge resembles our patch, lies behind an SOB and will stay there.

We have proposed that the universe is lumpy and moving at every observable scale, regular in its patterns and random in its details, like a sandpile or an earthquake record, and kept in motion by the gathering and dispersing of its matter. The proposal asks cosmology to do something harder than averaging. It also asks cosmology to stop presenting a convenience as a discovery.

What seems clearly not right is a model whose founding assumption is untestable in principle and whose fit requires 95 percent of the universe to be invisible. The better question is not how smooth the universe is. It is what we would see if we stopped averaging it into smoothness.

The smooth universe is the biggest ghost on the biggest wall in science.

the-exhaust-stroke-cosmic-expansion-as-n:
## Abstract

We propose that the accelerating expansion of the universe needs no dark energy. It is the residue of a recycling process with two strokes. In the dispersal stroke, which thermodynamics records as rising entropy, bound matter is broken down and released as radiation, outflows and decay products. In the gathering stroke, which we call gravity, diffuse matter is drawn back into bound structures. We begin from a premise developed elsewhere in our work: space is a material medium, and particles are its excitations. On that premise, dispersal does more than spread matter out. It returns matter to the medium and adds to it. When dispersal outruns gathering, the medium grows, and a growing medium is what an observer records as expansion.

The thesis accounts for when the acceleration began, about four billion years after cosmic star formation peaked, and it predicts that the acceleration should weaken as star formation declines, which is the trend the 2025 DESI results hint at. It also removes the need for a cosmological constant and replaces the heat death with a cycle. Its main weakness is quantitative: on standard accounting the radiation emitted by stars is far too small to drive the expansion. We state this objection in full, identify what the thesis would need in order to answer it, and propose tests that do not depend on settling it first.

## 1. Introduction

> Prediction does not equal truth. It’s local and non-transferable.

In 1998 two teams measuring distant supernovae found them dimmer than a decelerating universe allowed. The expansion of the universe, they concluded, has been speeding up. The standard account attributes the speed-up to dark energy, a property of empty space that makes up about 68 percent of the cosmic energy budget. Nobody has detected it directly, and nobody knows what it is. Its simplest form, Einstein’s cosmological constant, is the quantity that quantum field theory overpredicts by roughly 120 orders of magnitude.

The account has two further problems, and both bear on the thesis of this paper. The first is timing. Dark energy is said to have been present all along, yet it took over from matter only in the last six billion years or so. Physicists call this the coincidence problem: why should the take-over happen in the epoch when observers exist to see it? The second is the ending. If dark energy is constant and entropy only rises, the universe ends cold, dark and even, the heat death that William Thomson foresaw in 1852. That ending is a forecast for an object nobody has watched finish anything.

We propose a different reading of the same evidence. Entropy and gravity are two strokes of one engine. Entropy is the dispersal stroke: stars burn, solids break down, atoms decay, and bound matter is released into the surrounding medium as radiation and loose particles. Gravity is the gathering stroke: diffuse matter falls back into stars, galaxies and the dense objects at galactic centers. Given a material space, the dispersal stroke adds to the medium. Our thesis is that **cosmic expansion is the net of dispersal over gathering**: where the universe releases more than it gathers, the medium grows, and the growth is what we measure as expansion.

The paper sets out the premises (section 2), describes the two strokes (section 3) and states the thesis (section 4). It then presents the evidence in its favor (section 5), calls its supporting witnesses (section 6), meets the main objections (section 7), lists tests (section 8) and draws the consequences for the long-run fate of the universe (section 9).

We write as natural philosophers, not as working cosmologists. The thesis is offered as a coherent alternative that fits the observations and makes predictions. Where a claim is our best guess rather than an established result, we label it _pending_.

## 2. Premises

> Space is the singular field of Reality.

The thesis rests on three premises. None is new on its own. What is new is putting them together.

**Premise 1: space is a material medium.** Empty space reacts. It carries light at a fixed speed set by its electric and magnetic properties. Quantum field theory credits it with a zero-point energy and with fluctuations that have measurable effects, such as the Casimir force between uncharged plates. Something that reacts is something. We take the vacuum to be the most common substance there is, not a stage on which substances perform. This is close to the nineteenth-century ether, with one difference: the ether was a medium matter moved through, while ours is the medium matter is made of. Hendrik Lorentz showed in the 1900s that a medium of that kind can reproduce the predictions of special relativity, because motion through it hides its own wind. Physics chose Einstein’s geometric reading on grounds of economy, not because the medium was refuted.

**Premise 2: particles are excitations of the medium.** Standard field theory already says this: an electron is a quantum of the electron field, and a photon is a quantum of the electromagnetic field. We take the further step of treating the many fields as different motions of one substance. Lasting particles, the electron and the proton, are stable knots in the medium. Light is a disturbance crossing it. The short-lived particles found in colliders are splashes from knocking knots together.

**Premise 3: the medium is built up by what it carries.** This premise does the work in the thesis. Leibniz argued against Newton that space is not a container but the set of relations among things: no things, no space. In 2010 Mark Van Raamsdonk argued, in the language of quantum gravity, that connected spacetime is built from quantum entanglement among its parts, so that removing the entanglement pulls space apart. We do not adopt either position whole. We take from both the idea that the extent of space is not fixed in advance but depends on what is in it. Matter woven tight in knots contributes little to the extent of the medium. Matter released into free radiation and loose particles contributes more. The medium grows by what is let loose in it.

Premise 3 is the least established of the three. It is also the one the thesis needs. We return to it under the objections in section 7.

## 3. Two strokes

> Things break and stuff happens.

**Dispersal.** Over cosmic time, most of what happens to bound matter loosens it. Stars fuse hydrogen and radiate away about 0.7 percent of the mass they burn. The Sun alone turns about four million tonnes of itself into light every second and sheds more as solar wind. Supernovae blow the outer layers of stars back into interstellar space. Galactic winds and the jets from active galactic nuclei drive gas out of galaxies altogether. Radioactive nuclei break into lighter pieces. Solids weather into dust and dust into gas. On paper, even black holes eventually evaporate into radiation. Thermodynamics records all of this as rising entropy: the same energy spread over more ways of being arranged.

**Gathering.** Gravity runs the other way. Diffuse gas cools and falls into clouds, clouds collapse into stars, galaxies merge into larger galaxies, and the massive dark objects at galactic centers gather gas and stars and grow. The four million solar masses at the center of our own galaxy, and the billions of solar masses at the centers of giant ellipticals, are gathering’s largest products.

**How the books are kept.** The standard account counts gathering as an increase of entropy too. A collapsing cloud heats up and radiates, and the radiation carries away more entropy than the clump loses. Roger Penrose argued in 1979 that gravitating systems reverse the usual rule, so that a smooth gas has _low_ gravitational entropy and a clumped one has high entropy, with a black hole the most entropic object of all. That bookkeeping is internally consistent. It also blurs a physical difference that the thesis depends on. Matter falling into a dense object is being bound. Matter leaving a star as light is being released. Whatever number the ledger assigns to each, the two processes move matter in opposite directions: one into knots, the other out of them.

We therefore use plain names for the two flows and avoid the word entropy where it would hide the distinction:

- **Dispersal rate, D:** the rate at which bound matter is released into the medium as radiation, outflow or decay, per unit of cosmic volume.
- **Gathering rate, G:** the rate at which diffuse matter is bound into structures, by accretion, collapse or merger, per unit of cosmic volume.

The two are coupled. Gathering builds the stars whose burning is the main source of dispersal, and dispersal supplies the gas that gathering collects again. The coupling is what makes the system a recycling engine and not a one-way slide.

## 4. The thesis

> The power stroke and the exhaust stroke, entropy and gravity: a recycling system.

**Statement.** Over any region large enough to be typical of the universe, the rate at which the medium grows is set by the excess of dispersal over gathering. Expansion is that growth as an observer records it. Where dispersal and gathering balance, the universe coasts on the momentum of its early state. Where gathering wins, the expansion is braked. Where dispersal wins, the expansion runs faster than coasting would allow, which is what the supernova teams saw in 1998.

**Schematic form.** Let V be the volume of a typical region, so that the expansion rate is H = V̇/3V. The thesis says:

%% V̇ / 3V = H~c~(t) + κ [ D(t) − G(t) ]

Here H~c~ is the coasting rate, the rate a universe would have if nothing were added to or taken from its medium. In Edward Milne’s coasting model of the 1930s it falls as one over cosmic time. κ is a coupling constant that converts net release into growth of the medium. D and G are the dispersal and gathering rates of section 3. The relation is schematic. It fixes the sign and the history of the effect, not its size: κ is unknown, and section 7 explains why its size is the hardest part of the problem.

**What it replaces.** In the standard model the expansion history is governed by three ingredients: matter, which brakes; radiation, which brakes harder; and dark energy, a constant push. In the thesis, the push is not constant. It is a running account of what the universe’s structures are doing, and it rises and falls with them.

**Why the lag matters.** Gathering and dispersal do not peak together. Gas is gathered into a star in a few million years, but a star releases what it holds over its whole life, which for a star like the Sun is about ten billion years. Stars are delayed-release devices. A universe that formed most of its stars in a burst would therefore see gathering fall off first and dispersal persist, so that the net would turn from negative to positive some billions of years after the burst. Section 5 compares that expectation with the record.

## 5. Evidence and consistency

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

**The timing.** The history of cosmic star formation is now well measured. In their 2014 review, Piero Madau and Mark Dickinson found that the rate peaked about 3.5 billion years after the Big Bang, at redshift 1.9, and has declined exponentially since, falling by a factor of e every 3.9 billion years. The rate today is roughly a tenth of the peak. The expansion, meanwhile, switched from slowing to speeding up at a redshift of roughly 0.6 to 0.8, some seven to eight billion years after the Big Bang. The acceleration therefore began about four billion years after the peak of star formation. That is the lag section 4 expects from stars acting as delayed-release devices: gathering fell off with the decline of star formation, while the stars already formed went on releasing what they held.

**The coincidence problem.** On the standard account it is an unexplained accident that dark energy took over in the epoch when observers exist. On the thesis it is not an accident at all. Observers are built from carbon, oxygen and iron, which only exist after generations of stars have formed, burned and dispersed. Acceleration also requires generations of stars that have formed and are dispersing. Both are products of the same stellar era, so they appear together for the same reason.

**The early braking.** Before the switch, the expansion was slowing. The standard account puts this down to the gravity of matter. The thesis says the same thing in its own terms: the first several billion years were the great age of gathering, when gas fell into halos, galaxies assembled and the star-forming burst was being fueled. Gathering exceeded dispersal, and the net braked the expansion.

**A push that changes.** If the thesis is right, the push behind the acceleration cannot be constant. It must follow the net of dispersal over gathering, and with star formation now at a tenth of its peak, it should be weakening. In March 2025 the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) released its second set of results. On their own, the DESI measurements fit a constant dark energy. Combined with the cosmic microwave background and supernova data, they favored a dark energy whose strength has been declining in recent cosmic time, at a significance the collaboration put between 2.8 and 4.2 standard deviations depending on the supernova sample. That is short of discovery, and it may yet fade. But the direction of the hint is the direction the thesis requires, and a constant does not. _Pending._

**The same everywhere.** Expansion is observed to be nearly uniform on large scales, including across the great voids, where there are few stars. That might seem to tie the growth of the medium to where the stars are. It does not, because what stars release does not stay with them. Starlight from every galaxy that has ever shone fills all of space, including the voids, as the extragalactic background light. The release happens in galaxies; the addition to the medium happens everywhere the released light and matter go.

**Growing and thinning.** In earlier work we suggested that redshift may partly reflect a medium that was denser in the past and has been thinning since. The thesis is consistent with that. Smoke from a fire spreads over a larger and larger volume even as each part of it grows thinner. A medium can grow in extent and fall in density at the same time, provided its extent grows faster than its content.

**The first and greatest release.** One further pattern is suggestive. The largest dispersal event in cosmic history was the earliest: the annihilation of matter and antimatter, which left about a billion photons for every surviving particle of matter. That event coincides with the period of fastest expansion in the universe’s history. The standard account explains the early expansion by other means, and we do not claim the coincidence as proof. We note only that the two greatest episodes of release, the annihilation at the start and the stellar era now, line up with the two episodes in which the expansion ran fastest. _Pending._

## 6. Supporting witnesses

> Criticism is fair. Controversy is destructive.

The thesis is our own. Five lines of work stand as witnesses to parts of it, and none of them puts the parts together.

**Expansion as the emergence of space.** The nearest relative is Thanu Padmanabhan’s 2012 proposal that cosmic space is not a pre-existing arena but something that emerges as cosmic time proceeds. In his model the volume of the observable universe grows at a rate set by the difference between the number of degrees of freedom on its boundary and the number in its bulk, a relation he wrote as dV/dt = N_sur − N_bulk in natural units. He showed that this “quest for holographic equipartition” reproduces the standard expansion history, including the late acceleration. Padmanabhan’s growth is driven by a mismatch in the accounting of information. Ours is driven by a physical process, the release of bound matter into the medium. The two share the central move: the expansion is the medium coming into being, and its rate is set by an imbalance.

**Steady state.** In 1948 Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle proposed that matter is continuously created as the universe expands, so that its density never changes. The thesis is the steady state turned inside out. Hoyle had new matter appearing to fill expanding space; we have released matter making new space. The steady state was sunk in 1965 by the microwave background, which shows the universe had a hot, dense past. The thesis has no quarrel with that past.

**Black holes coupled to expansion.** In 2023 Duncan Farrah and colleagues reported that the central black holes of elliptical galaxies appear to have grown in mass faster than accretion can explain, in step with the expansion, and proposed that such black holes could be the source of dark energy. Their claim has been contested, and the evidence is not settled. It shares with the thesis the idea that the push behind the acceleration comes from the universe’s structures rather than from empty space, but it puts the source in the gathered objects, where we put it in the released matter.

**Gravity from thermodynamics.** In 1995 Ted Jacobson derived Einstein’s field equations from the thermodynamics of local horizons, treating them as an equation of state. In 2011 Erik Verlinde proposed that gravity is an entropic force. Both tie gravity and entropy closer than the standard account does. Neither treats them as opposing strokes of a cycle, which is our proposal.

**Expansion without dark energy.** Several programs explain the acceleration without a new substance. The backreaction approach, developed by Thomas Buchert and others, and David Wiltshire’s timescape model argue that averaging over a lumpy universe produces an apparent acceleration. In December 2024 a team led by Wiltshire reported that the timescape model fits a large sample of 1,535 supernovae better than the standard model does. These programs share our view that the acceleration is a product of structure, not of empty space, though they locate the effect in how observers average rather than in what the medium does.

## 7. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: the energy is far too small.** This is the strongest objection, and we state it at full strength. All the starlight ever emitted, the extragalactic background light, has a total intensity of about 100 nanowatts per square meter per steradian, roughly a tenth of the microwave background. Only a few percent of the universe’s ordinary matter has ever been fused in stars, and fusion releases 0.7 percent of the mass fused. The energy released by all the stars in history therefore comes to roughly one part in a hundred thousand of the cosmic energy budget. Dark energy is about 68 percent of it. On any accounting in which the push behind the expansion is measured in energy, stellar dispersal falls short by a factor of about a hundred thousand.

_Reply._ The objection is decisive within general relativity, where the expansion responds to the energy and pressure of what space contains and space itself contributes nothing. The thesis rejects that premise. On premise 3 the quantity that matters is how much medium is produced when bound matter is released, and the energy carried off is only one measure of that. In the schematic relation this is the coupling κ. For the thesis to work, κ must be very large: a small release of energy must yield a large growth of the medium. We do not have a theory of the medium that fixes κ, and we will not pretend to. Counting quanta instead of energy does not rescue the thesis either. A star turns each fusion’s energy into millions of low-energy photons, but the number of starlight photons is still tiny beside the number of photons in the microwave background. The honest position is that the thesis needs a large coupling, that this is a demand on any future theory of the medium, and that the tests in section 8 can be run without knowing κ in advance.

**Objection 2: radiation brakes the expansion.** In general relativity, radiation has positive pressure and slows the expansion harder than matter does. Releasing matter as light should make the universe decelerate, not accelerate.

_Reply._ That follows from the same premise as objection 1, that the expansion is a response to what space contains. The thesis says the expansion is the growth of what space is. General relativity is untouched where it has been tested: in the solar system, in binary pulsars and in merging black holes, all of them bound systems where gathering dominates. The thesis departs from it only at the scale of the whole universe, which is also where its predictions have needed dark energy and dark matter to fit the data.

**Objection 3: something from nothing.** If the medium grows, where does the new medium come from?

_Reply._ From the released matter. Nothing is created. On premise 3, the extent of the medium depends on what is loose in it, so matter going from bound to loose adds to the extent without adding any new substance. It is worth noting that the standard account has no better answer here. In general relativity, energy is not conserved globally in an expanding universe, and a constant dark energy means that ever more of it fills ever more space.

**Objection 4: why don’t galaxies and solar systems expand?** If release grows the medium, the Milky Way, which is full of shining stars, should swell.

_Reply._ It does not, for the same reason it does not swell on the standard account: within bound systems, gathering dominates. The growth the thesis describes is a net effect, visible only at scales where the books are averaged over released light crossing empty voids. Inside a galaxy, gravity’s grip far exceeds any local addition to the medium.

**Objection 5: the microwave background and the baryon acoustic scale.** The standard model fits the detailed pattern of the microwave background and the scale of baryon acoustic oscillations with great precision. Any rival must match both.

_Reply._ In the early universe the thesis and the standard model agree: a hot, dense, expanding state, with stars not yet formed and the dispersal term negligible apart from the annihilation era. The pattern in the background is set in that era. What depends on the later history is the distance to the background, which the thesis must reproduce through its own late-time expansion history. Whether a push that rises and falls with the stellar era can match that distance as well as a constant does is the first calculation a serious test would need. DESI’s preference for a declining push suggests it may. _Pending._

**Objection 6: a free parameter can fit anything.** A coupling chosen to match the observed acceleration explains nothing.

_Reply._ κ is fixed once, by the size of the acceleration today. After that the thesis has no freedom left. The shape of the expansion history in time is fixed by the measured histories of star formation and gas accretion, which are observed independently of cosmology. If the shape is wrong, the thesis is wrong. That is a stronger test than a cosmological constant faces, since a constant has nothing to fit except its one value.

## 8. Predictions and tests

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

The thesis stands or falls on the shape of the expansion history, and that shape can be predicted from data gathered without any cosmological assumption. Five tests follow.

1. **The push follows the stars.** Build the net release history of the universe from independent astronomical records: the star formation history, the rate at which aging stars return mass to space, the output of active galactic nuclei, and the rate at which galaxies accrete gas. Fix κ once with today’s acceleration. The thesis predicts the whole history of the effective push from that one curve. If DESI, the Euclid mission and the Rubin Observatory’s supernova survey reconstruct a push whose rise and fall does not match the release history, the thesis is refuted.
2. **The switch matches the crossover.** The expansion should have changed from braking to pushing when the net release history crossed from negative to positive. The crossover can be computed from galaxy surveys alone. The thesis predicts it at a redshift of roughly 0.6 to 0.8, where the switch is observed.
3. **The push is weakening, and will go on weakening.** Star formation is now a tenth of its peak and still falling. The thesis predicts that the effective push has passed its maximum and is declining. DESI’s 2025 results lean that way. Its final results, and Euclid’s, should strengthen the trend if the thesis is right and erase it if a constant is.
4. **The chemistry keeps time.** Every heavy element in the universe was made by stars and released by them. The cumulative production of heavy elements is therefore an independent record of the dispersal stroke. The thesis predicts that the expansion’s extra push tracks the growth of cosmic metallicity, with the lag set by the lifetimes of the stars that do the releasing.
5. **No push inside bound systems.** The thesis predicts no anomalous expansion within galaxies, groups or bound clusters, where gathering dominates. Any detected local effect of that kind would count against it.

One further question is worth checking, though we do not make it a test. The expansion rate measured nearby is higher than the rate inferred from the microwave background under the standard model, the so-called Hubble tension. A push that arose late and was not included in the standard model’s extrapolation from the early universe could bear on that gap. Whether it narrows or widens it depends on details we have not computed. _Pending._

## 9. The recycling engine

> Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

Put the two strokes together and the universe looks less like a clock running down and more like an engine. Gathering is the power stroke: it pulls diffuse matter into stars, where it is compressed and ignited. Dispersal is the exhaust stroke: the stars release what they hold, back into the medium. The exhaust is collected again by the next round of gathering, which builds the next generation of stars from the remains of the last. Every atom of carbon in a living body has been through at least one turn of that cycle.

The standard account follows only one stroke to its end. Entropy rises, the stars burn out, and the universe finishes cold and even, with nothing left to happen. Nobody has seen a universe finish. The far future lies behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. A forecast for the far side of an SOB is a story, not an observation, and this one depends on two assumptions: that dark energy is a constant that will drive everything apart forever, and that gathering will eventually lose every contest with dispersal. The thesis removes the first, since the push weakens as the stars do. It also questions the second.

At the centers of galaxies, gathering has been winning for billions of years. The massive dark objects there accumulate gas, stars and each other, growing denser and hotter with each merger, while jets thousands of light-years long show that some of what they gather is already being thrown back. In earlier essays we read these objects not as holes but as the quiet phase of an eruption: mass piling up and heat rising until the pressure can no longer be held, in the way a geyser gathers water and heat underground between eruptions. On that reading, the end of the stellar era is not the end of the engine. Gathering continues where dispersal has faded, and what it gathers may in time be released on a scale that resembles the hot, dense state from which our own expansion began. _Pending._

This is the cosmological consequence of the thesis. The heat death is not where the evidence leads. It is where one stroke of a two-stroke engine leads if the other is left out.

## 10. Conclusion

> We can be certain of what we invent, never of what we observe.

Dark energy was introduced to explain one observation: since about six billion years ago, the expansion has been speeding up. It has never been detected, its predicted size is wrong by 120 orders of magnitude, and it cannot say why it took over when it did. We have proposed that it is not needed. If space is a material medium that grows by what is released into it, then the expansion is the net of two opposing processes that astronomers already observe and measure: the dispersal of bound matter, which thermodynamics calls entropy, and the gathering of diffuse matter, which we call gravity.

The thesis explains the timing of the acceleration as the lag between the peak of star formation and the peak of stellar release. It explains the coincidence problem by tying both observers and acceleration to the same stellar era. It predicts a push that weakens as star formation declines, which is the direction of the 2025 DESI results. And it replaces the heat death with a recycling engine.

Its debt is the coupling between release and growth. On standard accounting the energy of starlight is a hundred thousand times too small to matter, and the thesis survives that objection only by denying that energy is the right measure. That denial has to be paid for eventually by a working theory of the medium. Until then the thesis offers what a placeholder cannot: a push tied to things we can see, with a history fixed by records gathered independently, and a shape that the next generation of surveys can confirm or refute.

What seems clearly not right is an expansion driven by an ingredient nobody has found, ending in a heat death nobody can witness. The better question is not what dark energy is made of. It is whether there was ever anything there to name, or only the exhaust of the stars, adding up.
