for-its-own-sake-or-for-ours:
## Abstract

Ask what science is for and two answers come back. The older one, which we call the pack’s answer, holds that knowledge is the first line of defense, the sword and shield of survival, aimed at shelter, nutrition and connection. The newer one, which we call the answer from the full table, holds that the highest knowledge is pursued for its own sake. Through Vannevar Bush’s 1945 report, the second answer became the charter of public science funding. We argue that the two answers have produced very different records, that the institutions built on the second have properties that work against discovery, and that the public which pays has been told a simpler story than the one its money buys.

We make five arguments. Institutions are nouns, built to hold still, and discovery is a verb; they cannot schedule it, and they tend to scorn the people who produce it. Intelligent insiders become trapped in failing programs by seven ordinary mechanisms, none of which requires bad faith. Spokesmen for science present patches as discoveries, which discredits the honest work at the bench. The books of public science mix open research with secret work and industrial subsidy, so its value cannot be judged. And there are tested ways to buy more discovery for less money.

## 1. Introduction

> Hunger creates its own perspective.

Science is the most successful enterprise our species has built, and in some of its branches the most expensive. Those two facts sit uneasily together. The success is concentrated where science serves human needs: food, medicine, power and communication. Much of the expense is concentrated where it serves its own curiosity: colliders, cosmological surveys and the search for particles nobody has found.

This paper asks why, and what the public that pays is entitled to know. Our thesis is that **public science has been chartered on the answer from the full table, knowledge for its own sake, while its record of success comes overwhelmingly from the pack’s answer, knowledge for survival; and that the institutions built on the first answer have properties that impede the discovery they exist to produce.**

None of this is a case against wonder or against basic research. Wonder is real, and some of it is worth paying for. The trouble is the casual way the bill is passed to people who are never asked whether they would rather have the story or the bread. We offer suggested causes throughout, not accusations. The paper’s arguments about institutions apply to all large research enterprises, but we take most examples from physics, where the gap between cost and return is widest.

## 2. Two answers

> Knowledge is the first line of defense, the sword and shield of survival.

**The pack’s answer.** We are pack predators, and for as long as there have been bands of us, knowing things was how we stayed alive: where the water was, when the frost would come, which berry would kill. Knowledge was always aimed at the same three goals, shelter, nutrition and connection. Connection carries the other two, since nobody hunts alone or raises a roof alone, which may be why the pack’s oldest punishments go straight for it: exile forces you out, prison forces you in, and for most of our 300,000 years the last resort was to remove you from the pack for good. On this answer every discipline climbs a ladder with no ground and no ceiling, because the pack keeps needing it to. The sciences’ goals are humanity’s goals in more precise focus.

**The answer from the full table.** Around 350 BC Aristotle described the highest kind of knowing as pursued for its own sake and not for any useful end, and he was frank about when it begins: after the necessities of life have been secured. Knowledge for its own sake was born at a full table. The idea traveled well. John Henry Newman told the universities in 1852 that knowledge is “capable of being its own end.” In 1939 Abraham Flexner, founder of the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton, published “The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge.” In 1945 Vannevar Bush handed President Truman _Science, the Endless Frontier_, which defined basic research as work “performed without thought of practical ends” and argued that the government should pay for it. Much of the world’s public science funding still runs on that blueprint. Aristotle supplied the ideal, Flexner the excuse and Bush the checkbook.

**The voice that got lost.** In 1605 Francis Bacon, who did as much as anyone to shape the modern scientific method, wrote that its purpose was “the relief of man’s estate.” Science kept his method and mislaid his goal.

## 3. Nouns and verbs

> You can’t ask a noun to do a verb’s work.

**Discovery happens.** In 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to find mold killing the bacteria on a dish he had left out, and penicillin followed. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson could not get rid of a hiss in their antenna, and it turned out to be the afterglow of the early universe. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a screen glowing in his darkened laboratory and found X-rays. Breakthroughs turn up in unexpected places, with unexpected people, usually while someone is looking for something else.

**Institutions hold still.** A university, a funding agency or a national laboratory is a noun: a fixed thing, built to last and to do tomorrow what it did today. It does to discovery what language does to motion. It freezes it into a thing that can be owned. Grant applications ask researchers to describe what they will discover before they have discovered it. Five-year plans schedule breakthroughs. Progress reports count deliverables, as though insight came by the crate.

**Scorn first, dependence later.** Because the institution cannot produce what only happens, it lives off the people who can, usually after resisting them. Katalin Karikó spent years in America unable to fund her work on messenger RNA and was demoted; her work became the basis of the vaccines that ended the pandemic lockdowns, and she shared the 2023 Nobel Prize. Michael Faraday, a blacksmith’s son apprenticed to a bookbinder, was opposed for membership of the Royal Society by his own patron, Humphry Davy. Alfred Wegener was ridiculed for half a century for saying the continents move. Lynn Margulis’s paper on the origin of the cell’s power plants was rejected by about fifteen journals before it was published in 1967.

**Genius is cheap.** The patent clerk who rethought gravity did it on a clerk’s wage. The bookbinder’s apprentice needed a bench and some wire. The horse dealer’s son from Belfast, John Bell, set the terms of the deepest debate in modern physics on the side of his day job. It is the institutions that are expensive. Evolution only works with variation to select from, and an institution that crushes its misfits removes the mutations it will someday need.

## 4. The smart insider’s trap

> If mankind were perfectible, it would have happened by now.

For about fourteen hundred years, generations of brilliant astronomers in Greece, Persia, the Arab world and medieval Europe kept tuning Ptolemy’s circles on circles. Very few asked whether the Earth was in the middle at all. They were not fools. The most dangerous trap in science is not stupidity. It is intelligence, organized.

**Monetized and weaponized.** Before the Second World War, physics was a small craft of a few thousand people in university laboratories. The Manhattan Project employed about 130,000 people, cost roughly $2 billion in 1940s money and ended a war. Physics was monetized and weaponized in the same stroke and has not separated from either. Nuclear weapons knowledge is “born secret” under American law, and in 1954 Robert Oppenheimer, who had led the bomb project and later opposed the hydrogen bomb, was stripped of his security clearance. In his farewell address in 1961 President Eisenhower warned not only of the military-industrial complex but of public policy becoming “the captive of a scientific-technological elite.”

**Seven springs.** Money and secrecy do not explain everything. Dark matter and inflation belong to cosmology, which is open and has no weapons. We suggest seven ordinary mechanisms, each rational for the individual, that together make the system absurd.

1. **Sunk cost.** After fifty years and billions of dollars, quitting means admitting waste. Barry Staw showed in 1976 that people escalate their commitment to failing courses of action they chose.
2. **Identity.** A theory is a life’s work, and giving it up means saying the life was spent on the wrong thing.
3. **Safety in numbers.** John Maynard Keynes observed that it is better for one’s reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally.
4. **No exit.** A theory is abandoned only when a rival is ready, and nobody funds the rival.
5. **The institution takes over.** Organizations outlive their purposes and come to be run for their own continuation. The machine needs the next machine.
6. **Salaries.** Upton Sinclair: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it.”
7. **Intelligence makes it worse.** Studies of motivated reasoning, among them Dan Kahan’s, find that greater skill makes people better at defending what they already believe, not at changing their minds.

**A thought collective.** Ludwik Fleck’s term from 1935 describes a group whose shared way of thinking makes certain questions invisible. Harriet Zuckerman found in the 1970s that more than half of America’s Nobel laureates had trained under earlier laureates. The same schools train the leaders, who review each other’s papers and grants. That is more resistant than a conspiracy, because no one in it is doing anything wrong.

## 5. Patches, spokesmen and the bench

> Criticism is fair. Controversy is destructive.

The courts have an old rule for witnesses: _falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus_, false in one thing, false in all. It applies to deliberate falsehood, not honest error. A witness who gets a date wrong keeps his credibility. A witness who knowingly dresses up a guess as a fact loses it.

Modern physics carries four well-known failures: a prediction for the energy of empty space that misses the measured value by about 120 orders of magnitude, two measurements of the expansion rate that will not agree, galaxies that spin too fast for their visible matter, and two foundational theories that contradict each other where they meet. Each failure has been answered with a patch: dark energy, dark matter, inflation. Imre Lakatos gave the test for a patch. A healthy research program, meeting trouble, predicts something new that then checks out. A degenerating one adds a patch that predicts nothing new and plugs the hole.

The patches are then presented to the public as settled discoveries. We do not attribute this to the working physicists. It was working physicists who measured the expansion rate twice and refused to fudge the gap, and astronomers who clocked the galaxies spinning too fast. The evidence against the story comes from inside the field. The presentation comes from its spokesmen: the bestseller authors, the laboratory press offices, the documentary presenters and the grant-winning names who turn every patch into a triumph.

The cost falls on the honest witnesses. When spokesmen are caught overselling, the public’s trust in science falls, and it falls on the people at the bench who were telling the truth all along. Every time science oversells a story, it spends trust it will need later.

## 6. Two sets of books

> Often the truth doesn’t set you free. It just gets you in trouble.

Nobody can judge whether research is good value without knowing what it is for. A machine that looks like waste as physics may be excellent value as something else, or it may simply be waste. From outside, nobody can tell. We do not oppose secret science; nations have secrets, and some are worth keeping. We oppose mixed books.

**The rule on paper.** In 1985 President Reagan signed National Security Decision Directive 189, which holds that federally funded basic research should remain unrestricted “to the maximum extent possible,” and that where national security requires control, the means is classification, decided at the start. It was reaffirmed by Condoleezza Rice as National Security Advisor in 2001 and by the Pentagon in 2010, and cited again by the White House in 2021. On paper, the rule is clean: classify it or publish it.

**The books in practice.** The national laboratories at Los Alamos and Livermore do open and weapons work under the same roofs, with the same staff and often the same machines. The largest laser in the world, at Livermore, is presented as fusion research, which it does, while its principal mission is maintaining nuclear weapons. How its costs are split is not visible to the taxpayer. The country already knows how to do better. Since 2007 the United States has published the total of its intelligence budget each year without saying what the money buys.

**The CERN subsidy.** CERN runs an industrial return policy. It tracks, for each member state, the value of contracts won by its companies against its share of the budget, classes under-returning states as “poorly balanced” and gives their firms preferential access to later contracts. The European Space Agency’s founding rules contain the same “geographical return” principle. The money a country sends to Geneva is designed to come home as orders for its industry. That is legitimate industrial and diplomatic policy. It is not what the public is told it is buying.

**The referee that was fired.** In 1972 Congress created the Office of Technology Assessment to advise it independently. In 1984 the office published a study by a young physicist, Ashton Carter, concluding that President Reagan’s missile shield was very unlikely to work as promised. In 1995 Congress abolished the office to save about $20 million a year. The official reason was budget cuts, and nobody has proven otherwise. In 2010, as a senior Pentagon official, the same Ashton Carter signed the memorandum reaffirming the 1985 rule. The rule survived. The referee did not.

## 7. What each table served up

> Science is strongest where it can touch, and weakest where it can only watch.

Argument will not settle which answer is right. The record may.

**From the pack’s table.** The Haber-Bosch process, developed just before the First World War, draws fertilizer from the air; by 2008 it was estimated to feed nearly half the people alive. Vaccines, by the World Health Organization’s estimate, have saved at least 154 million lives in fifty years, and smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. The transistor, the laser and fiber optics, products of the working half of physics, carry every phone call and light every screen. These are the white knights in lab coats, scaling their ladders in defense of the realm.

**From the full table.** The Large Hadron Collider found the Higgs boson in 2012. It won a Nobel Prize, and no use for it has been found. The collider has found nothing new since, and decades of searching for dark matter have come up empty. The proposed answer is the Future Circular Collider, a tunnel 91 kilometers around, its first stage costed at roughly 15 billion Swiss francs and ready in the 2040s: a bigger machine to look for what the last one could not find.

**The spinoff defense.** The full table’s answer is the spinoff. The World Wide Web was built at CERN, and detectors built for physics have found their way into hospitals. Both are real. Both were accidents along the road rather than the destination, and if better hospital scanners are wanted, it is cheaper to pay for scanners.

Prestige in science seems to run backwards: the further a question sits from any use, the higher it ranks. Bush’s definition turned that prestige into a budget line. And those who decide have usually eaten well, so the full table’s answer looks to them like common sense. To anyone who has missed meals, no question about the first second of the universe is worth a loaf of bread.

## 8. Fewer hammers, more thinkers

> Individuals learn the hard way. Groups almost never do.

Nobody can pick a winning idea in advance. Cost-effective research therefore cannot mean backing the right idea. It can only mean building a system that gives the right idea the best chance of turning up, at the lowest price. Five methods have been tried, and each has a record.

1. **Spread the bets.** Anyone who deals horses knows not to put everything on one animal. Big science does the opposite, putting billions on a single machine and doubling the bet when it loses. The first stage of the proposed collider would fund thousands of small research groups for a decade.
2. **Pay for results, not promises.** In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize for finding longitude at sea, and the answer came from John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter, not from the astronomers. In 2004 a $10 million prize for private spaceflight drew about two dozen teams, who spent around $100 million chasing it. A prize costs nothing unless someone delivers.
3. **Fund people, not projects.** The Howard Hughes Medical Institute funds chosen scientists for years at a time, with freedom to change direction. In 2011 Pierre Azoulay, Joshua Graff Zivin and Gustavo Manso compared Hughes investigators with similar scientists funded project by project, and found the Hughes group produced more breakthrough papers, and more outright flops, as people allowed to take risks should.
4. **Let chance help.** Reviewers tend to mark down the most original proposals. Since 2013 New Zealand’s Health Research Council has awarded some grants by lottery among proposals that pass a quality screen, and the Swiss National Science Foundation now uses a lottery to break ties. A lottery gives the oddball’s idea the same ticket as the safe one.
5. **Put a clock on placeholders.** The neutrino was proposed in 1930 and found in 1956. Dark matter has had about fifty years. Any program hunting something unseen could face a review date: find it, show real progress or explain to an independent referee why the hunt should go on.

What the five have in common is that they move power away from the guild and toward the people and ideas it tends to overlook.

## 9. Supporting witnesses

> If science can read the stars, it ought to be able to sense the wind.

The argument is our own. These witnesses support parts of it.

**Eisenhower** warned in 1961 that “the free university, historically the fountainhead of free ideas and scientific discovery,” was being transformed by government contracts, and that a contract could become “virtually a substitute for intellectual curiosity.”

**Robert Merton** described in 1942 the norms science claims for itself, among them disinterestedness and organized skepticism. In 1968 he named the Matthew effect, under which credit flows to those who already have it. Together they describe the gap between science’s ideals and its institutions.

**Thomas Kuhn and Ludwik Fleck** showed how a scientific community’s shared frame determines which questions can be asked, and how anomalies are shelved until a crisis forces a change.

**C. P. Snow** warned in 1959 that the sciences and the humanities could no longer speak to each other. In 1996 Alan Sokal had a deliberately meaningless article accepted by a leading cultural studies journal. Between them they show what happens when disciplines become guilds with private languages: the public is shut out of the conversation about its own world.

**The metascience movement**, including the reproducibility studies of the last fifteen years, has given empirical weight to suspicions about incentives that this paper states in general terms.

## 10. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: useful results come from useless research.** Flexner’s point stands. Quantum mechanics was pursued out of curiosity and gave us the transistor; nobody could have funded the transistor directly in 1925.

_Reply._ Granted, and it is the strongest case for basic research. It is a case for curiosity at the bench, which is cheap, not for any particular machine, which is not. The transistor came from people, ideas and modest laboratories. The thesis does not oppose basic research. It opposes a charter that exempts the most expensive basic research from ever answering to the people who pay for it.

**Objection 2: the spinoffs justify the cost.** The web alone has repaid CERN many times over.

_Reply._ The web was an accident of the road. A program whose returns are accidental cannot be justified by them in advance, any more than a gambler can be justified by the one time he won. If the spinoffs are the point, funding them directly is cheaper.

**Objection 3: national security requires secrecy.** The public cannot be told everything about weapons research.

_Reply._ Agreed, and the thesis asks for nothing secret. It asks that the existence and size of the secret share be stated, as the intelligence budget already is, so that the open share can be judged on its own merits.

**Objection 4: lotteries and clocks are anti-scientific.** Science should allocate by merit, and some searches take a long time.

_Reply._ Lotteries are used only among proposals already judged sound, where reviewers cannot reliably rank them. Clocks do not end a search; they require it to explain itself to someone outside the guild. Both are already in use and both have records.

**Objection 5: this is anti-science sentiment.** Criticism of science’s institutions gives ammunition to those who reject science itself.

_Reply._ Criticism is fair; controversy is destructive. This paper criticizes institutions and spokesmen in the name of the method and the people at the bench. The surest way to protect science from its enemies is to stop handing them the evidence that its spokesmen overreach.

## 11. Conclusion

> It’s the Big Bang gang that gives the frontier a bad name.

Science answers to two charters. The pack’s charter, knowledge as the first line of defense, has fed half the world, saved hundreds of millions of lives and connected everyone. The charter from the full table, knowledge for its own sake, has given wonder its due and, in its most expensive branches, has given the public stories in place of bread. Frontier is a good word; the frontier is where the ladders go. It is the Big Bang gang, the expensive pursuit of unanswerable questions on public money, that gives the frontier a bad name.

We have argued that institutions cannot schedule discovery and tend to scorn the people who produce it, that intelligent insiders become trapped by ordinary mechanisms, that spokesmen sell patches as discoveries at the expense of honest workers, that the books of public science are mixed beyond judging, and that tested methods exist for buying more discovery for less.

What seems clearly not right is spending the pack’s money as though the pack’s needs had all been met. The better question is the one in the title. Every science could say, in plain words, which of the three it serves: a roof, a meal or each other. The knights in lab coats could answer in a sentence. The Big Bang gang might need a very long grant application.

For its own sake, or for ours?

## Abstract

We argue that the parts of Reality cannot be fully understood without the whole, and that the whole cannot be seen from inside. A car is known by what it does on the highway, not by its twenty-five thousand components; you cannot deduce a car from rebuilding a carburetor. Physics has spent a century rebuilding carburetors. We propose a different method in five steps: survey what is observed about the whole, infer its shape, imagine what lies outside it, guess at its cause, then run the reasoning backward from the whole to the particle and see whether it holds.

Applying the method yields four findings. First, almost everything we know about the universe as a whole is the account light gives of its own journey: we measure the messenger, never the sender. Second, light traveling straight across the visible universe, which physics reports as “flatness,” tells us nothing about the shape of the container. Third, unless Reality is infinite and therefore unmeasurable, it is a bounded body, a ball, with a real center that no observer inside can locate, and a membrane beyond which lies the unknowable. Fourth, an observer inside might still detect which way the ball leans, and three independent lopsidednesses in the sky may be such clues. The questions that remain, where it started and what lies beyond, are past our operational horizon. Our insignificance knows no bounds.

## 1. Introduction

> You can’t deduce a car from rebuilding a carburetor.

A car on the highway is one thing. It has a speed, a direction, a fuel and an exhaust, and it is described by what it does. It is also some twenty-five thousand components traveling in a shell. Both descriptions are true. Only the first tells you what a car is. A carburetor on a workbench is a casting with jets and a float. In the engine it is the thing that mixes fuel with air so the car can move. Its identity comes from the whole.

Physics has worked the other way for a century, taking the universe apart to find out what it is. The parts have been catalogued with extraordinary precision, and they refuse to add up. The collider, the brain scanner and the gene sequencer have each reached the same wall: more parts, measured more finely, have not told anyone what the whole is. In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson put the problem in three words, “More is different”: every level of nature has rules of its own that cannot be read off the level below.

Our thesis is the strong form of Anderson’s point: **if we can’t see the whole, we can’t really understand the parts.** We can understand how a part works. We cannot understand what it is. And the whole of Reality cannot be seen, because there is nowhere outside it to stand.

This paper does not give up at that wall. It proposes a method for learning what can be learned about a whole from inside it, applies the method, and reports what it finds and where it stops.

## 2. The method

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

The method is the one a detective uses on a cold case: keep the evidence, throw out the old story and reason from the scene. It has five steps.

1. **Survey.** List what is observed about the whole, with no theory attached.
2. **Shape.** Infer what shape the whole could have, given the survey.
3. **Outside.** Imagine what could lie beyond the whole. Anything brought back from this step is a dream, labeled _pending_.
4. **Cause.** Guess at what could have produced a whole of that shape.
5. **Reverse.** Run the reasoning backward, from the whole down to the particle, and see whether it holds together.

Steps two to four are what the philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce called abduction: reasoning from clues to the best explanation available. Peirce held that abduction is the only kind of reasoning that introduces a new idea, since deduction only unpacks what is already assumed and induction only generalizes what is already seen. The fifth step is what keeps abduction honest. An explanation of the whole that cannot be run back down to the particle has explained nothing.

## 3. Step one: the survey

> We know what we sense. We assume what it is.

Here is what is observed about the universe as a whole, stated without theory.

1. **The light is stretched.** Light from distant galaxies arrives shifted toward the red, more the farther away they are. Read as growth, the growth slowed for billions of years, then sped up.
2. **There is an old glow.** A faint radiation arrives from every direction at 2.7 degrees above absolute zero, even to one part in a hundred thousand.
3. **Light crosses it straight.** Over the greatest distances we can see, light arrives without overall bending or distortion.
4. **It is lumpy.** Matter lies in a web of walls and filaments around enormous voids, with some structures billions of light-years long.
5. **It is matter, not antimatter.** One part in a billion more of one twin than the other.
6. **It runs the same everywhere.** Light from the most distant quasars carries the same chemical fingerprints, and the same constants, as light from a candle.
7. **It is not spinning.** No overall rotation has been detected.
8. **It has a rest frame.** The old glow defines a stillness, and we move through it at about 370 kilometers per second.
9. **It runs one way.** Overall it runs down, while pockets of order keep forming.
10. **We see only part of it.** Our view stops at a horizon set by how far light has had time to travel.

We first drafted item 3 in the language of physics: “the universe is flat.” Section 5 explains why we dropped the word.

## 4. The messenger and the sender

> We measure the reaction, never the reactors.

Read the survey again and ask, of each item, whose feature it is. Light arriving straight is something light does. Light arriving stretched is something that happened to the light. Most of the list turns out to be the photon’s report on its own journey.

| Item | Whose feature it is | What it reports
| 1. Stretched light | The messenger | What happened to light on its way
| 2. The old glow | The messenger | The oldest light, arriving now
| 3. Straight light | The messenger | How light travels through the interior
| 8. The rest frame | The messenger | The frame of the old glow
| 10. The horizon | The messenger | How far light has had time to come
| 4. Lumpy | The sources, read through light | Where light comes from
| 6. The same everywhere | The sources, read through light | Distant atoms emit the same colors as near ones
| 5. Matter, not antimatter | Matter we can touch | Sampled locally, extended by inference
| 9. Runs one way | Matter we can touch | Seen in every process we can watch
| 7. Not spinning | Neither | An absence in the light, not a presence

The finding is plain. Almost everything we believe about the universe as a whole is the photon’s travel diary. We measure the messenger, never the sender. A few other messengers exist, neutrinos and gravitational waves, and they tell the same kind of story.

This matters for everything that follows. If space is a material medium, as our companion paper The Singular Field argues, then a photon that has crossed it for billions of years may have been stretched, cooled and delayed by the crossing itself. Some of what is called the history of the universe may be the history of the trip. Before any shape can be inferred, the survey has to separate what the light went through from what the whole must be for the light to arrive as it does.

## 5. Straight light and the container

> Geometry obscures reality.

**What physics says.** Cosmologists report that the universe is “flat”: across the largest scales, space keeps Euclid’s rules, so that triangles add to 180 degrees and parallel lines stay parallel. The measurement uses the spots in the old glow. Their real size is known from the physics of the early universe, and they appear about one degree across, the size they would appear if their light came to us undistorted. Combined with other measurements, the “curvature” is zero to within about two parts in a thousand.

**What is observed.** Strip the geometry away and the observation is simpler: light crosses the whole visible universe straight, with nothing on the largest scale bending, magnifying or shrinking it. “Flat” and “curved” are the stories laid over that. The words are borrowed from surfaces, a tabletop and a globe, both two-dimensional skins seen from outside. Carried into three dimensions, they invite the mind to picture space bending into a fourth direction that is not there. Curved spacetime makes the same move. In both cases geometry obscures what was actually seen.

**What it tells us about the whole.** Nothing about its shape. Imagine the universe as a basketball holding floating marbles. Light from each marble travels in a straight line to every other marble. The membrane of the basketball is still round. Straight light inside reports how light travels through the interior. It does not report the shape of the container, because no light inside ever touches the container.

Physics treats flatness as evidence that the universe is either infinite or so large that its edges are irrelevant, and as evidence of a precise balance in its density that was then explained by inflation. Neither conclusion follows from straight light. A bounded container, with a membrane far beyond our horizon, gives exactly the same observation.

## 6. Step two: the shape

> All observation is self-centered. Reality does not possess a self.

**Infinite or a ball.** There is no third option. Either Reality has no boundary, in which case it can never be measured as a whole and lies permanently behind an SOB, a scientific observational boundary, a place where our methods run out though something surely lies beyond. Or it has a boundary, in which case it is a body with an inside and an outside. Unless Reality is infinite and therefore unmeasurable, it is a basketball.

**Why round.** “Ball” is likely the right shape, not just the right word. Everything in nature large enough to gather itself becomes round: planets, stars and the dense cores of galaxies. Gravity pulls equally in every direction. In our companion paper The Exhaust Stroke, gathering is one of the two strokes of the cosmic engine. A whole that gathers would round itself off.

**The interior.** Inside, the ball is a volume of medium in which light travels straight. No geometry word is needed to describe it.

**The center no one can find.** Every observer inside sees its own horizon as an even sphere around itself and naturally concludes that it stands in the middle. All observation is self-centered. Standard cosmology noticed that every point looks central and concluded that there is no center. Those are different claims. A ball has a real center. No marble inside it can locate the center, because doing so would require seeing the membrane. The center is not absent. It lies behind an SOB, with the membrane itself.

The shape, then, is a bounded ball of medium, round because it gathers, with a real center no observer inside can locate and a membrane beyond the horizon. _Pending._

## 7. Step three: beyond the membrane

> Experience is real. Knowledge is optional.

**What we can say.** Nothing that settles anything. At the membrane our methods run out, so we cannot detect what lies beyond, not even whether it is anything at all. Whether there is nothing out there, and whether nothing can exist, cannot be settled from inside. Our definition of an SOB ends with the words “though something surely lies beyond.” Read carefully, “something” there is not a claim that there is stuff beyond the wall. It is a substitute word for the unknowable, a name for what goes in the place we cannot see. It is an honest placeholder: unlike dark matter, it claims no thing at all.

**What we can imagine.** Step three is openly imagination, and anything brought back from it is a dream. Three dreams are worth testing:

1. **More medium, thinner.** The ball is a dense region within a wider, rarer medium, as a star is dense within thin interstellar gas. The membrane is where the density falls away.
2. **Other balls.** Ours is one gathering among many, each gathering, erupting and dispersing in turn.
3. **The unknowable proper.** Beyond the membrane there is nothing an observer of our kind could ever register, and the dream stops at the wall.

**One test.** Suppose the membrane is transparent and nothing lies beyond. Light reaching the edge would leave and never return, and nothing would come in. An observer near the edge would see the sky thin out on that side: fewer galaxies, a weaker glow, a dark direction. We see no dark direction. Either the ball is far larger than the part of it we can see, or its edge is not transparent.

## 8. Step four: reading the lean from inside

> Things break and stuff happens.

If Reality had a definite shape seen from outside, it might show where it started. Shapes record their history: a crater shows the direction of the impact, and a spray of debris points back to the blast. A bounded ball that began from one place would carry that place in its shape, as its center and perhaps as a lopsidedness. From outside, the question would answer itself at a glance. From inside, we can at best feel which way the ball leans. An observer off-center in a ball would find three kinds of trace.

- **A lopsided sky.** More of everything in one direction than the other. In 2021 Nathan Secrest and colleagues counted about 1.36 million quasars and found the sky lopsided by more than twice the amount our motion explains, at a significance of 4.9 standard deviations.
- **An expansion that differs by direction.** Debris from a blast moves faster the farther it is from the start, so the rate measured toward the center and away from it would differ. Konstantinos Migkas and colleagues reported in 2020 that the apparent expansion rate measured from hundreds of galaxy clusters seems to vary across the sky.
- **An uneven glow.** The Planck team catalogued a difference in the strength of the old glow between two halves of the sky, and in 2005 Kate Land and João Magueijo noted that its largest patterns line up along a common axis, which they called “the axis of evil.”

The standard model treats each of these as a fluke, an error or a local effect. On the ball, they are what an off-center observer should expect. The quasar lopsidedness points roughly the same way as our motion through the glow, which is why it is usually read as motion alone. If the three traces were shown to share a common direction beyond what our motion explains, that would be a weak but real hint of where the center lies, and so of where it started. _Pending._

## 9. Step five: running it backward

> Space is the singular field of Reality.

The last step tests the picture by reversing it: begin with the whole and descend to the particle, and see whether each level follows from the one above.

1. **The whole.** A bounded ball of one medium, gathering and dispersing.
2. **Its large-scale structure.** A body that gathers and disperses does not settle into evenness. Gathering builds walls and clusters, dispersal empties voids. The lumpy web of item 4 is what such a whole produces, as our companion paper The Smooth Universe Is an Assumption argues.
3. **Its motion.** Within a bounded ball, expansion is the net of dispersal over gathering, and it rises and falls with the stellar era, as The Exhaust Stroke proposes. Item 1, the stretched light, is in part the record of that motion and in part the record of the light’s long trip through the medium.
4. **Its dense cores.** Gathering at its most extreme makes the dense objects at the centers of galaxies, which on our reading are not holes but stores of gathered mass and heat, as What Black Hole? argues.
5. **Its matter.** If the medium is the only substance, every particle is a knot in it, and the uniform constants of item 6 are the medium’s properties showing through every knot, as The Singular Field argues.
6. **Its pairs.** A twist in a continuous medium cannot be made without a counter-twist, which is why matter appears in pairs and charge always balances, and why the surplus of item 5 is a remainder of an unequal split, as Two argues.

Run backward, the picture holds together at every level we can check. That is not proof. It is the test step five exists to apply, and the picture passes it.

## 10. The operational horizon

> Our insignificance knows no bounds.

Some things are unknowable. Others are only unreachable.

The method takes us a long way and then stops. Where Reality started, what lies beyond the membrane, and whether the membrane is transparent are questions we can think through but cannot operate on. They lie past what we call the operational horizon.

The operational horizon is related to the SOB but not identical with it. An SOB is where our _methods_ run out: no technique of observation, however refined, reaches past it. The operational horizon is where our _reach_ runs out: our instruments, our lifespans, our place inside the ball. Most of the time the two are the same wall. Sometimes they are not. A question can be answerable in principle and still beyond anything we will ever be positioned to do. Where the universe started may be such a question: written into its shape, readable from outside, and forever out of our reach.

The honest conclusion is not despair. It is proportion. We are marbles in a ball we cannot see, reading the diary of light that crossed it before our species existed. Our insignificance knows no bounds. That is not a reason to stop asking. It is the reason the asking matters.

## 11. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: reductionism works.** Taking things apart has given us chemistry, genetics and the transistor. Holism has given us nothing comparable.

_Reply._ Reductionism works superbly for how a part works, and the thesis grants that fully. A mechanic can rebuild a carburetor without knowing where the car is going. What reductionism has not delivered is what the parts are, because that comes from the whole. Both statements are true, and science’s success at the first has hidden its silence on the second.

**Objection 2: the universe has no center.** Every observer sees galaxies receding in the same pattern, faster the farther they are, so no point is special.

_Reply._ The same is true inside an explosion. Each piece of debris sees every other piece receding faster the farther away it is, and each concludes it is at the center. In the 1930s Edward Milne built a model of exactly that kind, a ball of particles flying apart from a point into ordinary space, and showed that it reproduces the observed pattern of recession with every observer seeing himself at the middle. The pattern shows that every point looks central. It does not show that there is no center.

**Objection 3: the lopsided sky is our motion, or a fluke.** The quasar excess, the uneven glow and the varying expansion rate each have conventional explanations.

_Reply._ Perhaps. Each has been offered one, and none has been settled. The ball does not need any one of them to be real. It predicts that, if we are off-center, such traces should exist and share a direction. That is a test, and it is _pending_.

**Objection 4: the messenger argument proves too much.** All observation comes through signals. If the photon’s diary is unreliable, so is every observation.

_Reply._ It applies to all observation, and that is the point. What distinguishes cosmology is the length of the trip. Light from the old glow has been traveling for nearly the whole history of the universe. A signal that has crossed a medium for that long has more opportunity to be changed by the crossing than any signal in a laboratory, and the standard account assumes it was changed in only one way, by expansion.

**Objection 5: a ball whose membrane is beyond the horizon cannot be tested.** The thesis hides its key feature where no one can look.

_Reply._ So does the alternative. An infinite universe is equally beyond any test. The difference is that the ball makes predictions inside the horizon: an off-center observer should see a consistent lean, and a transparent edge within reach would show a dark side. The infinite, even universe predicts no lean at all. Those are tests the ball can fail.

## 12. Conclusion

> If we can’t see the whole, we can’t really understand the parts.

A car is known by what it does, not by its components, and you cannot deduce a car from rebuilding a carburetor. We have argued that the same holds for Reality: the parts are understood in how they work and never in what they are, because what they are comes from a whole we cannot see.

The method we proposed, survey, shape, outside, cause and reverse, took us further than we expected. The survey turned out to be mostly the photon’s travel diary. Straight light turned out to say nothing about the container. The shape came down to a choice between the infinite, which can never be measured, and a ball, round because it gathers, with a real center no one inside can find. Beyond its membrane lies something, our substitute word for the unknowable. From inside, we may still feel which way the ball leans. Run backward from the whole to the particle, the picture holds together with the rest of our work.

What seems clearly not right is the belief that the whole will appear once the parts are counted finely enough, and its companion claim that because every point looks central, there is no center. The better question is not what the universe is made of. It is what the whole must be, for the parts to behave the way they do.

Where it started, and what lies beyond, are past our operational horizon. Our insignificance knows no bounds.

## Abstract

The story of the Garden of Eden has been read for millennia as a story about knowledge: a forbidden tree, a fatal curiosity and a punishment for wanting to know. We argue that this is an incomplete reading. The text, read with attention to its own words, is about one particular knowledge, the knowledge of death. The tree is introduced with a warning about dying, its first effect is the awareness of being exposed, the sentence it brings is mortality, and the exile is explicitly a separation from a second tree, the tree of life. Older Mesopotamian stories of Gilgamesh and Adapa tell the same tale of lost immortality.

Read this way, the Garden marks the moment the first priority of all life, staying alive, became conscious. Every animal stays alive; only an animal that knows it will die can ask whether, and why. That is Hamlet’s question, and humanity’s. We call it the principal duality, to be or not to be, and argue that it lies inside every decision as a choice between this and nothing. We trace what the incomplete reading has cost, a long suspicion of curiosity, and what the rereading offers: a real goal for science, the defense and advance of life, resting on the same ground as the oldest story we tell.

## 1. Introduction

> The Garden isn’t about knowledge. It’s about the knowledge of death.

Few stories have been read more often or with more consequence than the third chapter of Genesis. A man and a woman live in a garden where food grows on trees. They are forbidden one tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A serpent persuades them to eat. They are expelled, sentenced to toil, pain and death, and barred from returning by a flaming sword.

The usual reading makes the story about knowledge in general. Curiosity was the sin, the desire to know was the transgression, and human suffering is the price of wanting to understand. That reading has shaped attitudes to learning, to science and to curiosity itself for a very long time.

Our thesis is that **the Garden is not about knowledge in general but about the knowledge of death**, and that once this is seen, the story stops being a warning against curiosity and becomes the oldest account of the moment life’s first priority, staying alive, became a question. We make the case from the text itself (section 3), from older stories (section 4) and from what the sciences of the mind say about self-awareness (section 5). We then follow the question through Hamlet (section 6), name the principal duality it creates (section 7) and ask what the incomplete reading has cost (section 8).

The paper sits beside our earlier essay “This Isn’t the Garden of Eden,” which read the story as a memory of leaving the trees for the grass. Both readings can stand. The departure was a change of ground, and it was also a change of mind.

## 2. The Fundamental Priority

> Life’s first priority: staying alive.

Every living thing, from the first cell to the reader of this sentence, has one priority that comes before all others: staying alive. A cell builds a wall to keep the outside out. An immune system tells self from non-self and attacks the rest. An animal flees, fights, freezes or feeds. Whatever else life does, it does on the condition that it is still alive to do it.

Knowledge serves that priority. In our earlier work we called knowledge the first line of defense, the sword and shield of survival. The question comes from the senses, and the answer comes from experience, if we live that long; the instinct to question is the _sine qua non_ of survival. Defense and offense are the two ways the priority is served. The shield protects the pack from what Reality throws at it, and the sword takes the ground the pack needs. The best offense is a good defense and vice versa: a vaccine guards a people and lets it travel and grow, and a field that feeds a village also guards it against famine. They are two faces of one goal.

Nothing in this priority requires awareness. A bacterium swims away from poison without knowing it could die. The question this paper asks is what happened when the priority met a creature that did know.

## 3. The Garden reread

> The observations are real. The story isn’t.

Read the story in the King James words, with an eye on death rather than on knowledge, and death is present at every turn.

**Two trees from the start.** “The tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil” (2:9). The garden has two special trees, not one. The story will turn on keeping them apart.

**The warning names death.** “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” (2:17). The forbidden tree is defined from the first by what it does to life, not by what information it holds.

**The serpent’s half-truth.** “Ye shall not surely die” (3:4). And they did not drop dead; Adam lived, the text says, nine hundred and thirty years. What changed on the day they ate was not that they died. It was that they became creatures who would die, and knew it.

**The first thing they learn is exposure.** “The eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (3:7). They learn nothing about the world. They learn about themselves: that they are bodies, unprotected, able to be hurt.

**The sentence is mortality.** “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (3:19).

**The exile guards the other tree.** “Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever” (3:22). The cherubim and the flaming sword are placed “to keep the way of the tree of life” (3:24). The exile is explained, in the text’s own words, as keeping a creature that now knows death from also having endless life.

Read this way the story is coherent from beginning to end. A creature that knows it will die cannot also live forever. That knowledge, and that separation, is what the Garden is about. The phrase “good and evil” has been read by many scholars as a figure of speech meaning everything, from one end to the other, the way “high and low” means everyone. On that reading the forbidden knowledge is knowledge of the whole of life, and the whole of life includes its end.

## 4. Older witnesses

> Experience is real. Knowledge is optional.

The Garden story did not arise alone. Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers where Genesis places Eden, told the same tale earlier and more plainly.

**Gilgamesh.** In the Epic of Gilgamesh, whose oldest versions go back about four thousand years, the king of Uruk is shaken by the death of his friend Enkidu and sets out to escape death himself. He reaches the survivor of the great flood, who tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. Gilgamesh dives and brings it up. On the way home he stops to bathe, and a serpent smells the plant, takes it and sheds its skin as it goes. Gilgamesh sits down and weeps, and returns home mortal. A serpent and lost immortality, set beside the knowledge of a friend’s death, appear centuries before Genesis was written down.

**Adapa.** In the story of Adapa, a sage of the city of Eridu known from tablets of the fourteenth century BC, the god Anu summons Adapa to heaven and offers him the bread and water of life. Warned beforehand that he would be offered the bread and water of death, Adapa refuses, and so loses the immortality he was being offered. Wisdom he had; endless life he did not get.

The pattern is the same in all three. Humans gain or already have knowledge, and lose, or never gain, endless life. The stories are not about the danger of learning. They are about the boundary between a mind that knows and a life that ends.

This also settles the number. Genesis as a written text is about three thousand years old. The story it tells is older. Counting the Mesopotamian tradition behind it, humanity has been telling this story, and reading only half of it, for some four thousand years.

## 5. The eyes opened

> The question comes from the senses. The answer comes from experience, if we live that long.

The sciences of the mind tell a story that runs close to the Garden’s.

**The self arrives.** Put a dab of rouge on a toddler’s nose and set the child before a mirror. Somewhere around eighteen months to two years the child stops reaching for the baby in the glass and touches its own nose. Gordon Gallup showed in 1970 that chimpanzees pass the same test. A few other animals may. The eyes are opened: a creature sees itself.

**Death becomes knowable.** A creature that sees itself can, in time, see that it will end. Elephants linger over the bones of their dead, and chimpanzees attend to dying companions. Whether any animal but ours anticipates its own death is not known. In humans the understanding that death is universal, irreversible and personal arrives in childhood and never leaves.

**The mind defends itself.** In 2013 the biologist Ajit Varki and Danny Brower argued that full self-awareness could only have evolved if it came packaged with the power to deny mortality, because a creature that truly grasped its own death might stop striving. In 2019 researchers at Bar-Ilan University found that the brain’s prediction machinery declines to connect a person’s own face with words of death, though it links a stranger’s face readily. In 1973 Ernest Becker argued in _The Denial of Death_ that much of human culture is built to shield us from that knowledge.

Put beside the text, the science reads like a commentary. The eyes are opened and the creature knows it is exposed. It learns it will return to dust. And it is barred from the tree of life, not by a cherub with a sword, but by its own biology, which keeps the knowledge just far enough away to let it go on living.

## 6. Hamlet’s question

> To be or not to be: the principal duality, inherent in every decision.

Around 1600 Shakespeare put the Garden’s consequence into the mouth of a Danish prince.

> To be, or not to be, that is the question: Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles

A deer stays alive without asking whether to. Hamlet is the Fundamental Priority turned around and examined by the one animal able to examine it. Once a creature knows it will die, staying alive stops being only an instinct and becomes a question, one it can ask about itself.

Shakespeare also named the wall. Death, Hamlet says, is “the undiscover’d country, from whose bourn no traveller returns.” That is an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: a place where our methods run out, though something surely lies beyond. It is the oldest one and the most personal, and Hamlet’s hesitation before it is the hesitation of every observer at every wall: what lies past it cannot be known, and that is exactly what makes the choice so heavy.

In 1942 Albert Camus opened _The Myth of Sisyphus_ with the claim that there is only one truly serious philosophical problem, whether life is worth living, and that every other question comes after it. His answer was Sisyphus, rolling his boulder up the hill forever, whom “one must imagine happy.” The question Hamlet asked is the one every human being inherits from the Garden. The animal answers it without asking. We ask it, and answer it every day by going on.

## 7. The principal duality

> The basic choice: This or Nothing.

Hamlet’s question is not asked once, in a castle, in a crisis. In small change it is asked all day long. Cross the road or wait. Eat the strange berry or leave it. Take the new job or keep the safe one. Every decision weighs staying alive, in body or in some smaller sense, against what might be worth the risk. We call this the principal duality: to be or not to be, inherent in every decision.

It is the pair beneath the other pairs. In our paper Two we argued that two is the basic integer of existence and that every pair shows two faces of one thing: heads or tails, one coin; particle or wave, one substance. The Tao Te Ching said being and non-being produce each other. If that is so, the first pair is not up and down or plus and minus. It is being and not being, and every other pair is a version of it.

The everyday form of the duality is the pair that keeps every living mind alive: caution and curiosity. Caution leans toward _to be_, keeping what one has. Curiosity is willing to risk a little _not to be_ for something more. A creature of all caution starves in the cave; a creature of all curiosity meets the first snake. Every living thing balances the two. Only we know we are doing it.

And the choice is starker than it looks. It is never between this life and a better one somewhere else. There is no garden on offer. The basic choice is this, as it is, or nothing. That is the Garden’s last lesson, and our earlier essay’s title: this isn’t the Garden of Eden, and it is the only place we have.

## 8. What the incomplete reading cost

> Heads or tails, one coin. Particle or wave, one substance.

If the Garden is about knowledge in general, then curiosity is the original sin. That reading had consequences. In the fourth century Augustine listed curiosity, “the lust of the eyes,” among the temptations to be resisted. For centuries the desire to know more than one needed was treated as a form of pride. When Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky, he was looking into the place the old reading had fenced off, and he paid for it. Suspicion of the curious has never entirely gone away.

If the Garden is about the knowledge of death, curiosity is no sin at all. It is the instinct that serves the Fundamental Priority: the _sine qua non_ of survival. The knowledge that was gained in the Garden was not forbidden learning but a hard fact, that we will die, and everything humans have learned since, from fire to vaccines, has been an answer to it.

The modern world has made the opposite mistake. Having thrown off the suspicion of curiosity, it decided that knowledge needs no purpose at all, and that science is best pursued for its own sake. The two errors mirror each other. One treats knowledge as dangerous, the other as aimless. The rereading gives knowledge back its purpose. Life’s first priority is staying alive, and science’s real goal is the same: the defense and advance of life. The shield and the sword are carried by the same arm, for the same reason, and the reason was given at the gate of the Garden.

## 9. Supporting witnesses

> Intelligence should always be respected, no matter what form it comes in.

The reading is our own. Several thinkers stand near parts of it.

**Irenaeus**, a bishop of the second century, read the Garden not as a fall from perfection but as the beginning of humanity’s growing up: Adam and Eve as children, not yet ready for what they took. That softens the story’s verdict on curiosity, as our reading does.

**Kierkegaard**, in _The Concept of Anxiety_ (1844), read the Fall through anxiety, the dizziness of a creature that suddenly sees its own freedom and possibility. Anxiety in the face of what one might do, and might lose, is close kin to the principal duality.

**Heidegger**, in _Being and Time_ (1927), described human existence as “being-toward-death”: we are the beings who live in the knowledge of our own end, and that knowledge shapes everything we do.

**Camus** made whether life is worth living the one serious question of philosophy, and answered it with Sisyphus.

**Becker and Varki** supplied the science: culture as a defense against the knowledge of death, and self-awareness as something that could only evolve with that defense built in.

What none of them did was read the Garden itself, verse by verse, as a story about the knowledge of death, and connect it to the first priority of all life and to the purpose of science.

## 10. Objections and replies

> Always is not a word in science.

**Objection 1: the tree is about moral knowledge.** It is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not of death.

_Reply._ Its name speaks of good and evil; everything the text says about it speaks of death. It is introduced with a warning about dying, its effect is the awareness of exposure, its sentence is a return to dust, and the exile is explained by the tree of life. Many scholars read “good and evil” as a figure of speech for everything, the whole of experience. The whole of experience includes its end, and the story makes that end its subject.

**Objection 2: in Christian teaching, death is the punishment for sin.** The Fall brought death as a penalty for disobedience, not as an insight.

_Reply._ That is a reading, developed most fully by Augustine some four centuries after Paul, and it rests on the same incomplete reading. The text of Genesis gives its own reason for the exile in 3:22, and the reason is the tree of life: a creature that now knows good and evil must not also live forever. Whether that is a penalty or a condition, the content of what changed is the same: mortality, known.

**Objection 3: animals know death too.** Elephants mourn, and chimpanzees attend to their dying.

_Reply._ Perhaps some do, in some measure, and we do not claim otherwise. The story marks the moment the knowledge became complete: a creature that knows not only that others die but that it will, and that can turn the knowledge into a question about itself.

**Objection 4: this treats myth as history.** No garden, no serpent and no first couple are being claimed.

_Reply._ Correct, and we claim none of them. We read the story as people read all their oldest stories, as a memory in the only form a species without writing could keep it. What it remembers is not an event but a change: the arrival of the knowledge that we die.

## 11. Conclusion

> Reality is a given. What we make of it is not.

The Garden of Eden has been read for millennia as a warning against wanting to know. Read in its own words, it says something narrower and harder. The forbidden tree brings one knowledge above all: that we will die. The first priority of all life, staying alive, met a creature that could see itself, and became a question. Hamlet asked it aloud. Camus called it the only serious question there is. We ask it in small change in every decision we make, and answer it by going on.

The rereading changes what curiosity is. It is not the original sin. It is the instinct that serves the oldest priority, and it gives science its real goal: not knowledge for its own sake, but the defense and advance of life, the shield and the sword carried by one arm.

What seems clearly not right is a reading that turned the knowledge of death into a sin of curiosity, and a modern answer that turned curiosity into an end without a purpose. The better question is not why we were punished for wanting to know. It is what we do with the knowledge we were given at the gate: that our time is short, and that the basic choice, every day, is this or nothing.
