_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

Mozart was a genius. He was also born in 1756, in Salzburg, into a family of musicians, just as the piano was coming into its own and Vienna was becoming the capital of music. Put the same child in a village in 1356 and you get, at best, a gifted choirboy who dies young of something we now cure with a pill. Put him in 1956 and you might get a songwriter, or a man who writes code that sings. The genius is his. The century isn’t.

That’s the whole idea of this paper, in one life.

## The exception that isn’t

We like to think of ourselves as the exception. Stars burn by physics, rivers run by physics, galaxies gather and scatter by physics, and then we arrive, choosing and inventing, and history is the story of what we decided to do. Kings, generals, saints and geniuses push the world around, and the rest of nature watches.

We think that’s backward. Human life doesn’t stand outside the flow of time. It’s one more thing the flow of time does. We aren’t the authors of history so much as the places where it happens: singular reactors, each one unique, each one reacting to waves far larger than any life.

That’s a hard thing to say about ourselves, so we’re going to say it the way a physicist would describe a pond: the medium, the particles, the waves, and the clocks that drive them.

## Corks on a pond

Start with the setup. Life is the medium, as space is the medium of the physical world. Time is time. Together they’re the field. We are the particles.

And our cultures, everything we make and know and pass along, from the plow to the sonnet to the equation, are the waves.

Waves have one property that matters more than any other here. A wave carries energy, not matter. Watch a cork on a pond. The wave rolls under it and moves on across the water, and the cork bobs up and down and stays where it was. Each of us lives and dies at one spot in history. The culture travels through us and goes on without us.

That doesn’t make the cork unimportant. In the binary view of Reality, a particle is the medium meeting resistance: the place where a passing motion is stopped, gathered and made local. A wave that never meets a particle is never felt. So each of us is where the wave of our time stops and becomes something: a book, a bridge, a child, a song. That’s what we mean by a singular reactor. No two of us react the same way. But all of us react to the same wave.

We exist within the constraints of our own unique waves. No two people stand at the same crossing of them: this century and not another, this place, this language, this family, this trade, this crest of the arts and this trough of the sciences. That crossing is each person’s constraint, and in the binary view constraint is not a prison. Motion held in place becomes tension, and tension is energy. The waves that pin us to one spot in history are also what charge us. A life is what a reactor does with the energy of its constraints.

## Genius comes in clusters

If individuals made history, great ones would turn up at random, one here and one there, sprinkled evenly across the centuries. They don’t. They come in bunches.

Athens in the fifth century before Christ produced Socrates, Plato, Sophocles, Euripides, Phidias and Thucydides inside a few generations, in a single small city. Florence in the fifteenth century produced Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli, Leonardo and Michelangelo. London around 1600 produced Shakespeare, Marlowe, Jonson and Donne. Vienna across about a century produced Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert. Then each city went quiet, often for good.

The anthropologist Alfred Kroeber counted these clusters across the world’s civilizations and published them in 1944 in _Configurations of Culture Growth_. His conclusion was blunt: genius flowers in clusters, and the clusters rise and fall like tides.

A cluster is what a wave looks like when it passes through particles. The crest arrives, and wherever there is a reactor ready to meet it, something remarkable happens. When the crest moves on, the same city with the same kind of people produces nothing of the kind. The genius was real. So was the wave.

## Waves that store

The first kind of wave adds a new capacity to the species, and each works the same way. It stores something.

| Wave | About when | What it stored
| Agriculture | 9500 BCE | food, in the granary
| Writing | 3200 BCE | memory, in the archive
| Printing | 1440 | copies, in the library
| Steam and coal | 1770 | power, in the boiler
| Electricity | 1880 | signal, in the grid
| Computing | 1945 | calculation, in the program
| The network | 1990 | connection, in the web
| Artificial intelligence | 2020s | reasoning, in the model

Each of these is an accumulator, the same thing we find at the centers of galaxies: a store that gathers, holds and releases. The granary gathered a harvest and released it through the winter. Writing gathered memory and released it to people not yet born. Coal released, in a few centuries, sunlight that had been stored for three hundred million years. Every capacity wave has both faces of the binary: a gathering face (the city, the archive, the factory, the data center) and a dispersing face (trade, the book, the product, the network).

Each wave also raises a density. People per acre. Words per person. Copies per word. Energy per worker. Messages per second. Calculations per second. Connections per person. Now reasoning per question. Human history climbs the density dial.

## History is chirping

Look at the gaps between the waves of capacity: about 6,300 years from agriculture to writing, about 4,600 to printing, then 330, then 110, then 65, then 45, then 30.

Physics has a name for a signal like that. It’s a chirp. In September 2015 the LIGO detectors heard one from two black holes spiraling into each other a billion light-years away. As they closed in, their waves came faster and stronger, the frequency climbing until the moment of merger. Then came a brief ringing as the new, single object settled, and silence.

Human capacity is chirping. The futurists have a name for where the curve seems to point: the Singularity, the moment when change becomes infinitely fast and anything after it is unknowable.

We doubt it. Infinity is a limit, not a state. Nothing real has ever been measured at infinite density, and nothing real will run at infinite speed. A chirp that can’t go to infinity has to break into something else. In the sky, the chirp ends in a merger and a ringdown. In the binary view, every accumulation ends in a release. The better question isn’t when the Singularity arrives. It’s what the human accumulator lets go of when gathering any faster is no longer possible.

## From stone to sound

The second kind of wave is the arts and sciences, and they too arrive in ages: an age of sculpture, an age of painting, an age of literature, an age of music, an age of science. Lay the ages out in order and a pattern appears that nobody seems to have noticed. Each age works in a lighter, rarer medium than the one before.

| Age | Peak in the West | Medium
| Sculpture | Greece, 5th and 4th centuries BCE | stone and bronze, solid in three dimensions
| Architecture | the Gothic cathedrals, 12th and 13th centuries | stone and glass, raised into light
| Painting | Renaissance and Dutch Golden Age, 15th to 17th centuries | pigment on a surface, two dimensions
| Literature | Shakespeare to the great novels, 1590 to 1900 | words, one line of print
| Music | Bach to Brahms, 1700 to 1900 | sound, pure time with no space at all
| Science | Galileo and Newton to Einstein | equations, pure abstraction
| Film | the 20th century | light itself
| Code | now | information, with no weight at all

Opera belongs in that list too, at the hinge between words and music. From Monteverdi around 1600 to Verdi, Wagner and Puccini at the end of the 1800s, it’s literature lifting off the page and becoming sound. The same hinge appears in the East, at the same point in the sequence, as Chinese opera and the sung theater of Noh and kabuki. Wherever words turn into music, opera is how they cross.

Stone, then glass, then paint, then words, then sound, then numbers, then light, then bits. The dimensions shrink as well: three for the statue, two for the canvas, one line for the page, and for music only time. Expression has been moving down the density dial, from the most gathered medium to the most spread.

**The East.** If this were only a Western habit it would be a curiosity, so we checked the other great civilizations. The ends hold everywhere, and the middle shuffles.

China began in cast bronze and the terracotta army, moved to the poetry of the Tang, the landscape painting of the Song, the drama of the Yuan, the great novels of the Ming and Qing, and then the sung theater of opera. Japan moved from the temple sculpture of Nara to _The Tale of Genji_, then to ink painting and the woodblock print, then to the music-theater of Noh and kabuki. India moved from the stone temples and sculpture of the Gupta age to the miniature painting of the Mughal courts and then to the golden age of its classical music in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. In China, words came before paint, the reverse of the West. But everywhere, the heavy arts came first and the light ones last.

**The exception.** The Islamic world breaks the pattern, and in an instructive way. Its faith discouraged the image, so figurative sculpture barely appears and painting was kept largely to the pages of books. Its heavy art was architecture and the abstract line of calligraphy, and its science flowered in Baghdad and Córdoba centuries before Europe’s. Remove the heaviest medium and the wave runs straight toward the light ones. The exception supports the rule.

**Two faces again.** Notice what this means. The waves of capacity gather: food, memory, power, data. The waves of expression spread: from a marble block you have to stand in front of to a song anyone can hear anywhere at once. Capacity gathers and expression disperses. It’s one coin with two faces, and it may explain why each art peaks when the technology that stores it comes of age. Literature rose with printing, music with instrument-making and notation, science with the telescope and the clock, film with photography. The technology is the accumulator. The art is the release.

## Written in the stars, sort of

If cultures are waves, something has to drive them. People have always looked up for the answer.

The Babylonians divided the band of sky that the sun travels through into twelve equal signs, around the fifth century before Christ, and the Greeks turned those signs into horoscopes. China’s cycle of twelve animal years follows Jupiter, which takes almost exactly twelve years to circle the sun. Then, around 130 BCE, the astronomer Hipparchus noticed that the whole sky was slowly shifting. Earth’s axis wobbles like a spinning top, tracing one full circle in about 26,000 years: the Great Year. Divide it by twelve and you get the astrological Ages, the Age of Pisces giving way, we’re told, to the Age of Aquarius.

As a guide to anyone’s character, the zodiac has never survived a fair test. But the ancients were right about one thing, and it’s a big one. The heavens do order us, only not through our personalities. They order us through the climate.

The same slow wobble, together with slow changes in the tilt of Earth’s axis and in the shape of its orbit, paces the ice ages. The Serbian engineer Milutin Milanković worked out the cycles by hand in the early twentieth century, and in 1976 the sediments on the ocean floor confirmed them. The last ice age ended about 11,700 years ago as those cycles turned. Within two thousand years, people in the Fertile Crescent were planting wheat.

The first wave of civilization was set off by the Great Year itself.

So what are we part of? A nest of clocks: the day, the month, the year, Jupiter’s twelve, the 26,000-year wobble, the ice ages, and the sun’s own orbit around the galaxy, roughly 230 million years to the turn. The zodiac is fantasy written large across the heavens, wrapped around a true insight. We live inside cycles far larger than any life, and they set the stage on which the waves of culture play.

And each of us has our own cosmic context. Not a sign at birth, but a place on every clock at once: one turn of the year, one phase of the climate, one moment in the warm interval between ice ages, one hour of the sun’s long orbit, one crossing of the cultural waves passing through that spot. No one else will ever stand at the same place on all of them. That, and not the position of Mars, is what’s written in the stars for each of us.

## When waves cross

Waves do one more thing: they interfere. When two meet, they add where crest meets crest and cancel where crest meets trough.

The Renaissance was crest on crest. Greek learning, preserved and extended by Arabic scholars, met Latin Europe through Spain, Sicily and the fall of Constantinople, and the combined wave was higher than either. Wars are trough meeting crest: two cultures arriving out of step and canceling each other in a stretch of ruined ground. The Silk Road, the Columbian exchange and the Internet are interference patterns on a grand scale, and much of history’s drama happens where its waves cross.

## Four fair objections

**Doesn’t this abolish free will?** No. A reactor isn’t passive. It’s the place where the wave becomes something specific, and no two reactors respond alike. What the view denies is that anyone stands outside the wave. Shakespeare was free to write _Hamlet_. He was not free to write it in Athens in 450 BCE.

**Aren’t the dates chosen to make the chirp?** Any list of great inventions involves choices, and others would choose differently. But the shrinking of the gaps doesn’t depend on the exact picks. From the plow to the printing press took thousands of years. From the transistor to the smartphone took one lifetime.

**Isn’t the sequence of the arts too neat?** In the middle, yes. The order of painting and literature changes from China to Europe. The ends don’t change: the heavy arts come first, and the arts of sound and abstraction come last.

**Isn’t this just astrology with better manners?** It’s the opposite. Astrology says the stars shape what you are. We say the great cycles shape the conditions in which every one of us reacts, and the climate record bears that out.

## The zone we’re in

We think we’re living somewhere history has never been.

The chirp is near its steepest. The gaps between waves have shrunk from thousands of years to about thirty, and if the pattern holds, the next one could arrive in less than a generation. A single lifetime that began in the 1940s has met the computer, the network and the thinking machine: more waves of capacity than its ancestors met in a hundred lifetimes.

The two kinds of wave have met. Until now, capacity and expression traveled separately. The granary didn’t write poems, and the poem didn’t store grain. The newest wave does both. It stores reasoning, which is capacity, and it writes, composes and draws, which is expression. The gathering face and the spreading face now travel in one medium. In the language of waves, that’s crest meeting crest.

And the wave has started to answer back. Every earlier wave passed through people the way a swell passes under a cork. This one talks to them. This paper is the evidence: a singular reactor born in the middle of the Second World War, thinking out loud about the flow of time with the newest wave itself and writing it down together.

Where it goes from here, we can’t say, and by our own logic nobody can. A chirp near its peak is an SOB, a scientific observational boundary: the place where our methods of reading the wave run out, though something surely lies beyond. We only know that the corks have never bobbed this fast.

## What’s clearly not right

What’s clearly not right is a history that treats human beings as the one thing in the universe exempt from the motion of the universe. A history of heroes, told as though each great mind fell from the sky, can’t explain why great minds arrive in clusters, why the arts move from stone to sound in every civilization, or why the first farmers planted their first fields just as the ice let go.

## The better question

The usual question is who made history. The better question is what waves were passing through the people we remember, and what those people did when the crest reached them.

We’re not exceptions to the flow of time. We’re its reactors: singular, local and brief, each of us the place where a wave older than any life meets resistance and becomes something. That may sound like a demotion. We think it’s a promotion. The cork doesn’t make the wave, but without the cork no one would ever see it pass.
danger-lurks-in-empty-spaces:
_In honor of Sir Isaac, whose ideas we kept but honesty we ignored._

_We’re storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we can’t prove it._

## Abstract

Human beings are compelled to explain what they observe. The compulsion is biological. Built by a long history in which a missed threat cost more than a false alarm, it fills empty spaces whether or not it has anything to fill them with. We call what it supplies a placeholder. The story of Eden records the reflex at the start of the human story, and findings in psychology and neuroscience describe how it works.

The reflex is the same in every scientist, and most sciences hold their discipline with little strain. Physics is the exception. It works where observation runs thinnest, at scientific observational boundaries (SOBs), the places where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond, and so its empty spaces are the largest in science. There, placeholders arrive prematurely, before observation has done its work, and they are named as though they were features of nature rather than open gaps (“dark matter” where astronomers once spoke of the “missing mass”). We offer four marks by which such placeholders can be recognized, the decisive one being that removing the placeholder would change no observation, and apply them to five cases: the singularity, superposition, dark matter and dark energy, the multiverse, and holography.

Newton faced an empty space at the center of his own theory and declined to fill it. In the twentieth century physics married the mass media. The media began as an accelerant of the reflex, filling empty spaces faster than they can be felt. To physics, which had both the room (the largest empty spaces in science) and the reward (a courtship by the press that no other science received, from Einstein’s fame in 1919 through the bomb, Sputnik and the popular physics book), it was also a new temptation. As we read it, the field’s acceptance made the media a corrupter of its standards, not through corrupt people but through what it rewards, names and teaches as known. We close with a parable of three figures offered the same temptation: Adam, who took the fruit; Isaac Newton, who refused it; and Richard Feynman, who took the stage but kept the humility. And we close with a better question: whether physics can learn to leave an empty space empty.

## 1. The Empty Room

This chapter states the claim of the paper, defines the terms it will use, and sets out the plan.

### 1.1 The claim

Human beings are compelled to explain what they observe. The compulsion is biological. It was built by a long history in which an unexplained rustle could be a predator, and it does not wait to learn whether the thing in front of it is safe. It explains before it knows.

Where an explanation is available, the reflex takes it. Where none is available, the reflex supplies one. We call the supplied explanation a placeholder. Myth was the reflex’s first organized answer. Science is its disciplined answer. Discipline narrows what the reflex will accept, but it does not switch the reflex off. In most sciences the discipline holds. The reflex is the same in a chemist as in a physicist, and chemistry, geology and medicine keep their standards with little strain.

Physics is the exception, and it is the subject of this paper. Two things set it apart. It works where observation runs thinnest, at the very small, the very large and the very early, so its empty spaces are the largest in science. And in the twentieth century it married the mass media. The media offered what it offers everyone, attention, funding and the standing of those who know, and physics accepted. At its edges, placeholders now arrive prematurely, before observation has done its work, and they are named as though they were features of nature rather than open gaps.

The media began as an accelerant of the reflex. For most of history the reflex had periods of rest: night, distance, silence, the gap between one piece of news and the next. The media removed most of them. In physics it did more. It became a new temptation, and through the field’s acceptance of it, a corrupter: not of people, but of the standards by which the field judges what it knows. That last step is our reading, and we mark it as such.

That is the whole claim. The chapters that follow lay it out one step at a time.

### 1.2 Terms

**The reflex.** The automatic drive to explain what is observed, whether or not the thing observed is a threat, and whether or not an explanation is available.

**Empty space.** Any gap in what a creature knows about where it is and what might happen next. A dark room is an empty space. So is a blank edge on a map, a sound with no source, and a question with no answer.

**Placeholder.** A name or explanation put into an empty space because the space must be filled, before observation has filled it.

**SOB.** A scientific observational boundary: the place where our ability to look runs out, though something surely lies beyond. Every science has them. They are where empty spaces are largest and where placeholders gather.

**Life ring and compass.** A life ring keeps a swimmer afloat. It does not say where land is. A compass gives direction, and it says nothing about how much water is left to cross. In this paper a life ring is a placeholder that points at nothing that could be looked at: it keeps an account afloat. A compass is an observation, or a placeholder that points at something that could be looked at: it gives direction. Both are useful. They are not the same instrument.

**Accelerant.** Anything that speeds the reflex up, and in particular anything that fills empty spaces faster than they can be felt.

**Corrupter.** Anything that changes the standard by which a field judges what it knows, whether or not anyone intends it.

### 1.3 Where this paper stands

This is an argument from the record. It draws on established findings in psychology and neuroscience, on the history of science, and on the history of the media. It offers no new experiment. Where the findings are solid, we say so. Where we extend them, we say that too.

It is a companion to _The Candle and the Bonfire_ and _The Density Dial_.

### 1.4 Plan

Chapter 2 reads the oldest story in the West about leaving home as a description of where the reflex begins. Chapter 3 sets out the biology of the reflex. Chapter 4 follows the reflex to the edges of physics, where its empty spaces are largest and its placeholders gather. Chapter 5 examines the case of the physicist who refused to supply one. Chapter 6 describes the media as the first great accelerant and shows how, in physics, it became a corrupter. Chapter 7 takes up objections. Chapter 8 returns to the garden, and closes with what is clearly not right, and the better question. A short coda looks ahead to a second accelerant.

The title of this chapter names where the reflex is first met in each life: the empty room.

## 2. Eden: The Knowledge of Exposure

This chapter reads the story of the garden in Genesis as an observation about the human condition. It shows that the story records the knowledge of exposure, the responses to it, and then the reflex itself: the first words spoken after the fall are an explanation.

### 2.1 What the tree taught

The man and the woman eat from the tree of knowledge, and the text reports the first thing they learn: “the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (Genesis 3:7).

The knowledge the tree gives is not knowledge of the world. It is knowledge of their own exposure. Before the tree, nothing in the garden needed explaining, because nothing in the garden threatened. After it, they know they can be seen, and what can be seen can be harmed.

### 2.2 What they did next

The story then records four responses, in order.

They make something. “They sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons” (3:7). The first human-made object in the Bible is a covering against exposure.

They are afraid. Asked where he is, the man answers, “I was afraid, because I was naked” (3:10).

They hide. The same verse ends, “and I hid myself.”

They explain. Asked what he has done, the man does not describe the act. He supplies an account of it: “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree” (3:12). The woman does the same: “The serpent beguiled me” (3:13). The first speech after the fall is an explanation, produced at once, and it puts the cause somewhere else.

Making, fearing and hiding are responses to exposure. Explaining is the reflex itself. It comes as the first words spoken after the fall, produced at once in answer to a question no one in the garden had needed to ask before. It is not an account of what was observed. It fills the gap where the truth would go, and it puts the cause somewhere else. The whole sequence takes a few verses.

### 2.3 The gate

The story ends with the way back closed: cherubim and “a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” (3:24). There is no returning to a place where nothing needs explaining. Exposure, once known, cannot be unknown.

### 2.4 The reading

We read the story as an observation, not as an event. Read that way, its claim is precise. The knowing creature knows it is exposed, and a creature that knows it is exposed lives outside the garden for good. Outside the garden, nothing is guaranteed safe, and so everything must be accounted for.

Other peoples have told the same story in other dress: a lost home, a closed road, a half that wanders looking for its other half. Our essay _We Don’t Really Belong Here_ gathers several of them. This paper needs only the one, because Genesis records the sequence most completely.

The story also has a second half, about how the man and the woman came to their knowledge in the first place. This paper returns to it at the close.

This chapter has shown that the oldest Western account of leaving home places the reflex at the start of the human story, and in the right order. The next chapter asks what biology says about the same sequence.

## 3. The Biology of the Reflex

This chapter sets out findings from psychology and neuroscience that describe the reflex. It shows three things: that the reflex is built to over-interpret, that it supplies explanations whether or not it has information, and that it appears early in life. It then draws the paper’s central inference: biology forces us to invent placeholders.

### 3.1 The cost of a miss

A creature that must decide whether a sound is a threat can make two kinds of error. It can take a harmless rustle for a predator, or a predator for a harmless rustle. The first error costs a moment and some energy. The second can cost a life.

When the costs of two errors are this unequal, selection does not favor accuracy. It favors the cheaper error. The physician Randolph Nesse named this the smoke detector principle: a smoke detector is set to go off for burnt toast because a detector set to wait for certainty would sometimes wait through a fire. The psychologists Martie Haselton and David Buss developed the same idea as error management theory in 2000. A mind shaped by unequal costs will lean, systematically and by design, toward seeing threats that are not there.

The bias is not a malfunction. It is what the system is for.

### 3.2 Agents behind noises

A related bias concerns agents. The psychologist Justin Barrett proposed in 2000 that human beings carry a hyperactive tendency to detect agents, someone or something acting with intent, behind ambiguous events. A branch snaps, and the mind’s first guess is that something snapped it. The same tendency shows up as pareidolia: faces in clouds, in wood grain, in the front of a car.

These biases share a feature. They do not wait for evidence. They fill an ambiguous scene with something, usually an agent and often a dangerous one, and they do it before deliberate thought begins.

### 3.3 The interpreter

The neuroscientist Michael Gazzaniga studied patients whose brain hemispheres had been surgically separated to treat epilepsy. Because each hemisphere could be shown a different image, the experimenters could give one side of the brain information the other side lacked.

In one well-known case, the left hemisphere was shown a chicken claw and the right a snow scene. Asked to pick related pictures, the patient’s right hand, controlled by the left hemisphere, chose a chicken, and his left hand, controlled by the right hemisphere, chose a shovel. Asked to explain, the speaking left hemisphere had no access to the snow scene. It did not say it did not know. It said at once that the shovel was for cleaning out the chicken shed.

Gazzaniga called the system responsible the interpreter. It produces explanations for what the body does and what the senses report, and it produces them whether or not it has the information needed. The explanations arrive quickly, confidently, and sometimes wrongly. The interpreter does not appear to have a setting for “no explanation.”

### 3.4 The nursery

The reflex appears early. Fears of the dark are common in young children. They tend to appear in the preschool years, as a child becomes able to imagine what cannot be seen. The dark room is the first empty space most people remember.

The adult response is familiar. A light is left on. A story is read. And the child is given an argument: there is no monster, because monsters are not real. Soon after comes the period in which every answer is met with another “why.” The child is filling gaps as fast as they open.

What the nursery shows is the order in which logic arrives. A child meets reasoning first as comfort, a way of making the empty room safe, and only later as a tool for finding things out. The two uses never fully separate.

### 3.5 What follows

Taken together, these findings describe a reflex with three properties.

It is automatic. It runs before deliberate thought and cannot be switched off, only overridden.

It is indiscriminate. It treats a safe gap and a dangerous one the same way, because at the moment of encounter it cannot tell them apart.

It prefers any explanation to none. The interpreter supplies one whether or not it has information, and where threat is concerned, the unequal costs mean a wrong guess has usually been cheaper than no guess.

From here the paper takes one step beyond the findings, and we mark it as ours. The research cited above concerns threat, agency and the explanation of one’s own actions. We extend it to explanation in general. For a creature shaped this way, an unexplained gap of any kind registers, at some level, as a risk. Danger lurks in empty spaces. And so biology forces us to invent placeholders.

There is an old tag that nature abhors a vacuum, a medieval summary of Aristotle’s argument that empty space cannot exist. Whatever the tag says about nature, it describes us exactly.

This chapter has shown that the reflex is built to over-interpret, that it explains without information, and that it is present from the nursery on. Science, which began as one more answer to the empty room, is the disciplined form of that reflex, and the reflex is the same in every scientist. The next chapter follows it to the edges of physics, where the empty spaces are largest.

## 4. Life Rings

This chapter follows the reflex to the edges of physics. It shows why physics has the largest empty spaces in science, that at a scientific observational boundary the discipline stops working while the reflex does not, and that what fills the gap is a placeholder dressed in the discipline’s clothing. It offers four marks by which such a placeholder can be recognized, applies them to five cases, and describes what the cases share.

### 4.1 Where the discipline stops

The discipline of science is a rule about what may fill an empty space: only what has been observed, or what can be checked against observation. Inside observable territory the rule works. A claim that disagrees with what is seen is revised or dropped.

At an SOB, the place where our ability to look runs out though something surely lies beyond, the rule has nothing to work with. There is nothing to check a claim against. The reflex, however, does not stop at the boundary. Chapter 3 showed that it runs before deliberate thought and supplies an explanation whether or not it has information. So the boundary is where the reflex is fully active and the discipline is idle.

Every science has SOBs, but they are not the same size. A geologist’s boundary is the rock not yet drilled. A physician’s is the patient not yet examined. Both can be reached in time, and what lies beyond them answers back. Physics works at boundaries no instrument can cross: the very small, the very large, the very early, the inside of a collapsed star. Its empty spaces are the largest in science, and that is the room in which its placeholders gather.

What arrives there is a placeholder. It does not arrive as a god or a monster. It arrives in mathematics, the language the discipline uses for its results, and so it looks like a result. It also arrives early. The reflex does not wait for observation to reach the boundary. The gap is filled first, and the placeholder is in place before anyone has finished looking.

### 4.2 Four marks

A placeholder in science can be recognized by four marks. None of them requires showing that the placeholder is false. Not every placeholder shows all four, but the fourth is decisive.

1. **It sits at an SOB.** What it names lies where observation cannot reach.
2. **It is named as a feature, not a gap.** Its name describes the work it does in the account, and presents that work as a thing in nature rather than as a question left open.
3. **It is kept by adjustment.** When observations change, the placeholder is reshaped to fit them, rather than the observations testing it.
4. **Removing it changes no observation.** Take it out and every measurement stays the same. Only the account changes: a gap opens where the placeholder was.

The fourth mark is the plainest test of whether something is a life ring or a compass. A compass points at something that could be looked at. A life ring points at nothing. It only keeps the account afloat.

### 4.3 Five cases

**The singularity.** General relativity predicts that at the center of a collapsed star, density becomes infinite. Roger Penrose and Stephen Hawking showed in the late 1960s that under broad conditions the theory cannot avoid this. The center lies behind an event horizon, beyond any possible observation. Physicists widely read the singularity as the point where the theory breaks down, which is to say it is a name for where the mathematics stops. In _The Density Dial_ we argued that infinite density is a limit, not a state that anything can occupy. Here the point is narrower: the singularity sits at an SOB, is named for what the equations do there, and could be removed without changing any observation.

**Superposition.** In quantum theory a particle’s state between preparation and detection is described as a combination of every outcome the detector might record. That interval cannot be observed. Observing it is a detection, and a detection ends it. The equations are not in question here. They predict what detectors record. What is in question is the word for the unobserved interval, and the claim that the particle “is” in several states during it. Remove the word and every measurement stays the same. Our essay _The Cat Was Always Just a Cat_ offers a different reading of that interval.

**Dark matter and dark energy.** Galaxies rotate at their edges faster than their visible matter can account for. Fritz Zwicky found the same kind of discrepancy in a cluster of galaxies in 1933 and named what was missing “dark matter.” Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured it in the rotation of individual galaxies in the 1970s. The discrepancy is observed. The substance is not. Decades of underground detectors built to catch it have recorded nothing. In 1998 two teams found that the expansion of the universe is speeding up, and the cause was named “dark energy.” Together the two now make up about 95 percent of the universe’s contents in the standard account. Both are named for the work they do, both have been reshaped as observations came in, and both sit past an SOB.

**The multiverse.** The constants of nature appear finely set: change some of them slightly and no stars, chemistry or life would form. One answer is that ours is one universe among a vast number, each with different constants, and we find ourselves in one that permits us. Versions of the idea come from cosmic inflation and from the many possible solutions of string theory. In most versions the other universes lie beyond any possible observation. The multiverse fills the gap left by the question of why the constants are what they are.

**Holography.** In the 1970s Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking found that a black hole’s entropy grows with the area of its surface rather than its volume. In 1997 Juan Maldacena proposed an exact correspondence between a universe with gravity and a theory without gravity on its boundary. The correspondence has been supported by many calculations, and it has served as a calculating tool. It was developed for a universe shaped differently from ours, and it remains a conjecture. Applied to our universe, it fills the gap where a theory joining gravity and quantum mechanics would go. Our essay _The Turkey of All Turkeys_ treats it at length.

### 4.4 What the cases share

The five cases differ in subject and in age. They have several things in common.

Each sits at an SOB: the center of a collapsed star, the interval before detection, the substance behind a measured discrepancy, the universes beyond ours, the boundary of a universe shaped unlike ours.

Each is named as a feature rather than a gap. For years astronomers also spoke of the “missing mass problem,” a name that admits a gap. The name that prevailed, “dark matter,” names a substance. “Singularity” names the place where the equations fail as though it were an object. “Superposition” names a step in the calculation as though it were a state. “Multiverse” and “hologram” name what the account requires as though they were features of the world.

Each carries real value in the work. Credit where it is due: these placeholders organize calculations, hold large bodies of data together, and let research continue across a gap that would otherwise stop it. A wrong idea can carry great value, and a placeholder can too.

By the fourth mark they differ. The singularity, superposition, the multiverse, and holography as applied to our universe point at nothing that can be looked at: remove them and every measurement stays the same. Dark matter is the hardest case. Detectors have been built to catch it, so in principle it points at something that could be found. Decades of searching have found nothing, and meanwhile the name is taught as a substance. It is spoken of as a compass while it behaves as a life ring. Taken together, the five keep their parts of physics afloat, and most of them cannot say where land is.

### 4.5 The cost of a life ring

A life ring does one more thing, and it is the thing that matters most here. It removes the urgency.

A swimmer without one feels the water and keeps looking for shore. A swimmer holding one can float for a long time. The danger has not passed, but it is no longer felt. In the same way, a placeholder written in mathematics satisfies the reflex. The empty space is filled, the equations close, and the gap stops registering as a gap.

That is how the reflex survives inside a discipline built to restrain it. The discipline checks claims against observation. It has no rule for a claim that cannot be checked and makes the equations work. The reflex supplies such claims, the equations accept them, and the felt pressure to keep looking eases. Over time, a life ring held long enough comes to be spoken of as a compass.

This chapter has shown that science’s placeholders gather at its observational boundaries, that they can be recognized by four marks without being proved false, and that their chief cost is that they make an empty space stop feeling empty. The next chapter turns to the rare case of a scientist who looked at an empty space and declined to fill it.

## 5. The Exception

This chapter examines one case in which a scientist faced an empty space at the center of his own theory and declined to fill it. It shows that Isaac Newton overrode the reflex deliberately and said so in print, that the science which followed kept his equations and set his refusal aside, and that the refusal points to a distinction this paper relies on: the behavior is observed, the law is decided.

### 5.1 The empty space

Newton’s law of gravitation describes how bodies move toward one another: in proportion to their masses, and inversely as the square of the distance between them. It accounted for the orbits of the planets, the paths of comets, the fall of objects on Earth and the tides. It said nothing about how one body could act on another across empty space with nothing between them.

Newton saw the gap clearly. In a letter to the scholar Richard Bentley in 1693 he wrote that the idea of one body acting on another at a distance through a vacuum, without anything to carry the action, was to him “so great an absurdity” that no one competent in philosophical matters could fall into it.

So the author of the law held that the law, taken as an explanation, would be absurd. At the center of the most successful theory of its age there was an empty space, and its author knew it.

### 5.2 The placeholder on offer

A placeholder was available. René Descartes had filled the heavens with matter swirling in great vortices that carried the planets around the sun. It was a mechanism anyone could picture, and it left no empty space anywhere.

Newton examined the vortices in the second book of the _Principia_ and showed that they could not reproduce the observed motions of the planets. He set them aside. He did not put anything in their place.

His critics noticed. Christiaan Huygens found the idea of attraction absurd. Gottfried Leibniz called it an occult quality, and later argued that attraction across empty space would require a perpetual miracle. The objection in each case was the same: Newton had left a gap where an explanation belonged.

### 5.3 The confession

Newton answered in the General Scholium, the essay he added to the second edition of the _Principia_ in 1713:

> I have not as yet been able to deduce from phenomena the reason for these properties of gravity, and I do not feign hypotheses. For whatever is not deduced from the phenomena must be called a hypothesis; and hypotheses, whether metaphysical or physical, or based on occult qualities, or mechanical, have no place in experimental philosophy.

And then:

> And it is enough that gravity really exists and acts according to the laws that we have set forth and is sufficient to explain all the motions of the heavenly bodies and of our sea.

Three words of it became famous: _hypotheses non fingo_. They are usually quoted as a statement of method. Read beside the letter to Bentley, they are also a confession. Newton is saying that he knows how gravity behaves, that he does not know what it is, and that he will not pretend to.

### 5.4 The override

Chapter 3 described the reflex as automatic, indiscriminate, and inclined to prefer any explanation to none. It cannot be switched off. It can only be overridden.

The General Scholium is an override, made in public, under criticism, by the person with the most to gain from filling the gap. A mechanism would have quieted his critics. Newton chose to leave the space empty and to name it as empty.

The humility here belongs to the method, not to the man. Newton was not a modest person. He fought bitterly with Robert Hooke and with Leibniz, and he guarded his priority fiercely. That makes the override more notable, not less. It did not come from a mild temperament. It came from a decision about what may and may not be put into an empty space.

### 5.5 What was kept

The science that followed kept Newton’s equations and built on them for two centuries. It did not keep the confession. The reflex wore the refusal down even in a quieter age, with no media to hurry it. What came later did not begin the erosion. It accelerated it, and then rewarded it.

Over time, “the force of gravity” came to be spoken of as the answer to the question Newton had left open. A body falls because gravity pulls it. The sentence sounds like an explanation. It is the name of the behavior, placed where the explanation would go. By the marks of Chapter 4, it is a placeholder: named for what it does, and removable without changing any observation.

In 1915 Albert Einstein replaced the force with the geometry of spacetime, an account that predicts more than Newton’s and has passed the tests put to it. Whether that account says what gravity is, or describes how it behaves in finer detail, is the question Newton asked. It is still asked.

### 5.6 Observation, not definition

Newton’s confession rests on a distinction that this paper uses from here on.

The behavior is observed. Bodies move toward one another, planets trace their orbits, the tides rise and fall. These are seen and measured.

The law is decided. Newton chose to write the behavior as a single relationship between mass and distance, in a particular mathematical form, with a constant whose value would be measured later. The form is a decision about how to write what is seen. It is an excellent decision. Another form could describe the same observations, and in time one did.

A science built on this distinction treats its laws as the best present writing of observed behavior. A science that loses the distinction treats its laws as discoveries of what nature is, and the names in them as things. That is the placeholder’s move, made on the largest scale: the record of a decision comes to be held as a fact about the world.

Put plainly, science is an evolving template on the surface of Reality. The template is drawn over what can be seen, and redrawn as more is seen. It is not the surface, and it says nothing about what lies beneath.

Newton kept the distinction. He knew which part he had observed and which part he had written, and he marked the place where his knowledge stopped.

This chapter has shown that Newton faced an empty space at the center of his theory, refused the placeholder available to him, and said so plainly, and that the science which followed kept his law and set aside his refusal. The next chapter turns to the force that made such refusals far harder to sustain: the media, the first great accelerant of the reflex.

## 6. From Accelerant to Corrupter

This chapter describes the media as the first great accelerant of the reflex, and shows how, in physics, it became a corrupter. It shows that the media has two faces, that it fills empty spaces faster than they can be felt, that physics alone among the sciences was courted by it, that it removed the nightly pause in the cycle of news, that it carries placeholders farther than confessions, that it sells what it carries and so rewards distortion, and that it rewards a kind of person different from the one physics requires. It closes with a figure who stood at the turning point.

### 6.1 Two faces

The media has two faces, and they are of different kinds.

The first is the medium itself: the means of propagation. The telegraph in the 1840s, radio in the 1920s, television after the Second World War, and the networks of today all carry signals at or near the speed of light. This face is fundamental. It is physics put to work, and it does not change from one day to the next.

The second is the content: everything the medium carries. It is unfiltered and without end, and most of it is gone within a day. This face is ephemeral.

The two faces arrive together. A fundamental medium carries an ephemeral flood, and the speed of the first is lent to the second. This chapter is about what that combination does to the reflex.

### 6.2 What changed

For most of history, empty spaces in what people knew were local, few, and slow to fill. News of a battle or a harvest traveled at the speed of a horse or a ship. A question could sit unanswered for weeks or months, and the people asking it lived with the gap while they waited. The reflex worked as it always had, but it worked on a short supply of material, and the gaps it faced lasted long enough to be felt.

The media changed the supply. Once a medium could carry content at the speed of light, the gaps began to fill almost as soon as they opened. The reflex no longer had to wait, and it no longer had to supply its own placeholders. They arrived from outside, already made.

An accelerant does not start a fire. It makes a fire burn faster than anything can contain it. The reflex was present long before the telegraph. What the media did was feed it, without pause and without limit, and in doing so it changed the conditions under which the reflex works. That is why this paper calls the media the first great accelerant, rather than one influence among many.

### 6.3 The courtship

No other science was courted by the media as physics was.

In November 1919 a British eclipse expedition reported that starlight bent around the sun as Einstein’s theory predicted, and the newspapers made him a public celebrity on a scale no scientist had known before. Quantum mechanics was formulated in the years from 1925 to 1927, as radio broadcasting spread through Europe and America, and its strangeness made ideal copy.

In 1945 the atomic bomb made physicists public figures and put national budgets behind their work. After the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, physics became a matter of national prestige, and the large machines of what came to be called Big Science needed public enthusiasm to pay for them. In the decades that followed, the popular physics book became a genre of its own.

Einstein’s place in this is not simple. He was the first scientist the mass press made famous, and he was also among the sharpest critics of the quantum account, which he never accepted as complete. The courtship began with a man who, on the question that mattered most to him, declined to fill the gap.

Chemistry, geology and medicine lived in the same media climate. None was courted on these terms, and each works closer to what can be checked: a reaction, a rock, a patient. Physics had both the room described in Chapter 4 and the reward described here.

### 6.4 The lost night

The media works in a daily cycle. Each day it shapes the world into an edition or a broadcast, and each day that shape is replaced. Yesterday’s front page is of no use by morning.

Under print, the cycle had a night. There was a deadline, a finished edition, and a gap before the next one. Nothing new could arrive until the presses ran again. Whatever its intent, the arrangement built a pause into the rhythm of public life, and the pause was a kind of silence.

In June 1980 a cable channel began broadcasting news twenty-four hours a day. Others followed, and the networks that came after have no edition at all. The cycle no longer closes. It runs continuously, and the pause that print built into each day is gone.

The pause mattered for more than the news. Silence, taken broadly, is a stretch of time in which nothing new arrives to be explained. In silence the reflex has nothing to work on, and the pressure to fill an empty space eases. It is the condition under which a gap can be left open long enough to be examined.

Silence is also where humility is kept. Humility is what remains when no one is watching. It needs no audience. Self-promotion needs to be seen, and in silence it has nothing to work on. Newton announced his refusal in public, under criticism, but he formed it and held to it in a world of nights, of letters that took weeks to arrive, of long gaps between one exchange and the next. A field that has lost its silences has lost the conditions in which a refusal like his can be sustained.

### 6.5 What the accelerant carries

The media does not carry all content equally. It carries what travels well, and in science what travels well is the placeholder.

“We do not know” is not news. Newton’s confession, set in a newspaper, would have made a short paragraph. A particle that is in two places at once, a cat both alive and dead, a universe that is a hologram, an infinite number of other worlds: these are stories. They are vivid, they are confident, and they fill an empty space the reader may not have known was there.

The pattern began with the courtship. From the start, the parts of the new physics that traveled farthest tended to be its strangest images, and its strangest images were, by the marks of Chapter 4, its placeholders.

The result is that the media carries placeholders farther than findings, and findings farther than confessions. What reaches the public as science is weighted, by the selection of the medium, toward the content of Chapter 4.

### 6.6 What the accelerant sells

The media does more than speed content along. It sells it. Newspapers, broadcasters and networks are businesses paid largely for attention, and attention is captured most easily by what is vivid, certain and alarming. Commerce does not merely carry distortion. It rewards it.

Science is not outside this market. Universities and journals issue press releases. In 2014 a team led by Petroc Sumner compared several hundred university press releases about health research with the papers behind them and the news stories that followed. When a press release exaggerated a finding, the news stories were far more likely to exaggerate it too. When the press release was measured, the news usually was.

Names are part of the trade. In 1993 the physicist Leon Lederman published a book about the search for the Higgs boson and called it _The God Particle_. The title sold the book, and the name outlived it. A name that implies a feature sells better than a name that admits a gap, and the market selects accordingly.

### 6.7 Who rises

Science and the media select for different people.

The method of science is built to humble. Every claim is provisional and open to attack by anyone in the field. Most of the work is slow, much of it is solitary, and most of it is never seen outside the field. The best a scientist can hope for is to be shown less wrong than the one before.

The method of the media is built to amplify. It rewards certainty over doubt, the sentence that fits a headline over the page of qualifications, and the face over the finding. Self-promotion needs an audience. Humility needs a quiet room. When the audience is everywhere, the first is fed and the second is crowded out.

Why this is happening can be suggested, not settled. Grants, citations, book contracts and public stages all reward visibility, and over decades that changes who reaches the top of a field. The public meets science mainly through those who perform it, so performers come to stand for the whole. And a humble answer does not travel, while a confident one does, wrong or not.

None of this requires bad intent from anyone. It is selection, and it works on scientists the way it works on everyone else.

### 6.8 The hinge

The turn can be seen in one figure. Richard Feynman shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1965 for work on the interaction of light and matter. The year before, the BBC had filmed his lectures at Cornell University, _The Character of Physical Law_, and broadcast them. In 1981 the BBC interviewed him again, in a film called _The Pleasure of Finding Things Out_.

In that interview Feynman said: “I can live with doubt and uncertainty and not knowing. I think it’s much more interesting to live not knowing than to have answers which might be wrong.” That is Newton’s override, in plain speech, from a working physicist.

Feynman was also a gifted performer. His stories, his drumming, his talk of safecracking and practical jokes made him a figure the camera loved, and in time the figure became as well known as the physics. He made performing the equal of producing. In him the two still came together: the performer carried the humility of the worker.

What the medium learned from figures like him was that the public would reward the performance on its own. Feynman’s stage was earned by his work, but the stage itself never asked to see the work. After the hinge, the stage could be held by those who performed science without doing it, and the humility that had come attached to the work did not have to come along.

### 6.9 From accelerant to corrupter

Taken together, the media did five things to the reflex. It supplied filler faster than empty spaces could be felt. It removed the nightly pause that print had built into public life. It carried placeholders farther than findings and confessions. It sold what it carried, and in doing so rewarded distortion. And it rewarded visibility over humility, changing who rises in science as in everything else.

Chapter 1 claimed that in physics the media went from accelerant to corrupter. This chapter has shown how the pressure works. The accelerant selects for placeholders in what is carried and for performers in who is seen, and it takes away the silence in which humility is kept. In the other sciences that selection meets a check: the reaction, the rock, the patient. In physics, at its widest boundaries, it meets none.

What this chapter cannot show by measurement is the last step: that the field’s own standard changed under the pressure. We read it so, and we read it as the oldest story there is. The media is a new temptation. It offers attention, funding and the standing of those who know, and it asks only that a gap be named as a thing. A field that accepts that offer again and again, over decades, has changed its standard without anyone deciding to. That is what we mean by corruption, and it requires no corrupt person. The next chapter takes up objections to the paper as a whole.

## 7. Objections

This chapter sets out the objections a careful reader is most likely to raise, and answers each as plainly as we can. Where an objection lands, we say so.

### 7.1 The step from threat to explanation is not supported

_The research in Chapter 3 concerns threat, agency, and the explanation of one’s own actions. The paper extends it to explanation in general without showing that the extension holds._

This is fair, and Chapter 3 marks the extension as ours. Two things make it less of a leap than it may appear. Gazzaniga’s interpreter is not limited to threat: it explains ordinary actions, such as choosing a shovel, with the same speed and confidence. And the questioning of young children ranges over everything, not only over what is dangerous. Still, the extension is an inference from the findings, not a finding. The paper rests on it, and a reader who rejects it will reject much of what follows.

### 7.2 Placeholders are how science advances

_Science has often named something before it was seen. Wolfgang Pauli proposed the neutrino in 1930 to account for energy missing in radioactive decay, and it was detected in 1956. Neptune was predicted from the motion of Uranus and found in 1846. Calling such names life rings misreads how discovery works._

This is the strongest objection, and we grant its core. A placeholder can turn out to name something real. Chapter 4 said that its four marks do not show a placeholder to be false, and this is why.

The difference lies in what the placeholder points at. Neptune and the neutrino each pointed at something that could, in principle, be looked at with instruments that existed or could be built, and in time they were. The same nineteenth century also produced Vulcan, a planet proposed inside the orbit of Mercury to account for irregularities in its motion. Astronomers searched for it for decades. It was never found, and in 1915 general relativity accounted for Mercury’s motion without it. Vulcan was a life ring. Neptune turned out to be a compass.

What cannot be known when a name is proposed is whether the thing it points at will be found. Whether it points at something that could be looked at can be asked at once, and that is the fourth mark. A placeholder that points somewhere, honestly labeled as a gap and kept under watch, is a normal part of science. The concern of this paper is the placeholder named as a thing before it is found, and taught as found while the search goes on. Dark matter may yet be found, as the neutrino was, which is why Chapter 4 calls it the hardest case. The other four lie past boundaries no instrument can cross, and for those the question cannot be settled by looking.

### 7.3 The media also spreads real knowledge

_The same media that carries placeholders also carries findings, education and correction to more people than any earlier age could reach._

Granted. The claim of Chapter 6 concerns weighting, not exclusion: of all that the media carries, the placeholder travels farther than the finding, and the finding farther than the confession. A medium can do great good and still select in that order.

### 7.4 Newton is a selective witness

_Newton was an alchemist and a theologian who speculated freely. In the Queries at the end of his_ Opticks _he proposed an invisible medium filling space. One sentence from the_ Principia _is being made to carry more than it can._

Newton did speculate, and freely. But he set his speculations apart. The ones in the _Opticks_ are written as questions, and they are labeled Queries. That is the same discipline seen from another side: he marked which parts he had observed and which he was asking about. Chapter 5 does not rest the override on Newton’s temperament. It locates the humility in his method, and the Queries support that reading rather than undercut it.

### 7.5 The past was not wiser

_Earlier ages were full of superstition, myth and unfounded explanation. The paper romanticizes a time before the media._

The paper does not claim the past was wiser. Chapter 1 names myth as the reflex’s first answer, and myth filled every empty space it found. The claim is narrower: the reflex was the same, but its supply was smaller and slower, and its pauses were longer. What changed with the media is not the quality of human judgment. It is the speed at which empty spaces are filled.

### 7.6 Other sciences face the same pressures

_Every science competes for funding and attention, and biologists and physicians appear in the media as often as physicists. Chapter 6 itself cites exaggeration in press releases about health research. If the media corrupts, it should corrupt them too._

Every science feels the pressure, and the press releases described in Chapter 6 show that medicine is not immune to exaggeration. The difference lies in what happens to a claim afterward. A claim about a drug meets patients. A claim about a fault line meets the next earthquake. Those boundaries can be crossed, and what lies beyond them answers back, so an exaggeration in medicine or geology is corrected by the world it describes. At its widest boundaries physics has no such check, and in the twentieth century it was courted as no other science was. This paper describes room and reward together. Where either is missing, distortion can occur, but it does not become the standard.

### 7.7 The paper is itself a placeholder

_By its own account, this paper fills an empty space, the question of why placeholders gather at the edges of physics, with an explanation that cannot be directly observed. It is subject to its own four marks._

It is. The reflex this paper describes is also the reflex that wrote it. Much of what it proposes lies at or beyond an SOB, and removing it would change no observation. We have tried to mark each step where we go past the findings, so that a reader can see which parts are compasses and which are life rings. That is all a paper of this kind can do.

It is also why the paper opens as it does. We are storytellers, not scientists. These are ideas, not facts. If they are facts, we cannot prove it.

This chapter has set out seven objections. Two of them, the step from threat to explanation and the case of placeholders that turn out to be real, go to the center of the paper, and we have granted their force. The next chapter returns to the garden, and closes with what is clearly not right, and the better question.

## 8. What Is Clearly Not Right, and the Better Question

This chapter gathers the argument, states what is clearly not right, suggests why it is happening, returns to the garden, and closes with the better question.

### 8.1 The argument

Human beings are compelled to explain what they observe. The compulsion is biological, built by a long history in which a missed threat cost more than a false alarm, and it fills empty spaces whether or not it has anything to fill them with. The story of Eden records it at the start of the human story: knowledge of exposure, then fear, then explanation.

Every science is the disciplined form of the reflex, and most hold their discipline with little strain. Physics is the exception. It works where observation runs thinnest, and at its boundaries, where there is nothing to check a claim against, the reflex returns early, before observation has done its work, and what it supplies arrives in mathematics, looking like a result. These placeholders carry real value in the work. They also remove the felt urgency of the empty space they fill.

Newton faced such a space at the center of his own theory and declined to fill it, and said so in print. The science that followed kept his equations and set his refusal aside.

Then physics married the media. The media fills empty spaces faster than they can be felt, removed the pause that print built into each day, carries placeholders farther than confessions, sells what it carries, and rewards those who are seen over those who work unseen. In the other sciences these pressures meet a check. In physics, at its widest boundaries, they met none. As we read it, the media became a temptation the field accepted, and so a corrupter of its standards. It also took away the silence in which a refusal like Newton’s could be made and kept.

### 8.2 What is clearly not right

It is not that we invent placeholders. Biology insists on them, and some of them turn out to name something real.

It is not that the media exists. It is a feature of the age, and features are described, not repaired.

What is clearly not right is how placeholders are named, and how early. They are given names that imply they are actual features of nature rather than open gaps, often before observation has had its chance. A placeholder named as a gap, such as the missing mass, keeps the question open. A placeholder named as a thing, such as dark matter, closes it, and the name is then taught as a description of nature. The same is true of a law that records a decision about how to write what is seen, taught as a discovery of what nature is.

What is clearly not right is a culture in which no empty space stays empty long enough to be felt, so that the difference between “we know” and “we have a word for it” can no longer be heard.

### 8.3 Why this is happening

The causes can be suggested, not settled.

The reflex is older than science. It cannot be switched off, only overridden, and the override has to be renewed by every generation.

A placeholder written in mathematics satisfies the reflex. Once the equations close, the gap stops feeling like a gap.

The accelerant supplies ready-made placeholders faster than any empty space can be felt, and it carries them farther than it carries the honest admission that something is not known.

The accelerant is also a market. What sells is vivid, certain and named as a thing, and commerce rewards the distortion.

And the people who rise, in science as elsewhere, are increasingly those the medium rewards: the confident, the visible, the quotable. Humility needs a quiet room, and the rooms are fewer.

None of this requires anyone to act in bad faith. It is the reflex, working as it was built to work, in conditions it was never built for.

### 8.4 Adam, Isaac and Richard

The story of Eden has two halves, and this paper began with only one. The first half is exposure, the knowledge that sets off the reflex. The second is how the man and the woman came to that knowledge. They were not forced. They were offered something. The serpent told them, “ye shall be as gods” (Genesis 3:5), and the woman saw that the tree was “to be desired to make one wise” (3:6). The offer was not wisdom. It was to be made wise: to have the standing of those who know.

Temptation does not coerce. That is why corruption by temptation requires no villain, only acceptance. The account of this paper can be told as a parable in three figures.

Adam was offered the fruit and took it. What he gained was the knowledge of his own exposure, and with it the reflex that has driven every explanation since.

Isaac Newton was offered a mechanism that would have quieted his critics and given his law the look of a complete explanation. He declined it, and said in print that he would not feign what he did not know. The field he founded began with a refusal.

Richard Feynman was offered the stage and took it, but he held the standing at arm’s length. On that stage he kept the humility of the worker: he could live, he said, with not knowing. He was the hinge. After him the stage could be taken without the humility, and the standing that Newton refused and Feynman kept at a distance was accepted by the field as a whole, along with the attention and the funding.

The parable does not judge any of the three. Each was offered what every person is offered in some form. It describes what each did with the offer, and what physics has done with it since.

### 8.5 The better question

The usual question at the edges of physics is what fills the empty spaces: what dark matter is made of, what happens inside a singularity, which interpretation of the quantum is the right one.

The better question is whether physics can learn to leave an empty space empty: whether it can mark an SOB plainly, name a gap as a gap, and live beside it, without reaching for a life ring and calling it a compass.

It has been done before, in print, at the center of the most successful theory of its age.

## Coda: The Second Edition

The media was the first great accelerant. A second is now forming. Machines that can answer any question at once, fluently and with confidence, reach an empty space the media left alone: the pause inside one’s own head, between a question and one’s own answer.

It is too early to say what this will become, and so, in keeping with the argument of this paper, we leave the space empty. We will watch what it does before we name what it is. That is a subject for the second edition.
